title: Financial inclusion, information and communication technology diffusion, and economic growth: a panel data analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (fixed/random effects and two-step system GMM) of mobile, internet, fixed-telephone and ICT-import diffusion on GDP per capita growth and on financial inclusion in 41 economies (developed and developing); meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies, developed/developing mix) and outcome (families 1 and 5) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (with financial inclusion interactions)
exposure_measure: Mobile subscriptions per 100 people, internet users per 100 people, fixed telephone lines per 100 people, ICT goods imports (% of total goods imports); interactions of mobile x internet, internet x education, internet x services share, and ICT x financial-inclusion indicators. Sources: ITU, WDI.

sample.economies_or_groups: 41 countries listed in Table A1, labelled 'Developed' or 'Developing' by the authors (e.g. Austria, Japan, Switzerland, India, Brazil, Burundi, Uganda); 'dominated by developing countries'
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (authors' developed/developing split only; World Bank income groups not used; includes low-income e.g. Burundi, Uganda, Rwanda, Mozambique)

design.estimator: Fixed effects and random effects (ICT as determinant of financial inclusion); two-step system GMM (Blundell-Bond) for growth equations with lagged dependent variable
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged growth, government consumption, secondary gross enrolment, trade openness, inflation (growth models); log GDP, industry share, education, financial-access indicators (FE/RE models). Country and time effects stated in the FE equation. ICT and FI variables treated as endogenous and instrumented by internal lags; trade and inflation treated as exogenous.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, mobile subscriptions (system GMM, Table 5A col 1)
results.estimate: Current-year mobile +0.209; one-year lag -0.247 (growth in percentage points per unit of subscriptions per 100 people); net of the two terms is slightly negative (-0.038, authors do not compute it)
results.evidence: Table 5A p.29: 'mobile 0.209*** (0.0359); L.mobile -0.247*** (0.0331)'. Text p.31: 'one year lag values of these variables are having negative but significant effect'.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, internet users (system GMM, Table 5A col 2)
results.estimate: Current +0.242; lag -0.334 (net -0.092, not computed by authors)

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, fixed telephone lines (Table 5A col 3)
results.estimate: -0.0211 current; +0.115 lag
results.evidence: Table 5A p.29; text p.31: 'fixed telephone and ICT import ... are not having any significant effect'.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, ICT goods imports (Table 5A col 4)
results.estimate: -0.0204 current; +0.0721 lag
results.evidence: Table 5A p.29.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, mobile x internet interaction (Table 5B col 1)
results.estimate: Mobile +0.116, L.mobile -0.163, mobile x internet +0.00180, lag -0.00176
results.evidence: Table 5B p.30; text p.31-32: 'mobile when powered by internet have a better role'. Lagged terms offset current-year terms.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, financial inclusion x mobile interactions (Table 6)
results.estimate: Accounts +0.00323, lag -0.00471; mobile x accounts +6.46e-05, lag -6.24e-05; mobile x branches +0.000811, lag -0.000951
results.evidence: Table 6 p.34: 'Mbacct 6.46e-05*** (1.00e-05); L.mbacct -6.24e-05*** (9.47e-06)'. Authors conclude FI is a channel for ICT.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth, financial inclusion indicators alone (Table 4)
results.estimate: Accounts +0.0103 (lag -0.0106); ATM +0.168 (lag -0.218); branches +0.236 (lag -0.266); private credit +0.175 (lag -0.190); outstanding deposits -0.0757 (lag +0.0734)
results.evidence: Table 4 p.27; text p.24: 'previous year's values of these indicators are having negative effect on current year's growth'.

results.indicator: Financial inclusion (deposit accounts per 1,000 adults) as outcome of ICT, fixed effects (Table 3a)
results.estimate: Internet users +6.705; current mobile -0.098 (ns); 2-year lagged mobile +4.058; mobile x internet +0.038; fixed telephone -5.992 (ns) (accounts per 1,000 adults per unit)
results.evidence: Table 3(a) p.21: 'internet 6.705** (3.296)'; 'L2.mobile 4.058** (1.753)'. Text p.20: 'an increase in the number of mobile phone users takes a period of around two years'.

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of internet with secondary enrolment is negative (-0.00761, p<0.1) with positive lag (+0.00790, p<0.05); authors read this as education conditioning internet use but do not compute marginal effects
Internet x services share negative (-0.0377) with positive lag (0.0356); authors say internet in services speeds growth if the marginal effect is positive but do not compute it
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5B p.30-31: 'Netservice -0.0377***; L.netservice 0.0356***'.

heterogeneity.finding: Mobile effect on financial inclusion is positive only when internet access is adequate (mobile x internet interaction positive, p<0.1)
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3(a) p.21 and text p.20: 'positive effect on the financial inclusion only if there is also adequate facility of internet'.

heterogeneity.finding: Financial inclusion modifies ICT effect: positive interaction of mobile with accounts and branches in current year, offset by negative lags
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 6 p.34.

income_group_results.high: not reported (no split by income group; pooled sample)

n_specifications_reported: about 26 (Table 3a 5, Table 3b 5, Table 4 6, Table 5A 4, Table 5B 3, Table 6 3)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with internal lags is the only strategy. Sargan p-values of 0.99-1.00 in every model and no report of instrument counts against 41 groups suggest instrument proliferation, so the identification is not credible. A 12-year panel with a lagged dependent variable and inflated lags is used to claim 'causal link'. The authors treat all ICT terms as endogenous without justifying the instrument set.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Tables 4, 5A, 5B, 6 (Sargan 0.99-1.00); p.17 notes Roodman (2009) on too many instruments but no instrument count is given.

exposure_measurement.why: Penetration rates (mobile subscriptions, internet users, fixed lines) are standard ITU measures but capture access not intensity or quality; mobile subscriptions per 100 exceed 100 (max 162). ICT imports as a share of imports is a weak ICT proxy. Interpolated values for ICT imports.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table A2 p.39; pp.11-12; footnote on interpolation p.13-14.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 41 countries were retained only because all Financial Access Survey indicators were available, out of 175; selection by data availability, short 2004-2015 window, unbalanced panel and economy classification inconsistencies (Moldova, Ukraine, Bulgaria labelled 'Developed').
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.12-13: 'data for all the selected indicators of financial inclusion is only available for a set of 41 countries'; Table A1 p.38.

outcome_measurement.why: Annual GDP per capita growth is volatile and noisy over 12 years; financial inclusion measured by supply-side bank indicators only (accounts, ATMs, branches, credit, deposits), not usage or mobile money. Authors acknowledge GDP measurement problems in low-income countries.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.13 on GDP measurement; Table 1 p.11.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many ad hoc specifications with different endogenous/exogenous classifications; every key regressor enters with current and lagged terms of opposite sign, and interpretations are post hoc; interactions are added one at a time. Unit root tests on a T=12 panel are used to justify omitting cointegration tests. Statement 'Since all the variables are not stationary at first difference' is unclear. Inflation sign described as counter-intuitive.

selective_reporting.why: Net effects (current plus lag) are not computed or tested; positive current-year coefficients are emphasised in the abstract ('improve current year's growth') while negative lags largely cancel them. Marginal effects for interactions are not shown.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p.iii: 'both FI and ICT ... can improve current year's growth'; Table 5A p.29.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: The text file is the Madras School of Economics Working Paper 165/2017 (July 2017), whereas the assignment lists year 2020 and a journal-style title; the 2020 version may be a published version of this paper. If both are in the corpus, the working paper is an earlier version (DUP); a human should check. Appears to be a reproduction of the Andrianaivo-Kpodar framework applied to a 41-country mixed sample. Sargan p-values of 0.99-1.00 throughout (suspicious, symptom of too many instruments). Lagged terms are systematically negative and nearly cancel the contemporaneous positive terms; the paper's own text interprets lags as skill gaps without testing it. Introduction says sample period '2004-1015' (typo). No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: The Internet of Things and economic growth in a panel of countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel regression of TFP growth on cellular IoT connections per inhabitant (an ICT/mobile-connectivity exposure) for 82 economies, 2010-2017, with an OECD vs non-OECD split; outcome is productivity (family 1). A second, simulation-based growth-accounting projection is an add-on and not the basis for inclusion.
technology: Internet of Things (licensed cellular IoT / M2M connections)
exposure_measure: Change in log of licensed cellular IoT connections per inhabitant (GSMA Wireless Intelligence), used as a proxy for the intensity of IoT investment; mobile broadband connections per inhabitant included as a control. No official IoT investment data exist.

sample.economies_or_groups: 36 OECD and 46 non-OECD countries (Table 2); 8 extreme-outlier countries dropped (Kuwait, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Syria, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela, Yemen, Zimbabwe)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (OECD high-income plus non-OECD countries ranging from low income such as Malawi, Uganda, Tanzania to high income such as Singapore, Qatar); no World Bank income-group split, only OECD vs non-OECD
sample.years: 2010-2017 (574 country-year observations in first differences; 410 in three-year differences)

design.estimator: OLS in first differences (and three-year differences) with year dummies and cluster-robust standard errors; robustness with Stata rreg robust regression and within-group fixed-effects levels regression
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Change in log capital services, change in log labour services (composition-adjusted), change in log mobile broadband per inhabitant, year dummies; first differencing removes country fixed effects

results.indicator: TFP growth (change in ln TFP), first differences, IoT only
results.estimate: 0.026 (coefficient on change in ln IoT connections per inhabitant)

results.indicator: TFP growth, first differences, with mobile broadband control (headline specification)
results.estimate: 0.023; a 10 percentage point rise in IoT-connection growth per inhabitant is associated with 0.23 percentage point higher TFP growth
results.evidence: Table 4 column 2 and Section 5.3, p.269: 'a 10 percentage points (pp) increase in the growth of IoT connections per inhabitant is associated with 0.23 pp growth in TFP'

results.indicator: TFP growth, three-year differences
results.estimate: 0.036 (without MBB) and 0.031 (with MBB)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.015 and 0.014, both significant at 5%; N=410

results.indicator: TFP growth, OECD subsample, first differences
results.estimate: 0.021 (no MBB) and 0.017 (with MBB)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.011 and 0.010, significant at 10% only; N=252

results.indicator: TFP growth, non-OECD subsample, first differences
results.estimate: 0.023 (both specifications)

results.indicator: TFP growth, full sample when extreme-outlier countries are retained
results.estimate: not reported
results.uncertainty: stated only as 'insignificant'; coefficients not shown
results.evidence: Footnote 15, p.276: 'If these extreme outliers are not excluded, the IoT per inhabitant variable is insigniﬁcant in our regressions'

results.indicator: TFP growth, robust regression (rreg) retaining outliers with down-weighting
results.estimate: 0.03 (IoT only) and 0.02 (with MBB), first differences; 0.04 and 0.03 in three-year differences; N=630 and 450

results.indicator: Projected IoT contribution to growth (growth accounting simulation, 2018-2030, EU-13)
results.estimate: 0.99% pa including spillovers (0.19% pa direct capital contribution); range 0.013% to 1.74% pa across assumptions
results.uncertainty: not reported (scenario analysis, no sampling uncertainty)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.273: 'IDC estimate... 0.19% (0.99%)'; Section 6.4. This is a calibration/simulation using assumed parameters, not an estimate

heterogeneity.finding: OECD and non-OECD IoT coefficients are similar in size (0.017-0.021 vs 0.023) and both significant only at 10%; no formal test of difference reported. Authors attribute lower significance to smaller samples.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 and text p.269: 'The IoT coeﬃcient is similar and is signiﬁcant at the 10 percent level for both'

heterogeneity.finding: Longer (three-year) differences give larger coefficients (0.031-0.036 vs 0.023-0.026); equality with the one-year coefficients rejected at 1% in a sureg test. Authors suggest lagged effects or reduced measurement error.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 5.3, p.269 and footnote 17: 'positive and signiﬁcant at the 5 percent level, but with larger coeﬃcients'

income_group_results.high: OECD group (mostly high-income): 0.021* (no MBB), 0.017* (with MBB), N=252; significant at 10% only. No World Bank income-group split.
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (included in non-OECD group)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (included in non-OECD group)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (included in non-OECD group)

n_specifications_reported: about 20 coefficient sets across main tables (Tables 4, 5), appendix tables (A1-A4) and an unreported fixed-effects levels regression (results 'available upon request')

confounding_reverse_causation.why: OLS in first differences with no instrument and no GMM; authors say they could not find an instrument and lagging does not fix endogeneity. Countries with faster TFP growth may adopt IoT faster. Footnote 5 simply assumes the direction of causality. Causal-sounding 'contribution' calculations (e.g. $592 billion) are drawn from the coefficient. Authors themselves call the estimate an upper bound and possibly biased upward by early-year effects.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5.1, p.268: 'we have been unable to ﬁnd any suitable instrument for IoT connections'; footnote 5, p.275; Conclusions p.275

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is licensed cellular IoT connections per inhabitant from industry data (GSMA), not IoT investment or capital; excludes WiFi-based IoT; normalised by population rather than by business capital; the authors note that connections include non-business uses. Connection counts are concentrated in a few markets (China 61% of world connections in 2018). Short, rapidly growing series.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 5.1 p.267; footnote 3 p.275; footnote 7 p.275: 'data on IoT connections based on WiFi were not available'; p.270 discussion of connections vs devices

selection_of_countries_years.why: Eight countries removed as extreme TFP-growth outliers (Syria, Venezuela, Yemen, Zimbabwe and others), and the paper says the IoT coefficient is insignificant if they are retained. Sample is limited to countries covered by both TED and GSMA, 2010-2017, so it is tilted to richer and larger economies. The outlier rule (3 IQR) is stated.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Footnote 15, p.276; Section 5.3, p.268-269: 'After removing extreme outliers from our sample, we ﬁnd a signiﬁcant correlation'

outcome_measurement.why: TFP growth is a residual from the Conference Board Total Economy Database using composition-adjusted labour and capital services; measurement error in TFP for developing economies is likely, and the TFP residual can reflect output measurement problems. Authors note measurement error may be attenuated using longer differences.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 5.2, p.268: 'country data on growth in TFP and capital and labor services are from the Total Economy Database (2018)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications (first and three-year differences, with and without MBB, OECD split, alternative labour measures, robust regression, FE levels). Significant results depend on a data-driven outlier exclusion and are mostly significant only at 5% or 10%. Labour and capital services coefficients are negative and significant, which is unexpected and suggests the TFP construction interacts with the regressors. The preferred specification is not pre-specified.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 4, 5, A1-A4; footnote 15 and p.269; negative labour coefficient '-0.19**' in Table 4

selective_reporting.why: Fixed-effects levels results are described but not shown ('available upon request'); the no-outlier-exclusion regression is described as insignificant but the coefficients are not shown. On the other hand, the paper reports one-year, three-year, subsample and robust-regression results and flags its own caveats and upper-bound status.
selective_reporting.evidence: Footnote 38, p.276: 'Results are available upon request'; footnote 15, p.276

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Two parts: (1) the econometric analysis, which is the basis for inclusion, and (2) a growth-accounting simulation for 14 OECD countries (US plus EU-13), a calibration exercise with assumed parameters that does not count as estimation; the 0.99% pa figure depends on an assumed IoT investment starting value (IDC estimate vs Ericsson-implied 3% of CT investment gives a 75-fold range, 0.013% to 0.99%) and on an imported spillover multiplier of 4.1 from the authors' earlier work. Do not mix the 0.99% simulation figure with the regression estimates. Conflict of interest: first author is employed by Ericsson AB, which co-funded the project and has a commercial interest in ICT; disclosed in the Disclosure statement and Acknowledgements (p.277). Authors describe results as an 'association' and 'upper bound', though they also convert the coefficient into dollar 'contributions'. Footnote 2 and the introduction give different dollar conversions ($197 billion for 0.23 pp, $592 billion for 0.69 pp). The paper states that IoT 'is an innovational complementarity to ICT', so it is treated as an ICT/mobile-connectivity exposure for eligibility. Sample count of non-OECD observations differs between Table 5 (322) and rreg Table A4 (378) because rreg retains outlier observations; total obs 630 in Table A3 implies about 90 countries. No instructions embedded in the text were found.

title: Nexus between energy consumption, information and communications technology, and economic growth: An enquiry into emerging Asian countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 10 Asian economies (2000-2017) estimating the effect of internet and mobile subscriptions on GDP with FMOLS, DOLS and AMG. Meets the non-AI sample threshold of at least 10 economies and has a family 1 outcome.
technology: ICT in general (medium and high technology exports as proxy)
exposure_measure: Internet users (% of population, lnIT); mobile cellular subscriptions (number, lnMO); medium and high technology exports (% of manufactured exports, lnEX) used as an ICT-capability proxy because ICT investment or capital stock data were unavailable. Source: World Development Indicators.

sample.economies_or_groups: Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nepal, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Thailand (listed in Table 8). Text says selected as 'highest current GDP' emerging and developing Asian countries; the paper does not list them in the text.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (paper gives no income classification; sample spans lower-middle and upper-middle economies by my reading, not stated by the paper)

design.estimator: Pesaran and Breusch-Pagan CSD tests, IPS/Fisher and CIPS/CADF unit roots, Westerlund cointegration, Dumitrescu-Hurlin Granger non-causality (GDP as dependent variable), panel FMOLS and DOLS long-run elasticities, country-wise Augmented Mean Group (AMG)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Log-log model of GDP on electricity consumption (kWh per capita), energy use (kg oil eq per $1,000 GDP), income index (GNI per capita), internet, mobile, high-tech exports. No other controls; no explicit fixed effects described for FMOLS/DOLS.

results.indicator: Elasticity of GDP (current US$) with respect to mobile subscriptions, panel FMOLS/DOLS
results.estimate: FMOLS 0.7195; DOLS 0.7541 (log-log elasticity)

results.indicator: Elasticity of GDP (current US$) with respect to internet users, panel FMOLS/DOLS
results.estimate: FMOLS -0.5911; DOLS -0.5616 (log-log elasticity)
results.evidence: p.10, Table 7 lnIT -0.59107***; p.7 text: 'internet subscriptions negatively impact GDP ... decrease in growth by 0.59%'

results.indicator: Elasticity of GDP with respect to medium and high technology exports, panel FMOLS/DOLS
results.estimate: FMOLS 0.1331; DOLS 0.1241

results.indicator: Country-wise AMG coefficients on mobile subscriptions (10 countries)
results.estimate: Significant positive in India 0.0759, Indonesia 0.0870, Malaysia 0.3128, Thailand 0.0587 (10%); significant negative in Bangladesh -0.0987 and Cambodia -0.1060; insignificant elsewhere
results.uncertainty: Stars only (1/5/10% levels); no SEs reported
results.evidence: p.10, Table 8 lnMO column; p.8 text: 'mobile subscriptions also significantly impact ... Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Nepal'

results.indicator: Country-wise AMG coefficients on internet users (10 countries)
results.estimate: Insignificant in 8 of 10 countries; significant negative in Malaysia -0.4137 and Thailand -0.2656
results.uncertainty: Stars only (1/5/10% levels); no SEs reported
results.evidence: p.10, Table 8 lnIT column; p.8: 'impact of internet subscriptions is in fact insignificant is majority of the countries except for Malaysia and Thailand'

results.indicator: Dumitrescu-Hurlin Granger causality to GDP from internet, mobile, high-tech exports, electricity, energy use, income
results.estimate: Rejection of no-causality for all regressors: W-bar 3.79 (IN), 13.07 (MO), 4.28 (IT), 4.74 (EL), 7.96 (EN), 4.21 (EX)
results.evidence: p.9, Table 6 (GDP as dependent variable); only one causal direction is tabulated

heterogeneity.finding: Country-specific AMG estimates differ strongly: mobile coefficient positive and significant in India, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, negative in Bangladesh and Cambodia, insignificant in China, Philippines, Sri Lanka and Nepal. This contradicts the claim that results are consistent for all countries.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.10, Table 8; abstract: 'the results are consistent for all the countries analyzed'

heterogeneity.finding: The discussion says the ICT effect differs across income groups but cites Yousefi (2011); the paper estimates no income-group split.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.9, Section 5: 'impact of ICT on economic growth differs across different income group of countries (Yousefi, 2011)'

income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported as a group; country AMG results for China, Malaysia, Thailand given in Table 8 (the paper does not classify them)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported as a group; country AMG results for Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Nepal, Philippines, Sri Lanka given in Table 8 (the paper does not classify them)

n_specifications_reported: about 3 (FMOLS, DOLS, country-wise AMG with one equation each, plus causality tests); no robustness variants

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language and policy advice, but no instrument or timing strategy. Authors themselves find bidirectional causality between ICT and GDP. GNI per capita (income index) is included as a regressor alongside GDP, a mechanically related variable. The small set of regressors omits capital, labour and human capital.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.3 Eq. 1-3 (model has no capital or labour terms); p.9 Section 5 'bidirectional causality between all the variables'

exposure_measurement.why: Internet users (% pop) and mobile subscriptions are standard adoption measures, but mobile is entered in absolute numbers (not per capita) so it partly scales with population. High-tech exports are a weak proxy for ICT capability.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.2 and p.5: 'MO (in numbers)'; medium and high technological export used 'due to nonavailability of ICT investment or ICT capital stock'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 10 countries and 18 annual observations. Selection is described as 'highest current GDP' but Nepal and Cambodia are included and the countries are not named in the text. Text variously calls the sample 'emerging Asian', 'South Asian' and 'top 10 emerging South Asian' although it includes China, Indonesia and Thailand.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.1 abstract; p.5 Section 3.1; p.9 'South Asian countries under study'; p.10 Table 8

outcome_measurement.why: The dependent variable is current-price GDP in US dollars (levels), not real or per-capita GDP, so it mixes inflation and exchange-rate movements with output. The paper still calls it economic growth.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.5 Section 3.1: 'Y denotes the current GDP price in US dollars, as a measure of economic growth'; p.8 Table 1 GDP mean 856.34

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Panel with N=10 and T=18 uses FMOLS/DOLS/AMG with several nonstationarity and cointegration tests whose results are mixed (CIPS and Westerlund p-values 0.01-0.053, Gt only at 10%). First-generation unit root tests say all series are stationary at level, which conflicts with the cointegration framework. Variable-equation notation is inconsistent (beta3 and beta4 reused). No robustness checks.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.8 Tables 3-4; p.9 Table 5 (Gt p=.053); p.6 Eq. 3

selective_reporting.why: The abstract and conclusion say internet and mobile subscriptions have a positive effect on growth, but Table 7 shows a significant negative internet coefficient (-0.59) and Table 8 shows internet insignificant in most countries and mobile negative in some. The abstract says bidirectional causality but only the GDP-dependent direction is tabulated.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.1 abstract and p.10 Section 6 vs p.10 Table 7 lnIT -0.59107***; p.9 Table 6 title 'ln_GDP as dependent variable'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Headline claims conflict with the reported tables: the abstract states internet subscriptions have a positive impact, while Table 7 reports a negative and significant coefficient (about -0.59) and the AMG panel finds internet insignificant in 8 of 10 countries. The discussion also says the FMOLS/DOLS results show 'a significant impact' without noting direction. Energy outcomes (electricity use, energy use) are modelled as regressors for GDP, not as outcomes of ICT, so no family 6 result is extracted. Westerlund Z-values and p-values look inconsistent (Gt Z=-0.944 with p=.053). In Table 8, lnIN (income index) coefficients are large (up to 9.4) and Table 1 reports GDP mean 856 with max 12,062, suggesting GDP is in billions of US dollars; unit not stated. No injected instructions found in the text. Published in Journal of Public Affairs (Wiley, 2021).

title: Labor Market Exposure to AI: Cross-country Differences and Distributional Implications
decision_rationale: Maps AI occupational exposure descriptively and estimates no outcome from the six families. Moved from include to context after merge.
technology: artificial intelligence (occupational exposure to AI, AIOE of Felten et al. 2021, and complementarity-adjusted C-AIOE; AIOE: LLM only used in robustness)
exposure_measure: Occupation-level AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE, Felten et al. 2021, based on overlap of 10 AI applications with 52 O*NET abilities) and an authors' complementarity-adjusted measure C-AIOE = AIOE*(1-(theta-theta_min)), where theta is built from 11 O*NET work contexts and job zones (6 components). Occupation scores are mapped from US SOC 2010 to ISCO-08 and attached to worker microdata. This is potential exposure by occupation, not observed AI adoption.

sample.economies_or_groups: Advanced economies: US, UK. Emerging markets: Brazil, Colombia, India, South Africa.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (2 advanced economies and 4 emerging markets; World Bank income-group labels not reported)
sample.years: Survey years 2018-19 (India), 2019 (South Africa, US), 2022 (Brazil, Colombia, UK); no pooled panel
sample.unit: other (worker-level microdata aggregated to occupation exposure shares by country, demographic group and earnings decile)

design.estimator: Descriptive tabulation: cumulative employment shares and employment shares by exposure/complementarity quadrant, split by gender, education, age and earnings decile. Occupation-level correlations and PCA reported in appendix. No regression models reported.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: none; workers aged 16-64 and employed; cross-section per country; education harmonised into four categories (not available for India college categories)

results.indicator: Share of employment in high-AI-exposure occupations (above median AIOE), cross-country
results.estimate: UK about 40% of employment above 80th percentile of AIOE; US almost 30%; Brazil, Colombia, South Africa under 15%; India lowest. Roughly 40% of workers in Brazil, Colombia, South Africa in high-exposure occupations, 26% in India (14% high complementarity, 12% low).
results.uncertainty: not reported (descriptive shares, no standard errors)
results.evidence: Section 4.1, pp. 18-20, Fig 4a and Fig 5: 'UK emerges as the country with the highest aggregate exposure levels'

results.indicator: Share of employment in high-exposure and low-complementarity occupations (substitution risk), AEs vs EMs
results.estimate: UK 32%, US 29.7%; about 20% in Brazil, Colombia, South Africa; 12% in India. Gap between AEs and most EMs almost closed once complementarity is factored in (C-AIOE), India excepted.
results.evidence: Section 4.1, pp. 19-20: 'the gap in exposure across AEs and most EMs is almost fully closed'

results.indicator: Share of employment in high-exposure and high-complementarity occupations (potential beneficiaries)
results.estimate: UK 51.9% (text wording says 'highly complementary occupations'), US 49.8%; about 20% in Brazil, Colombia, South Africa; 14% in India.
results.evidence: Section 4.1, p. 20: 'UK leads in this metric, with 51.9 percent of workers engaged in highly complementary occupations'

results.indicator: Gender gap in exposure (share of women vs men in high-exposure occupations)
results.estimate: Women more exposed in 5 of 6 countries: US 68% women vs 51% men; Brazil 52% vs 32%. India reversed: 24% women vs 28% men.
results.evidence: Section 4.3.1, p. 23: 'in the US, 68 percent of women are in high exposure occupations compared to 51 percent of men'

results.indicator: Exposure across the earnings distribution (share in high-exposure occupations by earnings decile)
results.estimate: Positive association between earnings and high-exposure share in all countries; UK top decile almost all in high-exposure occupations. High-exposure low-complementarity jobs are more evenly spread across deciles; high-complementarity jobs concentrated in top deciles in all six countries, more so in EMs.
results.evidence: Section 4.4, p. 25: 'employment in high-complementarity occupations is concentrated in the top deciles of the earnings distribution'

results.indicator: Education gradient in exposure and complementarity
results.estimate: About 90% of college-educated workers in most countries are in high-exposure occupations; below 20% of those without high school in most countries (UK 40%). UK: high-exposure low-complementarity share 26% (middle school or below) vs 36% (college); high-exposure high-complementarity share 17% vs over 50%.
results.evidence: Section 4.3.2, p. 24: 'Only 17 percent of workers with middle school education or below find themselves in high-exposure and high-complementarity occupations'

results.indicator: Occupational structure as driver of cross-country exposure differences (professional, managerial, clerical, elementary and agricultural shares)
results.estimate: Professionals about 30% of UK employment vs just above 15% in US and under 10% in India and South Africa; managers 14.4% US vs 10.7% UK; agriculture over 30% of employment in India.
results.evidence: Section 4.2, pp. 21-23: 'Nearly 30 percent of workers in the UK are employed in professional occupations'

heterogeneity.finding: Advanced economies (US, UK) show higher unadjusted exposure than emerging markets, driven by larger shares of professional and managerial jobs; AEs also have more employment in high-exposure, high-complementarity jobs, so impacts are described as more polarised. After complementarity adjustment AE-EM differences narrow sharply except India. Groups are AE vs EM labels only, not formal income classes.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.1, p. 20-21: 'the US and UK point to greater polarization in exposure to AI for AEs'

heterogeneity.finding: Low exposure in India is attributed to a large agricultural workforce (over 30%); elementary occupations drive low exposure in the other EMs.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.2, p. 21: 'In India, this result is magnified by the extensive employment of workers in agriculture'

heterogeneity.finding: College-educated workers are more exposed and also more likely to be in high-complementarity jobs; adverse exposure is spread more evenly across education levels than the potential gains.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.3.2, p. 24: 'potential adverse impacts of AI might be distributed more evenly than the potential gains'

heterogeneity.finding: Gender (women more exposed except India) and age (youngest workers less exposed and, among exposed, less often in high-complementarity jobs; no clear pattern otherwise).
heterogeneity.evidence: Sections 4.3.1 and 4.3.3, pp. 23-25

income_group_results.high: US and UK: highest exposure (UK about 40% of employment above 80th percentile of AIOE, US almost 30%); about 30-32% of employment in high-exposure low-complementarity jobs and 50-52% in high-exposure high-complementarity jobs (Sections 4.1, pp. 18-20). Uses 'advanced economies' label; World Bank group not stated.
income_group_results.upper_middle: Brazil, Colombia, South Africa (World Bank group not stated in the paper): under 15% of employment above 80th percentile of AIOE; about 40% in high-exposure occupations, about half with high complementarity (p. 20).
income_group_results.lower_middle: India (World Bank group not stated in the paper): lowest exposure, 26% in high-exposure occupations, driven by agricultural employment (p. 20-21).
income_group_results.low: not reported (no low-income economy in sample)

n_specifications_reported: unclear (no regressions; baseline C-AIOE plus two robustness variants of the adjustment, w=0.5 and exponential form, and leave-one-out checks on the complementarity index)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: The paper makes no estimate of an effect of AI on any outcome. The title and abstract speak of 'impact' and 'distributional implications', but results are cross-sectional shares of workers in occupations with high exposure scores, with no counterfactual, no AI adoption data and no control for confounders. The authors acknowledge the analysis is static and partial equilibrium. Read as descriptive exposure mapping the problem is smaller, but it cannot support causal payoff claims.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Abstract and Section 6, p. 31: 'the analysis is static and in partial equilibrium, providing a snapshot view of exposure in one year'

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is a US-based occupation-level index (O*NET, crowd-sourced mapping of AI applications to abilities) applied to other countries through crosswalks, assuming occupation task content is the same across countries. It does not measure actual AI adoption or capability in each economy. The complementarity index theta relies on the authors' own choice of 11 work contexts out of 57 and on treating an ordinal job-zone as cardinal; the authors flag both.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2.3, pp. 10-12 and footnote 6, p. 9: 'the selection of O*NET contexts relies on our own judgement'; 'assumption that key tasks and skills... do not change across countries'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Six economies chosen apparently by availability of occupation-coded labour force microdata; four EMs but no low-income economy. Survey years differ (2018-19, 2019, 2022), and some surveys use 3-digit ISCO (India). No selection rationale beyond data availability is given. Avoiding 2020-21 is justified in a footnote.

outcome_measurement.why: The 'outcome' is the share of workers whose occupation falls above the median on the exposure or complementarity index; no realised employment, wage or displacement outcomes are observed. Earnings are gross pay from main job in different periodicity and units across countries (monthly, weekly, annual), compared only through within-country deciles. High/low thresholds are medians of the occupation distribution, so shares depend on this arbitrary cut.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3, p. 17: 'Earnings are computed as gross (pre-tax) income... except for the UK... weekly earnings, and the US... annual earnings'; Fig 5 note on median cut-offs

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: No regression specifications. Researcher choices lie in constructing theta (context selection, equal weights, linear and exponential adjustment forms, median thresholds). Robustness is shown for weight w=0.5, exponential form, leave-one-out components, PCA and alternative exposure measures; the authors note the Briggs-Kodnani replication gives a negative correlation with their baseline.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Sections 2.5 and 5, pp. 14-15, 28-29; Appendix A.1-A.2, Tables A.3-A.5

selective_reporting.why: Descriptive outputs are reported for all six countries and for all demographic splits, including the exception (India reverses the gender pattern) and the Briggs-Kodnani discrepancy. No sign of selective presentation, but no uncertainty measures are given and most results are in figures.

venue_quality_concern: possible (IMF Working Paper, not peer reviewed; 'research in progress... to elicit comments')
notes: Descriptive exposure study; no regression coefficients, standard errors or confidence intervals anywhere, so estimate fields hold reported shares. Eligibility is borderline: AI exposure is an occupational potential measure rather than observed adoption, and outcomes are composition shares rather than realised labour-market effects; reviewers may prefer to recode as context. Text quirks: the 51.9% UK figure is described as share 'engaged in highly complementarity occupations' while Fig 5 is defined as high-exposure and high-complementarity, so the exact definition is slightly unclear; the front-page recommended citation misspells 'Wokring' and the abstract lists JEL J23 twice. Pages cited are the paper's own page numbers. No embedded instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

title: Enhancing human development in developing regions: Do ICT and transport infrastructure matter?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel IV-GMM study of 79 developing countries relating broadband, internet, mobile and fixed-telephone penetration to HDI, schooling, life expectancy and child and maternal mortality (family 5). Meets the 10-economy threshold for non-AI technologies.
technology: ICT goods imports (also transport infrastructure as a parallel exposure)
exposure_measure: Log of WDI penetration indicators: fixed broadband subscriptions per 100, fixed telephone subscriptions per 100, individuals using the internet (% pop), mobile cellular subscriptions per 100, ICT goods imports (% of goods imports). Each ICT indicator entered one at a time in separate regressions (Table 1).

sample.economies_or_groups: South Asia (7), sub-Saharan Africa (about 44) and Latin America-Caribbean (about 27); list in Appendix Table 1
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed developing (not reported by income group; list includes some high-income Caribbean states such as Bahamas and Barbados, and Seychelles)
sample.years: 1990-2018 (unbalanced; N between 281 and 740 for HDI, 54 to 175 for maternal mortality)

design.estimator: Static two-step IV-GMM (Baum et al. 2002), log-log; Driscoll-Kraay estimator as robustness (Tables 3A-3C)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Controls: ln GDP per capita, trade openness, urbanisation, FDI, private credit, remittances, electric power losses; regional dummies (SSA, LAC vs SAR); no country fixed effects in Eq. 2 beyond a mu_i term that is not clearly implemented. The instrument is never named.

results.indicator: Human Development Index (log) on internet users (% pop, log)
results.estimate: 0.020 (elasticity; 10% rise in internet use -> 0.20% rise in HDI)
results.evidence: Table 2A col 8; p.8 text: 'broadband, internet and mobile phone penetration ... enhance human development'

results.indicator: Human Development Index (log) on mobile cellular subscriptions (log)
results.evidence: Table 2A col 9

results.indicator: Human Development Index (log) on fixed broadband (log)
results.evidence: Table 2A col 5

results.indicator: Human Development Index (log) on fixed telephone (log) and on ICT goods imports (log)
results.estimate: telephone 0.019; ICT goods 0.001
results.evidence: Table 2A cols 6-7

results.indicator: Human capital index (schooling and returns) on ICT indicators
results.estimate: broadband 0.007*, telephone 0.025***, internet 0.018***, mobile 0.015***; ICT goods -0.006 ns
results.evidence: Table 2B cols 5-9

results.indicator: Life expectancy (log) on ICT indicators
results.estimate: broadband 0.012***, telephone 0.026***, internet 0.011***, mobile 0.011***; ICT goods -0.012**
results.evidence: Table 2C cols 5-9

results.indicator: Under-five deaths (log) on ICT indicators
results.estimate: broadband -0.219***, telephone -0.582***, internet -0.200***, mobile -0.199***; ICT goods +0.519*** (worse). Negative sign means fewer deaths
results.evidence: Table 2D cols 5-9

results.indicator: Maternal mortality ratio (log) on ICT indicators
results.estimate: broadband -0.070**, telephone -0.278***, internet -0.077**; mobile -0.033 ns; ICT goods 0.085 ns
results.evidence: Table 2E cols 5-9

heterogeneity.finding: Region (SAR, SSA, LAC) via marginal-effect plots from interaction models in supplementary material. ICT slopes on HDI positive in all three regions for broadband, telephone, internet and mobile; ICT goods negative in SAR and LAC but positive in SSA. Maternal mortality slopes for broadband, internet and mobile negative in SAR and LAC but positive in SSA. Interaction estimates and SEs are not in the main text.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.2.1-4.2.5, Figs 1B, 1D, 1F, 1H, 1J; p.12 'broadband penetration slope is positive for all the regions'

heterogeneity.finding: No analysis by World Bank income group; only regional dummies. SSA has lower HDI, schooling and life expectancy and higher child and maternal mortality than South Asia.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.11, regional dummies paragraph; Table 2A SSA coefficients about -0.12 to -0.23

n_specifications_reported: about 45 main IV-GMM regressions (9 ICT/transport indicators x 5 outcomes) plus 45 Driscoll-Kraay regressions plus regional interaction models (supplementary)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('impact', 'improve'). IV-GMM is claimed, but the instrument is never identified or justified in the text; tables say 'a single instrument was used' while listing 11-12 instruments; Hansen J reported as 0.000 for exactly identified models, which is not meaningful. Wealthier and healthier countries adopt ICT earlier, so reverse causation is plausible.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.1 p.5-6; Table 2B note 'instruments are exactly identified ... a single instrument'; Table 2A-2E 'No. of instruments 11/12'

exposure_measurement.why: Standard WDI penetration rates, log-transformed (log of values near zero produces extreme minima, e.g. -10.95 for internet use). ICT goods imports is a weak proxy for adoption. Each indicator is entered alone, so overlap among ICT measures is not handled.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample set 'strictly based on data availability'; unbalanced panels with N varying from 54 to 785 across models. Only three developing regions, so generalisation to other income groups is limited. Maternal mortality models rest on 54-175 observations.

outcome_measurement.why: HDI includes an income component and is mechanically related to the GDP-per-capita control. Maternal mortality is a modelled estimate with sparse years. Under-five mortality is a count (number of deaths) rather than a rate, so it scales with population.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 1 (lnunfd 'Number of under-five deaths'; lnmmrm 'modelled estimate')

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many indicator x outcome combinations, each in a separate regression with a single instrument and no stated first stage. F-statistics identical across Tables 2B, 2C and 2D (132664.515, 68711.829, ...), which indicates copy-paste or a shared first stage; values of 50,000 to 200,000 are implausible. No lag structure or country fixed effects are described clearly.

selective_reporting.why: All indicator-outcome results are reported, including nulls and wrong-signed ICT goods. Regional interaction estimates are only in supplementary material and shown as plots. Some text claims in the conclusion do not match the tables (e.g. telephone is said to have a neutral effect on HDI but is listed with other ICT variables improving human capital, which matches; interpretation of mortality signs as 'enhance maternal mortality' is confusing).

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Transport infrastructure results are out of scope and not extracted. Text states ICT is more effective than transport but the paper does not test the difference formally. The instrument is not named anywhere in the main text. Hansen J p-values of 0.000 reported alongside the statement that models are exactly identified, and F-statistics duplicated across Tables 2B-2D, so the diagnostics are unreliable. Interpretation in text: '10% increase in broadband ... human development by 0.08%' consistent with log-log coefficient 0.008. Robustness (Driscoll-Kraay) is non-IV, so it does not address endogeneity. No instruction-like content found in the text.

title: Does the digital divide matter? The role of information and communication technology in cross-country level and growth estimates
decision_rationale: Own cross-country and panel estimation (94-99 economies, 1983-1997) of fixed lines, mobile phones, internet hosts and PCs on income per working-age person and its growth; meets exposure, sample and outcome (output/productivity) criteria.
technology: ICT in general: fixed telephone lines
exposure_measure: Four WDI diffusion proxies: main telephone lines per 1,000, internet hosts per 10,000, mobile phones per 1,000, PCs per 1,000; plus unweighted average of the four normalised indicators (composite). Enters as log of initial stock ln(A_ICT(0)) and growth rate g_ICT in cross-section, and as ln(A_ICT) in panel.

sample.n_economies: 94-99 in cross-section (47 for mobile or PC specifications); 97 (70-74 or 51 in subsamples) in panel; data appendix lists 116 countries
sample.economies_or_groups: World sample incl. OECD and non-OECD, from Algeria to Zimbabwe (see Data Appendix)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high to low); footnote splits sample into income terciles for descriptives only
sample.unit: country-year (cross-section averages for most regressions; panel with five subperiods)

design.estimator: Augmented Mankiw-Romer-Weil cross-section OLS with bootstrap standard errors (2000 replications); panel fixed effects; G2SLS fixed effects with lagged ICT instruments; growth/convergence regressions
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: ln(sk)-ln(n+g+d), ln(sh)-ln(n+g+d), initial income (growth equations); country fixed effects in panel; sensitivity to Levine-Renelt variables and freedom indices reported only as 'available upon request'

results.indicator: Log GDP per working-age person (PPP), cross-section 1991-97, elasticity of initial ICT stock ln(A_ICT(0))
results.estimate: 0.451 (phone lines), 0.301 (mobile), 0.438 (PCs), 0.388 (composite); 0.302 for composite 1983-97. Authors: 'elasticity of .3/.4'.
results.uncertainty: t = 10.18, 10.05, 12.69, 9.97, 8.48; flagged significant at 90-95% with bootstrap standard errors
results.evidence: p.24 Table 1; 'a ten percent higher stock of ICT variables at the beginning... 3/4 percent higher level of per capita GDP'

results.indicator: Log GDP per working-age person, cross-section, coefficient on ICT growth rate g_ICT
results.evidence: p.24 Table 1

results.indicator: Panel fixed effects and G2SLS: elasticity of ln(A_ICT) on income per worker
results.estimate: FE: 0.265 (phone), 0.051 (mobile), 0.138 (PCs), 0.027 (composite). G2SLS: 0.314, 0.094, 0.212, 0.120. Text says elasticity '.02/.12', which does not match the 0.314 in Table 2.
results.evidence: p.25 Table 2; p.16-17 text: 'The ICT elasticity in panel estimates is smaller (.02/.12)'

results.indicator: Growth of income per working-age person 1985-97: elasticity of initial ICT stock ln(A_ICT(1985))
results.estimate: 0.131 (phone), 0.060 (mobile), 0.121 (PCs), 0.063 (composite 1991-97 column); 0.102 (composite 1983-97). Authors: .06/.13.
results.evidence: p.26 Table 3; 'a ten percent higher stock... corresponds to a .6/1.3 percent higher rate of growth'

results.indicator: Growth equation: coefficient on ICT growth rate g_ICT
results.evidence: p.26 Table 3; abstract claims all four indicators 'significantly affect levels and growth'

heterogeneity.finding: OECD vs non-OECD split: ICT effect significant in both subsamples but stronger in OECD countries (results omitted, 'available upon request').
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 footnote 20: 'ICT effect is significant in both subsamples, even though it appears to be stronger in OECD countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Including ICT reduces the estimated elasticity of human capital and, for PCs and mobile phones, removes its significance; authors interpret this as part of human capital's contribution working through ICT (complementarity). Physical capital loses significance when composite ICT is included.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.13-15 and Table 1: 'sk is no more significant when ICT variables are included'

income_group_results.high: not reported separately (OECD stronger; numbers omitted)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (non-OECD significant but weaker; numbers omitted)

n_specifications_reported: about 24 columns across Tables 1-3; further specifications referred to but omitted

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Cross-section levels regressions on persistent ICT stocks; richer countries diffuse ICT faster, so reverse causality is likely. Only remedy is a lag of the initial ICT stock and G2SLS using own lags (t-2 to t-4) of ICT as instruments, which are not exogenous when ICT is persistent; no overidentification or weak-instrument tests. Authors concede results 'obviously risk to be affected by endogeneity'.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.13 footnote 18; p.16 G2SLS discussion; Table 2

exposure_measurement.why: Counts of lines, hosts, mobile phones and PCs per capita are crude access proxies without quality or usage; composite is an unweighted average of normalised indicators; internet hosts are noisy proxy (many zeros).
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.11 Sec 3.1; footnote 14 'power of PCs not available'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Samples driven by data availability: 94-99 countries for phone lines but only 47-51 for mobile/PC; short window 1991-97 for the individual indicators; mobile phone and PC series start between 1981 and 1996, so a 1985 initial stock cannot exist for many countries, yet Table 3 uses ln(A_ICT(1985)).
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.12 and Data Appendix pp.27-29; Table 3 p.26

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per working-age person at PPP from WDI is a standard productivity/income measure (labour input is population aged 15-64, not employment).

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four indicators x composite x several samples and periods; theory-driven MRW structure with restriction imposed; many robustness checks (alternative labour input, trend income, institutional controls, unrestricted coefficients) reported only as 'available upon request'.

selective_reporting.why: Abstract states all four proxies significantly affect levels and growth, but g_ICT is insignificant for phone lines and the composite (1991-97) in Table 3. Text elasticities (.02/.12 for panel) do not match Table 2 (up to 0.314). Table 1 gives the same R2 (0.9127) for the phone-line and composite columns, which looks like a transcription error. Conclusion contains a truncated sentence ('and finds .').
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; Table 3 p.26; Table 1 R2 row; Conclusions p.19

venue_quality_concern: possible (text supplied is a CEIS Tor Vergata working paper dated February 2003, not the 2005 journal version listed in the assignment; may differ from the published version)
notes: The file is the February 2003 working paper (CEIS Research Paper Series, Vol 2 No 4), while the assignment gives year 2005. Possible duplicate/earlier version of a later published article, so check whether the 2005 version is in the review set. Mobile phone sample is limited to 47 countries. Headline effect sizes are from a pre-2000 period and are not comparable to modern broadband or smartphone adoption. Table 3 column labels say 1991-1997 but the dependent variable is defined for 1985-1997. No instruction-like text found.

title: New technologies and jobs in Europe
decision_rationale: Own quantitative estimation of occupation-level AI (and software) exposure against employment shares and relative wages in 16 European countries (at least 3 economies for AI); labour-market outcome (family 3). Exposure is a potential-capability index, not measured adoption, but fits 'capability of AI'.
technology: artificial intelligence (occupational exposure indices: Webb 2020 patent-based AI score; Felten et al. AIOI)
robots (exposure used only as a control in robustness)
exposure_measure: Time-invariant occupation-level exposure scores built for the US (SOC) and crosswalked to ISCO 3-digit; transformed into employment-weighted percentiles by country-sector-occupation cell. Webb: textual overlap of patents and O*NET task descriptions. Felten et al. AIOI: EFF AI progress 2010-2015 linked to O*NET abilities (2019), standardised 0-1. Not a measure of actual AI adoption in Europe.

sample.economies_or_groups: 15 euro area countries (AT, BE, DE, EE, ES, FI, FR, GR, IE, IT, LT, LU, LV, NL, PT) plus the UK
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (paper does not classify; all 16 are European economies, high income by external classification)
sample.years: 2011-2019 (change 2011 to 2019; some countries use 2017/2018/2013 for wages)
sample.unit: other (country x sector x ISCO 3-digit occupation cell; about 6,767 cells for employment)

design.estimator: Weighted OLS (weights = cell average employment) of cell change in employment share (arc % change, winsorised 1%) or change in within-country wage centile on technology exposure; run pooled, by age/education tercile and country by country
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Sector and country dummies in headline spec; sector x country dummies and robot/software exposure controls in Table B1; SEs described as clustered by country in table notes (text says sector-clustered)

results.indicator: Change in sector-occupation employment share vs AI exposure (Webb), pooled 16 countries
results.estimate: 0.104 (dep var arc % change in employment share; exposure as 0-1 percentile); paper: moving 25 centiles = +2.6% in employment share; N=6767
results.evidence: Table 3 panel (a) col 1, p.17; text p.16: 'increase of sector-occupation employment share of 2.6%'

results.indicator: Change in sector-occupation employment share vs AI exposure (Felten et al. AIOI), pooled
results.estimate: 0.174 (same units); paper: +4.3% for a 25-centile move; N=5766
results.evidence: Table 3 panel (b) col 1, p.17

results.indicator: Change in employment share vs software exposure (Webb), pooled
results.evidence: Table 3 panel (c) col 1, p.17; 'null for the aggregate' (Conclusion p.25)

results.indicator: Change in relative wage centile vs AI exposure (Webb), pooled
results.evidence: Table 4 panel (a) col 1, p.18

results.indicator: Change in relative wage centile vs AI exposure (Felten et al.), pooled
results.estimate: -0.013; N=4872 (weakly significant only at 10%)
results.evidence: Table 4 panel (b) col 1, p.18; Conclusion: 'negative and hardly significant'

results.indicator: Change in relative wage centile vs software exposure (Webb), pooled
results.evidence: Table 4 panel (c) col 1, p.18

heterogeneity.finding: Positive AI-employment association is concentrated in high-education tercile cells (Webb 0.125**, SE 0.055; Felten 0.266***, SE 0.083); low and medium tercile coefficients are small and insignificant. Authors read this as skill-biased technological change.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 cols 5-7, p.17; 'driven by jobs that employ high skilled workers' p.18

heterogeneity.finding: By age: AI association strongest for cells with younger workers (Webb 0.212***, Felten 0.219***), about double the core/older groups; for software the sign is positive for younger (0.107***) and negative for core (-0.083*) and older (-0.117**) workers.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 cols 2-4, p.17

heterogeneity.finding: Country-level AI estimates correlate positively with DESI digital index (Spearman 0.40 Webb, 0.42 Felten); software correlation about zero (-0.08). No significance levels given, n=16 countries.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5, p.25

heterogeneity.finding: Country AI estimates correlate positively with governance (WGI 0.51 Webb, 0.31 Felten), negatively with product market regulation (-0.50, -0.30) and weakly negatively with employment protection (-0.08, -0.17). Positive employment association holds in most countries; negative for Greece (Webb) and Lithuania/Ireland (Felten).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5, p.25; Section 5.2 p.21

heterogeneity.finding: Country AI estimates correlate with PISA (0.30, 0.32) and tertiary share (0.31, 0.24), interpreted as complementarity or diffusion.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5, p.25

income_group_results.high: All 16 sample countries are European (high income by external classification; paper reports no income grouping). Pooled AI-employment association positive, wage association about zero.
income_group_results.upper_middle: not applicable (no such economies in sample)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not applicable (no such economies in sample)
income_group_results.low: not applicable (no such economies in sample)

n_specifications_reported: unclear (well over 100 coefficients: pooled 3 exposures x 7 subsamples x 2 outcomes, Table B1 variants, plus country-by-country regressions in Tables B2-B5, B7-B8)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Occupation exposure is predetermined and time-invariant (US-based, built from 2010-2015 AI progress and 2019 O*NET), which limits reverse causation, but there is no instrument or design to address confounding by occupation-level trends such as skill-biased demand shifts; only sector and country dummies. Authors use mostly associational language ('statistical associations', 'first approximation').
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5 p.15-16; Section 3 p.10 'implicit assumption that tasks are equally exposed'

exposure_measurement.why: Potential-exposure indices built for the US and applied to Europe, not actual AI adoption. The two AI measures correlate only moderately (rs=0.64) with little overlap in top/bottom occupations; Webb AI coefficient rises from 0.104 to 0.192 when software exposure is controlled (Table B1). Authors are explicit that these are proxies for potential automation.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 1-2 and p.11 (rs = 0.64); Table B1 p.44

selection_of_countries_years.why: 16 countries available in EU-LFS with wage deciles; start year fixed by the 2011 ISCO break; some wage reference years substituted (AT, ES, LT 2018; FI 2017; UK 2013 start). Homogeneous high-income European sample, short window.

outcome_measurement.why: Employment share change from EU-LFS 3-digit cells (winsorised) is reasonable; wages come only as deciles of monthly pay converted to cell centiles, which is coarse and tied to 2011 weights.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Simple, transparent main specification; many subgroup and country regressions, two AI measures, and alternative FE structures. SE clustering is inconsistent (text says sector-clustered, tables say country-clustered, 16 clusters).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 5 p.15 'standard errors are sector-clustered' vs Table 3 notes p.17 'clustered by country'

selective_reporting.why: Null and contrary findings reported (software null, wages null, negative country estimates, polarisation not supported); full country tables in the appendix.

venue_quality_concern: possible (NBER working paper, explicitly not peer-reviewed; authors affiliated with ECB, Banco de Espana, universities)
notes: Associations between potential exposure and employment share changes, not causal effects; the authors state results cannot be extrapolated and are silent on aggregate effects. Inconsistencies: SE clustering (sector in text, country in table notes); Table B1 note says columns 3 and 4 add software and robots respectively but rows show Robot in col 3 and Software in col 4. Table 3 reports Webb software 2011-2019 and Appendix Table B6 reports a negative software association for 2000-2010 (-0.171***). Software exposure is also estimated, so stream coded 'both'. Appendix A figures were not reviewed in detail. No instructions embedded in the text were found.

title: Job creation and destruction in the digital age: Assessing heterogeneous effects across European Union countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of ICT investment stock and total employment in 27 EU countries, 1995-2019, with its own estimation (OLS, 2SRI, GMM). Meets the exposure (ICT), sample (27 economies) and outcome (labour market) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (ICT capital stock: computer hardware, telecom equipment, software and databases)
exposure_measure: Stock of ICT investment built with the perpetual inventory method from Eurostat gross fixed capital formation by asset (hardware N11321, telecom N11322, software/databases N1173), constant 2005 prices, 33% depreciation; also split into machine-based vs non-machine-based. Entered as log growth.

sample.economies_or_groups: EU27 member states
sample.income_groups_covered: mostly high income (EU members); income groups not reported or compared by the authors

design.estimator: Pooled OLS (no FE and with country FE), 2SRI/control-function estimator, with RE, difference GMM and two-step GMM as robustness. GDP-weighted regressions. Short-run labour demand equation in first differences of logs.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Growth of non-ICT capital stock, real cost per employee, population growth, change in tertiary-education share, recession dummy, country FE (in columns III-IV). Instruments for 2SRI are first and second lags of the ICT stock (log levels).

results.indicator: Growth rate of total employment (elasticity with respect to growth of ICT investment stock), EU27 pooled, 2SRI
results.estimate: 0.112 (elasticity); about 3.3 net jobs per EUR 100,000 increase in ICT investment stock
results.evidence: p.6 Table 4 col IV; p.7 text: 'an increase of EUR 100,000 in the ICT investment stock ... 3.3 jobs'

results.indicator: Growth of total employment, pooled OLS with country FE (exogenous ICT stock)
results.estimate: 0.0508 (about 1.5 jobs per EUR 100,000)
results.evidence: p.6 Table 4 col III; p.7 text

results.indicator: Country-specific elasticities of employment growth to ICT stock growth (27 country-by-country specifications)
results.estimate: Significant positive in 14 countries (e.g. Spain 0.731, Portugal 0.335, France 0.196, Sweden 0.081); no significant effect in 13 countries; Poland -0.001 (insignificant). Marginal effects 0.8 jobs (Sweden) to 50.7 jobs (Latvia) per EUR 100,000.
results.uncertainty: Significance stars only in main text (p<0.1 to p<0.01); SEs in online supplement Table S4, not reported in the text
results.evidence: p.7 Table 5; 'statistically significant and positive effect ... for fourteen countries'

results.indicator: Employment elasticity to ICT stock, by sub-period (2SRI)
results.uncertainty: p<0.01 both; SEs not shown in main text
results.evidence: p.8 Table 7

results.indicator: Robustness: difference GMM and two-step GMM, employment growth on ICT stock growth
results.estimate: 0.108 (both); RE estimate 0.0337
results.evidence: p.10 Table D1

heterogeneity.finding: Composition of ICT capital: employment effect per EUR 100,000 is larger in countries with a low share of non-machine (software) to machine-based ICT stock (6.8 vs 5.8 jobs; elasticities 0.134 vs 0.262), i.e. machine-based capital linked to larger job gains. Elasticity is actually higher above the median, so the ranking in jobs and in elasticities differs.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.8 Table 6; 'positive relationship ... is stronger when the share of non-machine-based investment ... is relatively low'

heterogeneity.finding: Countries with a lower share of high-skilled jobs have larger job gains per unit of ICT stock (9.8 vs 3.5 jobs vs medium-skilled comparison; 9.5 vs 4.0 vs low-skilled comparison); effect still positive where high-skilled share is high.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: median (P50) split of high-skilled share; no estimated threshold
heterogeneity.evidence: p.8 Table 6; 'countries with a lower share of high-skilled jobs ... have a higher rate of return'

heterogeneity.finding: Time: net job effect declines over time (5.9 to 3.6 jobs), attributed by the authors to rising high-skilled share and growth of non-machine ICT (the attribution is not tested directly).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.8 Table 7; 'effect of digitalisation on employment has declined over time'

income_group_results.high: not reported (no income-group split; sample is EU27)

n_specifications_reported: about 40 (4 baseline columns, 27 country interaction models, 6 group/median splits, 2 sub-periods, 3 robustness estimators, weighting and control variants in supplement)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors address endogeneity with 2SRI using lags of the ICT stock as instruments and report GMM and a Granger test. Lagged own-variable instruments are weak identification: Table C1 shows the first lag of the endogenous variable correlated with employment growth (r=0.1385, p=0.0007), which the authors label 'weakly correlated'. The residual term is only significant at 10%, and in Table C2 the correlation between error terms is 0.0074 (p=0.86). Causal wording ('effect') exceeds what the design establishes, but short-run differenced FE with GMM check is a reasonable panel design.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.5-6 section 4.2 and 5.1; Table 4 rho -0.0728*; Appendix C Tables C1-C2

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital stock from national accounts GFCF by asset, built with PIM, captures ICT investment directly and distinguishes machine and non-machine assets. Depreciation rates (33%) are taken from other studies and are assumed uniform across countries; missing values linearly interpolated.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.4-5 section 4.1; Table 3 note 'Missing values were replaced by means of linear interpolation'; Table A3

selection_of_countries_years.why: All 27 EU members, 1995-2019 (594 observations), no evident selection. Number of observations per country (22) is smaller than the differenced span would imply, reason not explained in the main text. Sample is EU only, limiting generalisation to developing economies.

outcome_measurement.why: Total employment in thousand persons from Eurostat national accounts; skill-level employment from labour force survey by occupation. Standard measure. Employment is persons, not hours.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many alternative specifications (27 country interactions, median splits, sub-period split at 2009) with choices of weights (GDP-weighted headline), instruments and lags. The skill and machine-share heterogeneity uses median splits, and country-by-country regressions pick OLS or 2SRI depending on rho significance. Headline results are stable across estimators.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.7 'twenty-seven alternative specifications'; Table 5 note on [1] OLS vs [2] 2SRI; p.6 'GDP-weighted'

selective_reporting.why: Main text reports only coefficients for the ICT variable in the country and group tables with significance stars; standard errors for country results, split samples and robustness are in the online supplement (Tables S1-S8), not in the paper. The pooled result is positive for all estimators and is reported with SEs.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.7 Table 5 (stars only), p.8 Tables 6-7 ('Based on Table S5-S8 in the online supplement')

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Elasticities of employment growth on ICT stock growth are small (0.05-0.11); the 'jobs per EUR 100,000' conversion is the authors' own transformation using the ratio of employment to stock, and is large in small countries (Latvia 50.7). Authors say results are short-run only. Table 6 shows an inconsistency worth a look: elasticities are larger above the median for non-machine share and lower for the high-skill splits, while job counts move the other way, because of scaling. Footnote 8 reports Granger tests giving 'unidirectional causal relationship' from digitalisation to employment (Table S1, not seen). No text in the paper attempted to direct the extraction. Page numbers are journal pages 1-10 of the PDF (Economic Modelling 126, 106405).

title: Empirical Analysis of Inclusive Growth, Information and Communication Technology Adoption, and Institutional Quality
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of up to 193 countries (2010-2019) with explicit income-group comparison; exposure is mobile and fixed telephone subscriptions (ICT/mobile telephony); outcome is HDI (living standards beyond income, family 5).
technology: ICT in general (internet users used as control)
exposure_measure: Natural log of mobile cellular subscriptions and of fixed telephone subscriptions (World Bank WDI). Summary statistics show absolute counts (mean 35.4 million mobile subscriptions), not per-capita penetration. Internet users (% of population) enters as a control. Also an institutional quality index (PCA of six WGI indicators) and its interaction with ICT.

sample.n_economies: 193 stated (Section 3); effective estimation samples are smaller: 152 groups in Table 5 (mobile), 151 (fixed); 47/25/39/41 groups (high/low/lower-mid/upper-mid) in Table 8
sample.economies_or_groups: World-wide panel split by 2020 World Bank income classification (Appendix Table A1)
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low

design.estimator: Panel fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay (PSCC) standard errors; IV-GMM; simultaneous (bootstrap) quantile regression at 25th/50th/75th percentiles
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Year dummies; labour force participation, gross capital formation, inflation, trade openness, internet users; one-period lag of regressors used in PSCC-FE and IV-GMM; instruments for IV-GMM are not described in the text; Hansen J p-values reported

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln mobile subscriptions, full sample, PSCC-FE
results.estimate: 0.0111 (Table 5 col 2); 0.0103 with IQI (col 3); 0.0112 with interaction (col 4); log-log so elasticity of HDI to mobile subscriptions about 0.01
results.evidence: Table 5, p. 10, row lnICT, cols 2-4; text: 'lnMOB exerts a positive and statistical effect at the 1% level'

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln fixed telephone subscriptions, full sample, PSCC-FE
results.evidence: Table 5, p. 10, row lnICT, cols 5-7; text: 'that of lnFTEL is negative'

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln mobile subscriptions, full sample, IV-GMM
results.estimate: 0.00708 (Table 6 col 3); 0.00673 (col 4); col 2 (ICT alone, no IQI) is -0.860 and insignificant
results.evidence: Table 6, p. 11, row lnICT; Hansen p = 0.319 (col 3)

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln fixed telephone subscriptions, full sample, IV-GMM
results.evidence: Table 6, p. 11, row lnICT, cols 5-7. Sign is opposite to PSCC-FE in Table 5 although the text says Table 6 'align[s] with those of Table 5'

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln mobile subscriptions across HDI quantiles (SQREG)
results.evidence: Table 7, p. 12, upper panel, row lnMOB

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln mobile subscriptions by income group, PSCC-FE
results.estimate: High 0.0137; Low 0.00147; Lower-middle 0.0143; Upper-middle 0.00534
results.evidence: Table 8, p. 13, row lnICT, mobile model

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln fixed telephone subscriptions by income group, PSCC-FE
results.estimate: High 0.00758; Low -0.0108; Lower-middle 0.0116; Upper-middle -0.00638
results.evidence: Table 8, p. 13, row lnICT, fixed telephone model

results.indicator: ln HDI on ln mobile subscriptions by income group, IV-GMM
results.estimate: High 0.0200; Low -0.00211; Lower-middle 0.0174; Upper-middle 0.00343
results.evidence: Table 9, p. 15, row lnICT, mobile model; text says 'positive impact in seven out of eight models'

results.indicator: Institutional quality x ICT interaction on ln HDI (PSCC-FE and IV-GMM, full sample)
results.estimate: Mobile: 0.000561 (PSCC-FE, ns), 0.00128 (IV-GMM, 10%). Fixed telephone: 0.00150 (PSCC-FE, 5%), -0.000983 (IV-GMM, 10%)
results.evidence: Tables 5 and 6, row IQI*lnICT, col 4 and col 7; text: 'interaction effect is observed to be sensitive to the choice of ICT indicator' (abstract)

heterogeneity.finding: Mobile subscriptions are positively and significantly associated with HDI in high-income and lower-middle-income groups (PSCC-FE and IV-GMM); insignificant in low-income; upper-middle is insignificant in PSCC-FE and weakly positive (10%) in IV-GMM. Fixed telephones: negative in low-income, positive in high and lower-middle (PSCC-FE).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 8, p. 13 and Table 9, p. 15; text p. 12: 'high- and lower-middle-income countries show significant positive outcomes, while the effect is negative for low-income countries regarding fixed telephones'

heterogeneity.finding: Institutional quality (IQI) is positive for HDI in the full sample and in high and upper-middle income countries; negative in lower-middle income (both estimators). ICT x IQI interaction is negative in high and upper-middle income (IV-GMM) and positive in lower-middle income, i.e. ICT narrows the institution gap in poorer groups. Interaction signs differ between PSCC-FE and IV-GMM for upper-middle (mobile), so the pattern is estimator-dependent.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 8-9, pp. 13-15; text p. 13: 'ICT attenuates the impact of IQI in high and upper-middle-income countries but improves IQI in low- and lower-middle-income countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Quantile regression: mobile coefficient positive and similar in size at all three HDI quantiles (0.0062-0.0076); no clear gradient across the HDI distribution.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 7, p. 12, lnMOB row

income_group_results.low: Mobile: +0.00147 (ns), -0.00211 (ns). Fixed phone: -0.0108 (1%, PSCC-FE); +0.886 (1%, IV-GMM, implausible magnitude, no year dummies, R2 = -7.735).

n_specifications_reported: about 60 regression columns (Table 5: 7 mobile/fixed columns; Table 6: 7; Table 7: 18 quantile columns; Tables 8 and 9: 8 each, plus the three-estimator repetition)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: HDI is regressed on ICT and institutions with causal language ('impact', policy recommendations). Endogeneity is handled by one-period lags and an IV-GMM whose instruments are not described; lagging does not remove reverse causality (richer countries adopt more ICT). Hansen p-values are close to 0.05 for some groups (0.0566 low income; 0.0891 upper-middle). Country fixed effects are not clearly included (year dummies only are listed) although the estimator is called 'fixed effects'.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.3 p. 8; Tables 5-6 notes 'Endogeneity corrected using one-period lag of the regressors'; Table 6 and 9 Hansen rows; text lists only year dummies

exposure_measurement.why: ICT is log of absolute number of subscriptions (mean 35.4 million, max 1.75 billion), not per capita, so the measure largely tracks population size. Mobile and fixed telephone penetration is narrow ICT. Internet users is included as a separate control, which absorbs part of the ICT effect.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 4 p. 9 (summary statistics, lnMOB mean 35,446,936); Table 3 p. 6; Section 3.1 p. 7

selection_of_countries_years.why: Stated sample is 193 countries but estimation samples cover about 150 countries and are unbalanced (e.g. 1322 obs. for 152 groups in a 10-year window; IV-GMM 1173). Short 10-year window. Choice based on data availability. Country list in Appendix A has an apparent duplicate (Congo, Dem. Rep. listed twice).
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3 p. 5; Table 5 observations/groups; Table 6 observations; Table A1 p. 16 rows 39-40

outcome_measurement.why: HDI used as proxy for 'inclusive growth'; HDI is a composite of income, schooling and life expectancy that moves slowly and is partly interpolated; it does not measure distribution of gains, so 'inclusive' is a loose label. Fits family 5 (living standards beyond income) rather than distribution.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1 p. 6: 'we chose to proxy inclusive growth using the human development index from UNDP (2019)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications across three estimators, two ICT indicators, with and without IQI, interactions, and four income groups. Sign of fixed telephone effect flips between PSCC-FE (negative) and IV-GMM (positive). Some IV-GMM sub-sample estimates are implausible (low income fixed phone IQI -3.315, ICT 0.886, R2 -7.735, no year dummies). Reported F-statistics of 10^6 in Table 5 suggest a specification or reporting problem. The text claims robustness although results differ.
