specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 5, 6, 8, 9; Table 9 low-income fixed telephone column; text p. 11 'most of the findings of the IV-GMM results ... align with those of Table 5'

selective_reporting.why: All specifications appear in tables, so nothing seems hidden, but the narrative stresses favourable results and glosses over sign reversals and inconsistencies between text and tables (e.g. text says IQI is negative in 'low' income in Table 9 while the table shows an insignificant positive; text describes the Table 5 interaction as 'positive though statistically significant' for fixed telephones only). No pre-registration or robustness beyond estimator switching.
selective_reporting.evidence: Text p. 13 (Table 9 discussion) versus Table 9 IQI row; abstract versus Tables 5-6

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Published in Economies (MDPI), 2023, 11(4), 124. Text-extraction is garbled in the figure and introduction pages (duplicated overlay text), but tables are readable. Odd content: the PCA paragraph reports 'explains 682.41% of the common variance' while Table 2 gives 0.8241 (typo). Labour force participation coefficient flips sign across estimators and income groups (Tables 5, 8, 9). The Table 5 note says endogeneity is corrected by lagging regressors, but the model equations are written contemporaneously. IV-GMM instruments not named in the text. The text calls the Table 6 interaction for fixed phones 'positive' while Table 6 col 7 shows -0.000983 and the Table 7 discussion says it is negative. No instructions to the reviewer or other embedded directives were found in the paper text.

title: Impact of digitization on carbon productivity: an empirical analysis of 136 countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 136 countries (2000-2020) with own estimation; exposure is internet penetration (mobile phone penetration as robustness); outcomes are carbon productivity (GDP per kg CO2; families 1/6) and income inequality (family 4).
exposure_measure: Share of internet users in population (ITU), logged, as digitization level; mobile phone penetration rate used as substitute measure in robustness test (Table 1, p.6; Table 9, p.10).

sample.economies_or_groups: 136 countries across Europe, America, Asia, Africa, Oceania; selected for data completeness (list in Appendices, not in main text)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, middle, low by World Bank standards; middle not split into upper/lower)

design.estimator: Country fixed-effects panel regression (main), random effects and OLS comparisons, three-step mediation models, panel quantile regression (Q10-Q90), system GMM robustness; sub-sample regressions by region, income and human capital
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country fixed effects; controls GDP growth rate, urbanization, population density, renewable energy share; no year/time effects stated in Eq. (1); standard-error type (clustering) not stated

results.indicator: Carbon productivity (GDP per kg CO2, log); inverse of carbon intensity
results.estimate: 0.0687 (log-log elasticity; 1% rise in internet users raises CP by 0.0687%), FE with all controls
results.evidence: Table 8 col (6), p.9: 'For every 1% increase in digitization level, CP increases by 0.0687%'

results.indicator: Carbon productivity, mobile phone penetration as exposure (robustness)
results.estimate: 0.0930 (elasticity)
results.evidence: Table 9 col (1), p.10

results.indicator: Carbon productivity, system GMM (dynamic, endogeneity-robust)
results.estimate: 0.0211 (elasticity), N=2720; about one third of FE estimate
results.evidence: Table 9 col (2), p.10

results.indicator: Carbon productivity, quantile regression Q10 to Q90
results.evidence: Table 11, p.11: effect rises with CP quantile

results.indicator: Income inequality (log top-10% pre-tax national income share)
results.estimate: -0.0707 (elasticity: digitization lowers top-10% share)
results.evidence: Table 10 col (2), p.10: 'digitization has an inhibitory effect on income inequality'

results.indicator: Carbon productivity by region (Europe/America/Asia/Africa/Oceania)
results.estimate: not reported in text (shown only in Figure 5); text states largest in Europe, not significant in Africa, negative in Oceania
results.evidence: p.11: 'In African countries, the impact ... is not significant. In Oceanian countries, digitization has a negative effect on CP'

heterogeneity.finding: Effect of digitization on CP declines with income level: high 0.0849 > middle 0.0579 > low 0.0408, all significant at 1%.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.12: 'coefficients of digitization in high-income, middle-income, and low-income countries are 0.0849, 0.0579, and 0.0408'

heterogeneity.finding: Larger effect in high human capital countries (0.0907) than middle (0.0694) and low (0.0429); all p<0.01.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.12, Fig. 7 text

heterogeneity.finding: Region: strongest in Europe, insignificant in Africa, negative in Oceania. Quantile: effect grows across CP distribution.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.11, Table 11

n_specifications_reported: approximately 25 (7 benchmark columns, 2 robustness, 5 mediation, 5 quantiles, plus about 11 sub-sample regressions in figures)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('impact') but identification relies on country fixed effects only; Eq. (1) has no year effects, so common trends in internet use and carbon productivity can drive the result; no instrument; system GMM is the only endogeneity check, with Hansen p=1.000 (suggests instrument proliferation) and a coefficient about a third of the FE estimate.

exposure_measurement.why: Internet users share is a one-dimensional proxy for 'digitization'; mobile penetration used as alternative; does not capture intensity of use, data centres or energy use of ICT.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Independent variable section p.5; Table 9 p.10

selection_of_countries_years.why: 136 countries with complete data in 2000-2020; countries with missing data (for example Bahrain, Oman, Guyana) dropped; balanced panel; no sensitivity to sample. Text once says 163 countries.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Data sources p.6; Introduction p.2 ('163 countries')

outcome_measurement.why: Carbon productivity is GDP per kg of territorial CO2 (World Bank), a ratio outcome that can move with GDP and offshoring; income inequality uses top-10% share.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Controls added stepwise across seven columns with coefficient rising from 0.0210 to 0.0687; standard errors' clustering not reported; several preliminary tests (CIPS, cointegration) not reflected in estimator choice; mediation uses simple Baron-Kenny steps.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 8 p.9; Mediating effect model p.4-5

selective_reporting.why: Region and income heterogeneity coefficients are shown only in figures; negative Oceania result and insignificant Africa result are reported, but the lower GMM estimate is described as confirming robustness.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Scientific Reports. Internal inconsistencies: introduction says 163 countries, elsewhere 136; Table 1 source labels for DIG and INC appear swapped (WID vs ITU). Table 1 says ECO is logged but text says all variables except growth are logged. Mediation shares (22.36%, 26.34%) reproduce from reported coefficients. Technological innovation (R&D/GDP) mediator effect of digitization is only significant at 10% (0.0387, SE 0.0213), yet claimed as mediator. Digitization is a log of internet-user share with minimum -8.15 in descriptives. Income-group sub-samples pool upper- and lower-middle countries. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extractor.

title: Artificial intelligence and global carbon inequality: Addressing the challenges and opportunities for SDG 10, SDG 12, and SDG 13
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with own estimation (POLS, SYS-GMM, UQR, dynamic threshold) on 67 countries over 1995-2019; exposure is AI proxied by industrial robot stock per capita; outcomes are carbon inequality between and within countries (families 4 and 6). Meets the AI criterion of at least 3 economies. Weak AI proxy is a risk-of-bias issue, not an eligibility one.
exposure_measure: Per capita industrial robot stock (IFR World Robotics), logged (LNAI). Alternative proxy in robustness: new robot installations per capita (AI2). Authors concede robots are 'far from being a comprehensive indicator of AI' (Sec 4.2.2).

sample.n_economies: 67 (56 when GVC position is used)
sample.economies_or_groups: 67 countries with IFR robot data and WID/WDI data; the country list is given only in Fig. 3 (image, not in extracted text). Authors say sample 'mainly involve[s] countries with comparative advantages in AI development'.
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (no income-group split; sample selected on IFR robot data availability, likely skewed to high and upper-middle income)

design.estimator: Pooled OLS; system GMM (Blundell-Bond) dynamic panel as preferred baseline; unconditional quantile regression (RIF); SYS-GMM with AI-quantile dummies; SYS-GMM moderation (AI x moderator); dynamic panel threshold model (Seo et al. 2019, xthenreg) with TRADE, GVCP, GOV, IT as thresholds; IV-GMM robustness using lagged AI.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Inter-country model: lagged DV, oil price, natural resource rents, GDP per capita. Intra-country model: lagged DV, renewable energy share, tertiary-sector share, share of population aged 80+. No explicit country or year fixed effects reported; control sets differ between the two equations. Instruments are internal lags (GMM-style).

results.indicator: Inter-country carbon inequality (population-weighted absolute percentage deviation of per capita CO2 from 67-country mean), log
results.estimate: SYS-GMM LNAI = 0.0016 (log-log elasticity); POLS LNAI = 0.1708. Text says each 1% rise in AI raises inter-country CI by '0.00016%' (does not match table coefficient 0.0016).
results.evidence: Table 6, col (3) and (1); Sec 5.2: 'Each 1% increase in AI applications enlarges the inter-country carbon inequality by 0.00016%'

results.indicator: Intra-country carbon inequality (ratio of top-10% to bottom-50% emitters' carbon emissions, WID), log
results.estimate: SYS-GMM LNAI = 0.0130 (elasticity); POLS LNAI = 0.0132
results.evidence: Table 6, col (4) and (2); Sec 5.2: 'carbon inequality within countries is boosted by 0.0130%'

results.indicator: Carbon inequality (distribution of per capita CO2 emissions) as resource-cost / carbon outcome; the paper does not estimate AI effect on emissions level or carbon intensity directly
results.estimate: Same coefficients as above (0.0016 inter; 0.0130 intra)
results.evidence: Table 6; AI energy requirement is asserted as a mechanism (abstract 'due to its energy requirements') but no energy-use variable is estimated

results.indicator: Robustness: IV-GMM with lagged AI as instrument
results.estimate: Inter 0.0071; intra 0.0122
results.uncertainty: t = 12.836 and 21.450; Sargan p = 1.0000 in both
results.evidence: Table 9 col (1)-(2)

results.indicator: Robustness: alternative dependent variables (unweighted CI_INTER2; top1%/bottom1% CI_INTRA2)
results.estimate: Inter 0.0145; intra 0.0222
results.evidence: Table 9 col (3)-(4)

results.indicator: Robustness: alternative AI proxy (new robot installations per capita, AI2)
results.estimate: Inter 0.0059; intra 0.0175
results.evidence: Table 9 col (5)-(6)

results.indicator: Unconditional quantile regression: AI effect across distribution of CI_INTER (Q10-Q90)
results.evidence: Table 7 cols (1)-(5); note UQR coefficients are two orders of magnitude larger than SYS-GMM 0.0016 for the same outcome

results.indicator: Unconditional quantile regression: AI effect across distribution of CI_INTRA
results.evidence: Table 7 cols (6)-(10)

results.indicator: AI level non-linearity (dummies for AI above median / 75th percentile), inter-country CI
results.estimate: LNAI 0.0050; LNAI*Q50 +0.0164; LNAI*Q75 -0.0447 (net marginal effect at top quartile about -0.0233 by simple sum, not reported by authors)
results.evidence: Table 8 col (1); Sec 5.3: 'when AI level further surpasses the third-quarter value, the impact of AI can significantly decline and become negative'

results.indicator: AI level non-linearity, intra-country CI
results.evidence: Table 8 col (2)

heterogeneity.finding: Trade openness weakens AI's inequality-raising effect on inter-country CI: interaction LNAI*LNTRADE = -0.0163 (t = -14.804). Threshold model: AI effect turns from positive to negative above LNTRADE = 4.737 (log of trade/GDP).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: LNTRADE = 4.737 (about 114% trade/GDP in levels if natural log; only about 4.5% of country-years above it by 2019)
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 10 col (1); Table 11 col (1); Fig. 8 text 'in 2014, 20.9% of countries exceeded the threshold, but by 2019, this figure had fallen dramatically to 4.5%'

heterogeneity.finding: Global value chain position weakens AI effect on inter-country CI: LNAI*LNGVCP = -0.0176 (t = -12.271); LNAI main effect itself negative (-0.0233) in this specification. Threshold: b_LNAI 0.0067 below, 0.0067-0.1332 = -0.1265 above.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 10 col (2); Table 11 col (2); Sec 5.6 'changes to -0.1265, with a decrease of -0.1332'

heterogeneity.finding: Government size weakens AI effect on intra-country CI: LNAI*LNGOV = -0.0064 (t = -6.118). Threshold: 0.0031 below, 0.0031-0.0078 = -0.0047 above.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 10 col (3); Table 11 col (3); Sec 5.6

heterogeneity.finding: Institutional transparency (control of corruption index, logged) weakens AI effect on intra-country CI: LNAI*LNIT = -0.0111 (t = -15.518). Threshold: 0.0096 below, 0.0096-0.0098 = -0.0002 above, i.e. essentially zero, threshold only significant at 10%.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: LNIT = -0.2166 (p < 0.10 only; about 85% of sample above)

heterogeneity.finding: Level of AI development: effect on inter-country CI rises above the median and then reverses above the 75th percentile of robot density; intra-country effect stays positive throughout.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: AI quantiles Q50 and Q75 (values not reported)
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 8; Sec 5.3

n_specifications_reported: about 30 columns across Tables 6-11 (2 POLS, 2 SYS-GMM, 10 UQR, 2 AI-quantile GMM, 6 robustness, 4 moderation, 4 threshold); each tested on two dependent variables

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('AI significantly amplifies CI'). Identification relies on internal lags in SYS-GMM and a lagged-AI IV-GMM; authors admit reverse causality 'cannot be completely ruled out'. Sargan p-values of 0.95 to 1.0000 suggest instrument proliferation, so over-identification tests are uninformative. Models contain few controls (no education, institutions, trade or income distribution in the baseline) and controls differ between equations. Industrial-robot density correlates with income and manufacturing structure, which independently shape per capita CO2 distribution. No country or year fixed effects reported.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Sec 5.4 'it is difficult to completely rule out the possibility that the level of AI development ... is influenced by ... carbon emission inequality'; Tables 6, 9 (Sargan p = 1.0000)

exposure_measurement.why: AI is proxied by industrial robot stock per capita, which captures automation in manufacturing, not machine learning, deep learning or generative AI. Authors acknowledge it is not a comprehensive indicator. Interpreting robot density as 'AI development' and its 'energy requirements' is not supported by measures of AI compute or energy.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Sec 4.2.2; Table 1: 'measured by the per capita industrial robot stocks'; 'Although industrial robots are far from being a comprehensive indicator of AI'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 67 countries chosen by availability of IFR robot and GVC data, 'mainly countries with comparative advantages in AI development'; 56 countries for GVC models. No income-group analysis, so results cannot speak to low-income countries. Panel ends in 2019, before generative AI.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sec 5.1 and 6.3: 'the sample countries mainly involve countries with comparative advantages in AI development'; Table 3 footnote (LNGVCP 56 countries)

outcome_measurement.why: Inter-country CI is constructed by the authors from WDI per capita CO2 (territorial or production-based, not clearly stated; the paper's own framework speaks of consumption- and investment-based emissions). Intra-country CI (top 10% / bottom 50% emitters) from WID is modelled/imputed at the group level, not a direct survey measure. Both are heavily transformed (log of an absolute-deviation index) and the inter-country measure is a country-year deviation from the sample mean, so it depends on sample composition. The paper does not say how the global mean or WID series are defined by year.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Sec 4.2.1 (CI_INTER formula and CI_INTRA definition); Table 1 'calculated by the authors'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications (POLS, SYS-GMM, UQR, quantile dummies, moderation, thresholds, IV-GMM) with different control sets by outcome, hypotheses H1b/H2b/H3b all reported as 'confirmed'. Estimated effect sizes are extremely unstable across estimators for the same outcome (0.0016 SYS-GMM vs 0.1708 POLS vs about 0.15-0.18 UQR). Unit-root tests show mixed integration orders yet levels models are estimated and cointegration is invoked as justification. t-statistics of 100 to 1,800 (e.g. L.Y t = 1876.54, 378.68) are implausibly large for GMM output. Threshold in LNIT significant only at 10%.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 6 vs Table 7; Table 9 R2 L.Y t = 1876.54; Table 4 mixed I(0)/I(1); Table 11 col (4)

selective_reporting.why: Internal inconsistencies point to transcription or reporting errors: text '0.00016%' vs table 0.0016; Sec 5.6 reports TRADE threshold result using GOV numbers (d_LNAI -0.0078, net -0.0047) while Table 11 col (1) gives d_LNAI = -0.0665; Sec 5.5 says governance moderators reduce 'inter-country' CI when they concern intra-country CI; Table 11 'd_Cons.' equals b_LNAI exactly in every column; Table 8 L.Y has negative t-statistics with positive coefficients; Eq. (6) lags CI_INTER instead of CI_INTRA; Tables 9-11 lack N in some columns. All reported hypotheses confirmed; no null results or failed tests reported. No pre-registration.
selective_reporting.evidence: Sec 5.6 vs Table 11 col (1); Table 11 d_Cons rows; Table 8 L.Y '(-402.78)'; Sec 5.5 'inhibit the increasing effect of AI on inter-country carbon inequality'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Journal is Geoscience Frontiers (Elsevier, open access); no venue concern. No embedded instructions to the reader found in the text. Key cautions for synthesis: (1) AI exposure is industrial robots only; (2) outcome is carbon inequality, not emissions level or carbon intensity, so it is only indirectly a resource-cost result; (3) the main SYS-GMM inter-country elasticity (0.0016) is economically negligible and differs by about two orders of magnitude from POLS and UQR estimates, and the text misstates it as 0.00016%; (4) several textual and table inconsistencies (see selective_reporting) mean exact numbers should be treated cautiously; (5) threshold values are in logs (LNTRADE 4.737, LNGVCP -1.071, LNGOV 2.907, LNIT -0.217), and the abstract rounds them to 4.74, -1.07, 2.90, -0.22; (6) the country list is only in Fig. 3 (image) and could not be read from the text, and no income-group results exist. Heterogeneity by income group is therefore unavailable.

title: Does digital financial inclusion moderate or exacerbate output volatility?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of about 40 EMDEs (2009-2017) using mobile money usage (mobile-telephony-based digital finance) as exposure and output volatility as outcome (family 1). Meets sample size (>=10 economies) and own estimation. Exposure is mobile-money, a narrow proxy within mobile telephony; judged eligible but borderline on exposure scope.
technology: mobile telephony (mobile money / digital financial inclusion)
exposure_measure: IMF Financial Access Survey: MM1 = number of mobile money transactions per 1,000 adults (access); MM2 = active mobile money accounts (usage); alternative normalisations (value of transactions, accounts per population) mentioned in footnote 2 only.

sample.n_economies: about 40 (38 in baseline FE with MM1; 26 with MM2; 32 and 24 in system-GMM)
sample.economies_or_groups: Selected emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs); country list not reported in text; selection based on availability of digital financial inclusion data
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (EMDEs, mixed)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects (country and year) with robust SEs; Blundell-Bond system GMM with lagged dependent variable as robustness; split-sample FE by median banking concentration
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year FE; covariates lagged one year: ln GDP per capita, inflation, change in government expenditure, trade openness, terms of trade, financial openness, REER volatility, credit volatility, VIX; bank concentration (top-3 bank asset share) in extended models. Outcome: 3-year rolling SD of GDP per capita growth.

results.indicator: Output volatility (3-yr rolling SD of GDP per capita growth) vs MM1 mobile money transactions per 1,000 adults, two-way FE
results.estimate: 0.119 (MM1 coefficient)

results.indicator: Output volatility vs MM2 active mobile money accounts, two-way FE
results.estimate: 0.318 (MM2 coefficient)

results.indicator: Output volatility vs MM1, system-GMM
Output volatility vs MM2, system-GMM
Output volatility vs MM1 in low-concentration banking sample
results.estimate: 0.139 (MM1, low concentration); MM2 0.448
results.evidence: Table 3 cols (3) and (6), p.1807

results.indicator: Output volatility vs MM1/MM2 in high-concentration banking sample
results.estimate: MM1 -0.109 (marginally negative); MM2 -0.150 (not significant)
results.uncertainty: MM1 SE 0.0628, p<0.1; MM2 SE 0.238, insignificant; N=47 and 38
results.evidence: Table 3 cols (2) and (5), p.1807

heterogeneity.finding: Banking concentration: positive effect on volatility only in countries below median concentration (60% top-3 bank asset share); in high-concentration countries MM1 effect is small negative (p<0.1) and MM2 insignificant. Sample split, not an interaction term.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 and text p.1808: 'consistent and significant only for the low concentration sample'

heterogeneity.finding: Fin. development index does not substitute for digital financial inclusion (Fin Dev index insignificant in Table 4 specifications); no moderation by income group tested.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4, p.1808: 'Fin Dev Index 1.546 (4.567)'

n_specifications_reported: about 16 columns across Tables 1-4 (plus unreported robustness in footnotes)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal-sounding language ('exacerbates', 'amplifies'). Only strategy is one-year lags of covariates (note the digital finance variable itself appears in Table 1 unlagged: 'MM1' not 't-1'), country and year FE, and a system-GMM with a 120/75-observation sample and no reported instrument diagnostics (AR tests, Hansen). Short panel of 9 years; reverse causation (volatile economies adopting mobile money) not addressed.

exposure_measurement.why: Mobile money transactions and active accounts are direct but narrow measures of digital financial inclusion; they capture a mobile-money-specific channel, not mobile or internet adoption generally. Levels not scaled consistently (MM2 is accounts, not normalised in main tables); well-known to be dominated by a few countries such as Kenya.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section II p.1805; Table 1 footnote p.1806

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample chosen 'solely on consistent availability' of mobile money data; unbalanced and small (26-38 countries, 100-158 obs); country list not reported; sample size varies across columns, and countries with mobile money data are likely selected on mobile money activity.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section II p.1805: 'based solely on consistent availability of panel data'; Tables 1-3 observations

outcome_measurement.why: 3-year rolling SD of GDP per capita growth over 2009-2017 induces overlapping windows and mechanical serial correlation in a short panel; standard in literature but noisy.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section II p.1805: 'three-year rolling standard deviation of growth rate of GDP per capita'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Sample split at the median concentration is post hoc ('we conjecture'), quadratic concentration term mentioned but not shown, alternative measures only in footnote, column numbering in Table 1 skips (2). Controls appear to include lagged levels and VIX with differing coefficient magnitudes across columns (VIX 4.4 vs 0.40), suggesting scale or sample instability.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section III p.1807; footnotes 2 and 3; Table 1 header '(1) (3) (4)'

selective_reporting.why: Several key robustness results are reported as 'not shown' or 'available on request' (quadratic concentration term) or only in a footnote. Headline emphasis on significant results; some conflicting results (insignificant MM2 in high concentration; wrong sign of concentration) are reported, though.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Short letter (Applied Economics Letters, 6 pages). Sample list of countries not given. Table 1 has no column (2); text says 'Column (1) before introducing proxies in columns (2-3)' but table shows (1), (3), (4). System-GMM text claims lagged dependent coefficient 'close to zero' whereas Table 2 shows 0.346 and 0.194 (inconsistency). Abstract says result 'persistently' amplifies volatility but no long-horizon or dynamic analysis is reported. Outcome is volatility, treated as family 1 (output); negative-for-stability finding implies a payoff cost. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: What drives labor market polarization in advanced countries? The role of China and technology
decision_rationale: Quantitative industry-country panel estimates of the effect of ICT capital intensity on employment polarization and industry employment in 18-19 European economies (>=10 economies, non-AI technology). Outcome is labour market (family 3) with a reallocation element (family 2).
technology: ICT in general (ICT capital services per hour worked)
exposure_measure: Log of ICT capital services per hour worked by industry-country-year (EU KLEMS); R&D intensity, offshoring (foreign value added share of exports) and Chinese net import penetration are the other regressors.

sample.n_economies: 19 (stated in text and Table 1 note; footnote 5 and Table A1 list only 18 names, Norway appears only in the Table 1 note)
sample.economies_or_groups: European OECD countries: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Germany, France, Finland, Greece, Portugal, Spain, Netherlands, UK, Slovenia, Slovakia, Sweden, Czech Republic, Italy, Hungary, Ireland (+ Norway per Table 1 note)
sample.income_groups_covered: high (advanced European economies; Central European members are the newest high-income). No middle- or low-income economies.
sample.years: 1996-2007 for within-industry polarization regressions; 1998-2010 (ICT only to 2007) for employment growth regressions

design.estimator: Weighted (by industry employment share) OLS panel with industry x country fixed effects, with and without country x year fixed effects; long-difference and stacked-difference employment growth regressions with country (or country x period) FE; standard errors clustered by country (18-19 clusters).
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Industry x country FE; country x year FE in preferred columns; offshoring, R&D intensity, Chinese net import penetration; union density, EPL, Kaitz index in baseline columns only.

results.indicator: Within-industry polarization, manufacturing: ln(high-paid/mid-paid employment), preferred specification with country x year FE
results.estimate: 0.128 (log-log elasticity; text: a 10 percent rise in ICT capital services raises the high/mid-paid employment ratio by 1.28 percent)
results.evidence: Table 5 col (3) and p.13: 'A ten percent increase in ICT-induced technological change causes a 1.28% increase in high-paid employment polarization'

results.indicator: Within-industry polarization, manufacturing: ln(high-paid/mid-paid), without time effects
results.estimate: 0.250 (elasticity)
results.evidence: Table 5 col (1)

results.indicator: Within-industry polarization, manufacturing: ln(low-paid/mid-paid)
results.estimate: 0.113 (col 2, no time effects); 0.003 (col 4, country x year FE)
results.evidence: Table 5 cols (2) and (4); asymmetry noted on p.13: no association with low-paid polarization

results.indicator: Within-industry polarization, non-manufacturing private sectors: ln(high/mid) and ln(low/mid)
results.estimate: Without time effects: 0.185 (high) and 0.133 (low). With country x year FE: -0.049 (high) and 0.008 (low).
results.uncertainty: Cols 1-2: se 0.032 and 0.038, p<0.01. Cols 3-4: se 0.105 and 0.127, insignificant
results.evidence: Table 6; p.15: 'In columns (3) and (4) ... We find that all significance is lost.'

results.indicator: Share of manufacturing high-paid within-industry polarization explained by ICT (counterfactual from Table 5 col 3)
results.estimate: about 33 percent explained by ICT (Chinese import competition about 4 percent; together about 37 percent on average; 5 percent in Slovenia to 76 percent in Germany); counterfactual excludes Hungary, Czech Republic, Netherlands and countries with missing ICT/China data
results.evidence: p.14-15: 'ICT induced technical change, which explains on average around 33 percent of the high-paid employment polarization in manufacturing'

results.indicator: Change in log industry employment (between-industry reallocation), manufacturing, change in ln ICT (x100)
results.estimate: -0.057 (col 1, long difference 1998-2007); -0.030 (col 3, with polarization interaction)
results.evidence: Table 8 cols (1), (3); p.22: 'we find no proof that technological change played any role in this reallocation of labor' (Conclusion)

results.indicator: Change in log industry employment, non-manufacturing, change in ln ICT (x100)
results.evidence: Table 9 cols (1), (3), (5)

heterogeneity.finding: Country group: ICT effect on high-paid manufacturing polarization is weaker in Central Europe (ICT x Central Europe -0.267, p<0.05 in col 1) and Southern Europe for the low-paid margin; authors say the difference is not robust to a country-specific time trend. Reference group is core Western Europe.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 7 and p.17: 'In Central- and Southern-European countries the correlation between ICT intensity and high-paying employment polarization is often weaker'

heterogeneity.finding: ICT effect on within-industry polarization is robust in manufacturing under country x year FE (high-paid margin) but not in non-manufacturing, where all significance disappears under country x year FE.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 5 and 6, cols (3)-(4)

heterogeneity.finding: No clear role for labour market institutions (union density, EPL, Kaitz index) in explaining polarization; institution interaction results in Tables B1-B2 are mixed (appendix not read in full in the available text).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.17-18: 'industries in different countries seem to show differing degrees of sensitivity ... independent of the type of labor market institutions'

income_group_results.high: All 18-19 sample countries are advanced European economies; see results above (ICT raises high-paid relative employment within manufacturing).

n_specifications_reported: about 30 columns in main text (Tables 5-9 and 7), plus appendix robustness tables B1-B5 referred to in text

confounding_reverse_causation.why: ICT capital intensity is not instrumented; authors use causal language ('causes', 'more causal in nature') on the basis of country x year fixed effects only. Industry-specific demand shocks, wage changes that drive ICT investment, and reverse causation are not addressed. For the employment regressions the authors themselves acknowledge endogeneity concerns and keep specifications basic.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.13 'ICT-induced technological change ... causes a 1.28% increase'; p.16 'we can state with a sufficient degree of certainty that these relations are causal'; p.20 endogeneity paragraph on Chinese imports

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital services per hour worked from EU KLEMS is a reasonable industry-level measure of ICT investment/use, but it is an input measure and there is no ICT data after 2007; R&D is a weaker technology proxy and is sensitive to specification. Offshoring series is interpolated.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2.3 p.9-10; footnote 10; p.23 (no ICT data after 2007)

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 18-19 European high-income economies, 1996-2007 for ICT; countries with missing data dropped; three countries (Hungary, Czech Republic, Netherlands) discarded from the headline counterfactual because predictions were about twice the observed polarization. Results cannot speak to developing economies.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Footnote 5 and footnote 20 p.14; footnote 6-7 on sample end years

outcome_measurement.why: Polarization is measured from employment shares in ISCO occupational groups ranked by average wage (high/mid/low-paid), not from wages; coarse 8-group classification and ELFS industry cells; authors state no wage polarization data.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.4 'Since the data do not suffice to carry out an analysis on wage polarization ... entirely concentrated on ... employment polarization'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many columns and subsamples (manufacturing vs non-manufacturing, with and without time effects, country groups). ICT effect on the headline outcome is significant only for the high-paid margin in manufacturing and disappears in non-manufacturing and in the employment-growth regressions. Authors present the more demanding country x year FE column as the basis for the headline.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 5-9; p.15 'all significance is lost' for non-manufacturing

selective_reporting.why: Most results reported including nulls; however a decomposition of net import penetration is 'not reported here', some robustness material is in appendices, and the counterfactual drops several countries. Abstract emphasises the significant ICT result for manufacturing.
selective_reporting.evidence: Footnote 25 p.22 'In a separate analysis (not reported here)'; footnote 20 p.14

venue_quality_concern: possible (VIVES/KU Leuven discussion paper, October 2017, OECD-funded; not itself peer reviewed, and the assignment lists year 2018 so a later published version may exist and could be a duplicate)
notes: Text version is VIVES Discussion Paper No. 61 (October 2017) while the assignment lists 2018; check whether a journal version is also in the corpus (possible DUP). Internal inconsistencies: sample stated as 19 countries but footnote 5 and Table A1 list 18 (Norway only in Table 1 note); the abstract says Chinese imports explain about a fifth of manufacturing job loss, text says 21 percent; Table A2 note cross-references columns (5) of Tables 5/6 that do not exist and appear swapped; Table 3 contains a likely typo (-0.40). Sample sizes differ across the text (Table 5 N=1937 vs 2053 between columns). ICT is only one of four regressors (R&D, offshoring, Chinese imports); this record extracts the ICT results only. No text attempting to direct the reviewer was found.

title: The unequal implications of Industry 4.0 adoption: evidence on productivity growth and convergence across Europe
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (14 European countries x 13 manufacturing industries, 2009-2019) with TFP growth outcome, but the exposure is import stocks of advanced industrial robots, additive manufacturing and industrial IoT, which are not ICT in general, mobile, internet/broadband, crypto-assets or AI. ICT capital enters only as a control variable, not as the exposure of interest.
exposure_measure: Sectoral stock of imports of 8-digit CN capital goods embodying AIR, AM and IIoT, allocated to industries with 2008 input-output weights (WIOD), perpetual inventory with 15% depreciation, as share of value added (Section 4.2, Eq. 7).

sample.economies_or_groups: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Spain, Finland, France, UK, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, Sweden (note 7); 13 manufacturing industries
sample.income_groups_covered: high (all European; income groups not compared by the authors)

design.estimator: WLS fixed effects (within-groups) distance-to-frontier model; GMM, LSDVC and FGLS as robustness
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: country-industry and year FE; R&D, ICT capital and import shares of value added with distance-to-frontier interactions

n_specifications_reported: not applicable
venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Screening had marked this INC. Excluded at full text on E2 because the exposure is Industry 4.0 capital goods (robots, AM, IIoT) rather than a listed technology; a reviewer who treats IIoT as ICT may reconsider. For reference only: headline Table 4 col (7), p. 1060, I40(t-1) = 0.329 (SE 0.102) with I40 x lnDTF = -0.313 (SE 0.089), 1760 obs; authors note reverse causality cannot be ruled out (Section 5.3, p. 1065). The Table 4 ICT capital control is positive in 2009-2019 (col 7: 0.491, SE 0.234) but is a control, not an identified exposure. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: The impact of the digital economy on green total factor productivity in Belt and Road countries: the mediating role of energy transition
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 40 Belt and Road economies (2006-2021) with its own estimation; exposure is an ICT-based digital economy index (broadband, fixed and mobile telephony, internet use, ICT trade); outcomes are green TFP (output, energy and CO2 based) and renewable energy shares.
technology: ICT in general (composite digital economy index: fixed broadband, fixed telephone, internet users, cellphone users, e-participation, ICT goods trade)
exposure_measure: Digital economy index (DE) built by principal component analysis from 10 indicators in four groups (infrastructure, social impact, digital trade, social support) and rescaled to 0-1; note that the index includes medium/high-tech manufacturing value added and per-capita service value added. Robustness uses the UN Online Service Index.

sample.economies_or_groups: Belt and Road countries in Europe/Central Asia/Caucasus, West and South Asia and ASEAN (e.g. Albania, Azerbaijan, Egypt, India, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, Russia)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, middle, low; income class assigned year by year using World Bank annual classification; low-income has only 16 observations)

design.estimator: OLS with country and year fixed effects, between-dimension panel FMOLS, panel-corrected standard errors (PCSE), DOLS (robustness), spatial Durbin/lag/error models with inverse-distance weights, three-step mediation model, lagged DE terms
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year fixed effects; controls lnFDI, lnService (service share), lnUrban, lnIC (industrial concentration), lnRGDP (GDP per capita)

results.indicator: Green total factor productivity (super-SBM with undesirable CO2 output, Global Malmquist-Luenberger) regressed on digital economy index, linear model
results.estimate: Fixed-effects OLS with controls: DE = -0.425 (Table 9 col 2); FMOLS -0.339 (col 3); PCSE -0.425 (col 5). DE scaled 0-1, GTFP mean 1.118 (Table 3). Authors read this as a 0.1 rise in DE lowering GTFP by about 0.04.
results.evidence: p.11 Table 9. 'columns (1), (3), and (5)... are consistently negative'; text oddly says 'a 0.1 decrease in DE will cause GTFP to decline by approximately 0.04'

results.indicator: GTFP on DE and DE squared (non-linear / U-shape)
results.estimate: PCSE: DE = -1.017, DE2 = +0.782 (Table 9 col 6); FMOLS: DE = -1.602, DE2 = +1.567 (col 4). Implied turning point about 0.5-0.65 of the index; net effect stays negative over the 0-1 range.
results.uncertainty: PCSE t = -7.56 and 5.53; FMOLS t = -5.903 and 5.135 (both p<0.01)
results.evidence: p.11 Table 9 and text: 'the total contribution of the digital economy to GTFP is consistently negative'

results.indicator: GTFP on lagged DE (1, 2 and 3 years)
results.evidence: p.11 Table 10; 'three-order lag term of DE has a significantly positive effect on GTFP'

results.indicator: Renewable energy consumption share (REC) and renewable generation (REG) on DE (energy transition mediator)
results.estimate: DE -> REC = 0.136; DE -> REG = 20.29 (Table 11 cols 1-2). REC -> GTFP = 0.157; REG -> GTFP = 0.001. DE coefficient on GTFP stays about -0.40 in both mediation columns (-0.404 and -0.408).
results.uncertainty: t = 2.79 and 3.31 (p<0.01); REC t = 2.80; REG t = 2.77. No Sobel or bootstrap test of indirect effect reported.
results.evidence: p.13 Table 11: 'digital economy can significantly raise REC and REG'

results.indicator: GTFP on DE, spatial Durbin model (direct, indirect, total effects)
results.estimate: SDM DE = -0.963, DE2 = +0.963 (Table 13 col 3). Direct DE = -0.962; indirect (spillover) DE = +4.803; total DE = +3.841; total DE2 = -3.157 (Table 14). Table 14 total effect is positive although the text says the total effect is negative.
results.uncertainty: SDM t = -2.55 / 2.39; direct t = -2.48; indirect t = 2.12; total t = 1.73 (p<0.1). R2 only 0.027 (SDM).
results.evidence: p.14 Tables 13-14; text: 'within the range of sample values, the total effect of the digital economy on GTFP is negative'

results.indicator: GTFP on DE with alternative exposure (UN Online Service Index) and robustness (pre-COVID sample, DOLS)
results.estimate: Online service index -0.161 (no controls) and -0.204 (with controls); DE excl. 2020-21: -0.374 / -0.463; DOLS DE -0.266, quadratic spec -1.299 with DE2 +1.182
results.evidence: p.16 Table 17

heterogeneity.finding: DE lowers GTFP in high-income (-0.860) and middle-income (-1.240) countries, larger in middle-income; low-income coefficient -6.305 is not significant (only 16 observations).
Region: negative and significant in the EU-group (-0.662) and non-ASEAN Asia (-0.287); positive but insignificant in ASEAN (0.212).

Non-linearity in DE: negative effect strengthens until DE about 0.6, then diminishes but net effect remains negative. Energy transition (renewables) partly offsets the negative effect (claimed, not formally tested).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.11: 'the turning point nearly occurs at DE equal to 0.6'

income_group_results.low: -6.305 (t -1.66), not significant, N=16 only (Cambodia, India, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan in early years)

n_specifications_reported: about 28 columns across Tables 9-17

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Fixed-effects panel with no instrument or exogenous timing; causal language ('will cause a decline'). DE index contains components (service value added per capita, medium/high-tech manufacturing share) that overlap with GDP per capita control and with the GDP output used in GTFP. Mediation is a plain three-step regression.

exposure_measurement.why: Composite PCA index of ICT infrastructure and use is a reasonable ICT proxy, but it mixes in non-ICT structural variables and uses fixed telephone and e-participation; weights from PCA not reported; rescaled to 0-1 so coefficients are hard to compare.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 40 Belt and Road participants chosen by data availability, not representative of the world; only 16 low-income observations; missing data filled by interpolation and regression; unbalanced samples (N 587-654).
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Abstract; Sec 3.2.3 'Missing data are supplemented by interpolation'; Table 16 N=16

outcome_measurement.why: GTFP is a DEA-derived index with CO2 as the only undesirable output; capital stock built by perpetual inventory with assumed 6% depreciation; GTFP is described both as a level and as a growth index (GML), leaving the interpretation unclear.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many estimators (OLS, FMOLS, PCSE, DOLS, SAR/SEM/SDM) and lag choices; sign of effect changes with lag (L3 positive). Panel unit-root table shows GTFP and DE as I(0) but text says all variables are order-one stationary; some variables I(1) yet levels are regressed. Tiny within R2 in FMOLS (0.216) and SDM (0.006-0.027). Textual cross-references to tables are wrong (mediation 'Table 6', DOLS 'Table 15').
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 7 p.10; Table 9 p.11; Table 13 p.14

selective_reporting.why: Headline says total effect is negative, but Table 14 reports a positive total DE effect (+3.841) and the 3-year lag is positive. Table 11 shows the direct DE coefficient barely moves after adding the mediators, so 'mediation' is not demonstrated. Paper is explicit about its limits (no dynamics, other mediators).
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 14 p.14 vs text p.14; Table 11 p.13; Limitations p.16

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Frontiers in Environmental Science (open access); a correction dated 02 July 2026 is stamped on the first page ('minor changes'). Internal inconsistencies to check: text says 'a 0.1 decrease in DE will cause GTFP to decline by approximately 0.04' while the coefficient is negative (an increase lowers GTFP); Table 14 total effect positive vs text negative; Table 9 col 1 OLS R2 0.763 with no controls; Table 15 text refers to DOLS but DOLS is in Table 17. GTFP is both productivity (family 1) and CO2-adjusted (family 6). Negative DE-GTFP result is opposite to most of the cited literature. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: Informality and aggregate labor productivity growth: Does ICT moderate the relationship?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 118 economies (1997-2017) with its own fixed-effects estimation; exposures are ICT capital deepening and internet penetration; outcome is aggregate labour productivity growth (family 1) and the study compares advanced vs emerging and developing economies.
technology: ICT in general (ICT capital services per worker)
exposure_measure: (a) ICT capital services per worker (hardware, communication equipment, software; perpetual inventory with hedonic deflators based on US ICT deflators), entered as growth rate (delta ln kIT) and log level (ln kIT); (b) change in percent of population using the internet (World Bank WDI). ICT is a moderator of informality's effect (interaction terms).

sample.economies_or_groups: Conference Board TED countries: 38 advanced economies and 80 emerging and developing economies (Table 1); 13 TED countries dropped for missing data
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (advanced vs emerging and developing; the latter spans upper-middle, lower-middle and low income plus Gulf high-income states; author notes grouping does not match World Bank income groups)
sample.years: 1997-2017 (11 countries start later, e.g. Myanmar and Yemen 2011, Ethiopia 2012)

design.estimator: Fixed-effects panel regression of labour productivity growth with country-clustered robust SEs; informality x ICT interactions; separate samples for global, emerging and developing, advanced. Also Jorgensonian growth accounting (descriptive, Table 3).
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year fixed effects; non-ICT capital deepening growth, employment growth, labour quality growth, change in internet penetration, change in institutional index (WGI PCA), change in trade openness. Variables in growth rates or first differences.

results.indicator: Interaction of change in informality with ICT capital deepening LEVEL (dINF x ln kIT) on labour productivity growth, global sample
results.estimate: Vulnerable emp .144; self-employment .179; agricultural emp .087; informal VA .383 (percentage points of productivity growth, coefficient units as in Table 5)
results.uncertainty: SE .082 (p<.10) for vulnerable; SE .091 (p<.10) for self-employment; SE .058 and .331 not significant for the other two
results.evidence: Table 5, p.14; text p.15: 'positive and significant only for ICT capital deepening levels when informality is measured using vulnerable and self-employment shares'

results.indicator: Interaction dINF x ln kIT, emerging and developing economies
results.estimate: Vulnerable .183; agricultural .117; self-employment .205; informal VA .183 (not significant)
results.uncertainty: SE .104, .067, .116, all p<.10; informal VA SE .347 not significant
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16; text p.17: 'coefficient of the interaction term is positive and statistically significant, with the size of the effect ranging from 0.12 to 0.2'

results.indicator: Interaction dINF x growth of ICT capital deepening, emerging and developing economies
results.estimate: Self-employment .017; vulnerable .013; agricultural .005; informal VA .028
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16; text p.17: 'significant only in the model with self-employment shares'

results.indicator: Interaction dINF x change in internet penetration (all samples)
results.estimate: Global: -.076 to .025; emerging and developing: -.048 to .024; advanced: -.175 to .072
results.uncertainty: Insignificant except advanced agricultural-employment model (.072, SE .036, p<.10)
results.evidence: Tables 5-7, pp.14,16,17; text p.17: 'interaction coefficient of changes in internet penetration is relatively small, statistically insignificant'

results.indicator: Direct effect of ICT capital deepening growth on labour productivity growth (global, with interactions)
results.estimate: Delta ln kIT: .042 (VA model), .026, .026, .029; advanced sample .055-.065
results.evidence: Table 5, p.14; Table 7, p.17; text p.15: 'growth rate of ICT capital deepening had a statistically significant and positive impact'. Coefficient is conditional on interaction terms evaluated at zero change in informality.

results.indicator: Direct effect of ICT capital deepening LEVEL on labour productivity growth (global)
results.uncertainty: SE .293, .307, .31, .308; significant at p<.05 in employment models for vulnerable and agricultural, p<.10 for self-employment
results.evidence: Table 5, p.14; author attributes to catch-up logic: 'levels of ICT capital deepening had a negative and statistically significant coefficient in all the employment share models' (p.14-15; self-employment is only p<.10)

results.indicator: Direct effect of change in internet penetration on labour productivity growth
results.estimate: Global .009 to .023; emerging and developing .012 to .037; advanced -.001 to .038
results.uncertainty: Global and EDE SEs .021-.042, insignificant; advanced .031* and .038** in two employment models
results.evidence: Tables 5-7, pp.14,16,17; text p.15: 'changes in internet penetration had a positive but statistically insignificant coefficient in all models'

results.indicator: Interaction dINF x growth of ICT capital deepening, advanced economies
results.estimate: Vulnerable -.027; agricultural -.034; informal VA -.144; self-employment -.024
results.evidence: Table 7, p.17; text p.17: 'ICT capital growth is negative and significant in two out of four models'

results.indicator: Moderation using informality-decline dummy: dINF_D x ln kIT, global and emerging and developing (robustness)
results.estimate: Global: .472, .375, .533 (employment measures), .199 (VA, ns); emerging and developing: .499, .488, .559, .351 (VA, ns)
results.uncertainty: Global SE .119, .133, .136 (p<.01); emerging and developing SE .187, .186, .197 (p<.05 to p<.01)
results.evidence: Tables A1-A2, pp.19-20; footnote 20 p.17: 'the moderating effect of ICT capital deepening levels becomes stronger'

results.indicator: Main effect of change in informality on labour productivity growth (baseline, no ICT interaction), global
results.estimate: Informal VA +.933; vulnerable -.545; agricultural -.407; self-employment -.518
results.evidence: Table 4, p.14; text p.13: informal VA 'positive impact ... significant at 10 percent' while employment measures 'negative and significant'

results.indicator: Main effect of change in informality, emerging and developing vs advanced (with interactions in model)
results.estimate: EDE: VA -.633 (ns), vulnerable -1.755, agricultural -1.139, self-employment -1.848; advanced: 7.422, .032, .148, -.755 (all ns)
results.evidence: Tables 6-7, pp.16-17; text p.15: 'impact is insignificant for all measures for the advanced group'. Coefficient is conditional on interaction terms.

heterogeneity.finding: Positive moderating effect of ICT capital deepening levels on informality's drag appears in emerging and developing economies (.12-.21) and is absent in advanced economies, where the level interaction is insignificant and the growth interaction is negative in two models. Informality's own effect is negative and significant only in emerging and developing economies.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 6-7, pp.16-17; text p.17: 'positive interaction effect of ICT appears to be unique to the emerging & developing economy sample'

heterogeneity.finding: Results depend on the informality proxy: employment-based proxies (vulnerable, self-employed, agricultural share) give significant main effects and level interactions; informal value-added share gives null or wrong-signed results throughout.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 4-6; text p.15: 'the value added measure also gains a negative, albeit insignificant, coefficient'

heterogeneity.finding: Direct effect of ICT capital deepening growth is larger in advanced (.055-.065) than in global or emerging and developing samples (about .02-.04); author cites this as consistent with higher ICT returns in richer countries.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 7 vs Table 6, p.15-17; text p.15: 'coefficient of ICT capital deepening growth is slightly higher in the advanced economies sample'

income_group_results.high: Advanced economies (38; grouping is Conference Board, not World Bank income): informality has no significant effect; ICT capital growth positive direct effect (.055-.065, p<.05); interaction with ICT capital growth negative in two models; ICT level interaction insignificant; internet interaction positive only in agricultural model (p<.10).
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group of 80 economies, which also includes high-income Gulf states)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group; author notes low-income countries likely dominate the group results)

n_specifications_reported: 24 regression models in main tables and appendix (6 tables x 4 informality proxies), plus an unreported lagged-ICT-level variant (footnote 18) and growth-accounting decomposition

confounding_reverse_causation.why: No instrument or event timing. Author argues first differences mitigate reverse causality (footnote 9) but concedes no suitable instrument for informality; ICT capital deepening and internet use are plausibly endogenous to productivity and informality. Conclusions use causal language ('ICT investment ... can help reduce the negative impact of informality').

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital services rely on US hedonic deflators adjusted by domestic inflation and a steady-state initial stock, so cross-country measurement error is likely; internet penetration captures mostly consumer use (author's own point). Informality proxies are weak (modelled value-added share; self-employment, vulnerable employment and agricultural share are indirect). Author notes the macro measures do not show ICT adoption within the informal sector.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.3-3.5 pp.7-8, footnote 13 p.7; Section 6 p.18: 'we implicitly assume that the informal sector is gradually incorporating ICT'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 118 of 131 TED countries retained; 13 dropped for missing data and 11 begin late (unbalanced panel). Data-poor and fragile economies likely under-represented. Author notes the advanced / emerging split is not income-based, and EDE group mixes Gulf high-income and low-income countries.

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity is GDP (PPP) per person engaged, not per hour; labour quality is partly econometrically imputed; TED data for developing countries rely on national accounts of uneven quality. Well-established source overall.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1-3.2, pp.7; footnote 6 p.5; footnote 17 p.13

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four informality proxies x three ICT moderators (growth, level, internet) x three samples; ICT level and its interaction added after referee suggestion; dummy-informality variant and unreported lagged-level variant. Interaction significance at p<.10 only, with many tests and no multiple-testing adjustment. Models in growth rates with country FE as well as year FE (author acknowledges FE are redundant in first differences). Signs and significance change with proxy.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 2.2, pp.5-6 and footnote 8; Tables 5-7; footnotes 18 and 20, pp.15,17

selective_reporting.why: All main tables show full coefficient sets, including null results, and the abstract says evidence is 'some' and 'modest'. However the lagged-level results (footnote 18) are not reported, the conclusion foregrounds the significant level interactions in employment-based models, and the VA-based null results and negative advanced-economy interactions are given little weight in the conclusions.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p.1; footnote 18 p.15; Section 6, p.18

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Included for family 1 (labour productivity growth); the study's primary question is a moderation effect of ICT on informality's drag, not the average effect of ICT, so direct ICT coefficients are conditional on interaction terms. Significance stars are at 10 percent for most key interaction results (author's table note: *p<.1). Internal inconsistencies noted: observations are 2411 in Table 4 but 2374 in Tables 5-7 and in the Table 2 note (791 + 1583 = 2374); text refers to 'equation (10)' for the perpetual inventory formula which is equation (5); footnote 9 says informality measures are 'four' while the text says 'three different indicators' in Section 3.5; Table 7 coefficient layout is garbled in the text extraction (row labels misaligned with coefficients) so Table 7 values for non-ICT capital, employment, labour quality, internet, institutions and trade were not used. Text states Table 6 effect range 0.12-0.2, which matches the table. The Table 5 text says level effect negative and significant in 'all' employment models but the self-employment model is only p<.10. No instruction-like content in the paper text.

title: Does artificial intelligence help in improving human capital based educational development? Evidence from 29 countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (FE, 2SLS, mediation) of AI development (Stanford Global AI Vibrancy score) on a schooling and education-quality index in 29 countries, with explicit developed/developing comparison. Meets AI sample rule (>=3 economies) and outcome family 5 (schooling), with a family 4 mediator (inequality).
technology: artificial intelligence (national AI development / vibrancy composite)
exposure_measure: Stanford Global AI Vibrancy Tool total score (8 pillars, 42 indicators), scaled 0-1 (original scaled down by 100%); robustness: Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, six AI pillar scores, 12 individual AI sub-indicators in logs (Sections 4.1, 5.4; Tables 4, A.2). Instruments: industrial robot stock/installations/total count.

sample.economies_or_groups: Mainly OECD and BRICS economies (e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, Malaysia, Turkey, Singapore, US, Japan, European countries); full list only shown in Fig. 1 panels
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (mostly high income; developing group includes large emerging economies); World Bank income groups not used, 'developed' vs 'developing' split only
sample.unit: country-year (analysed as country-month after quadratic interpolation; N=1740 in Table 2, 1734 in regressions)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects OLS (country and 'year' FE); subsample regressions (developed/developing; COVID/non-COVID); 2SLS with industrial-robot IVs; Sobel-Goodman mediation; PSM mentioned
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE, time FE; controls: ln GDP per capita, CPI growth, FX rate, personal expenditure growth, unemployment, population growth, and five Legatum education-quality sub-indices (adult, pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary)

results.indicator: HCBED index (World Bank HCI education component adjusted for learning-adjusted years of schooling and returns to education) on AI Vibrancy Index, full sample FE
results.estimate: 0.084 (HCBED units per unit of AI index, 0-1 scale; text misdescribes as 'a 1% increase in AI ... 0.084 increase')

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, developed-country subsample
results.uncertainty: SE 0.023, ** (p<0.05) in Table 3; text says significant at 10%
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (3), p.8; N=358; text p.8: 'coefficient for developed countries is 0.058, significant at the 10% level'

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, developing-country subsample
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (2), p.8; N=1376

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, COVID period (2020.01-2021.12)
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (4), p.8; N=690

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, pre-COVID period (2017.01-2019.12)
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (5), p.8; N=1044; text p.9: 'coefficient is negative (-0.024)'

results.indicator: HCBED2 (recomputed with HDI mean years of schooling) on AI
results.evidence: Table 4 Model (6), p.11

results.indicator: HCBED on Government AI Readiness Index
results.estimate: 0.004 per index unit (units not defined)
results.evidence: Table 4 Model (7), p.11

results.indicator: HCBED on AI pillars (separate regressions): Diversity, Education, Policy and Governance, Economy positive; R&D and Infrastructure not significant
results.estimate: Diversity 0.010, Education 0.009, Policy 0.002, Economy 0.000 (rounded, significant), R&D -0.000, Infrastructure 0.001 (ns)
results.evidence: Table 4 Models (8)-(13), p.11

results.indicator: HCBED on 12 individual AI sub-indicators (logs)
results.estimate: Significant positive: Legislative mentions 0.000, Study programs 0.002, Study program penetration 0.002, Strategy presence 0.001, Newly funded companies 0.004, Private investment 0.002, Journal publications 0.022, Patent grants 0.002; not significant: AI talent concentration, notable ML models, internet speed; gender equality 0.000*
results.uncertainty: SE reported per column, e.g. journal publications 0.005
results.evidence: Table A.2, p.19; each in a separate regression with different N (992-1734)

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, 2SLS with industrial-robot instruments (stock, installations, total count)
results.estimate: 0.260 (robot stock), 0.179 (robot installations), 0.244 (total robots)

results.indicator: Income inequality (Gini, OECD data) regressed on AI (mediator equation)
results.estimate: 2.400 (Gini units not specified)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16, Mechanism test (1): 'Economic_inequity 2.400*** (0.2966)'

results.indicator: Mediation via economic inequality: direct effect 0.057, indirect effect 0.027, total 0.084 (Sobel-Goodman)
results.estimate: indirect 0.027 (about one third of total effect)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16; text p.15: 'direct effect ... 0.057, while the indirect effect ... 0.027'

results.indicator: Education inequality (Legatum component) regressed on AI, and mediation via education inequality (indirect effect on HCBED)
results.estimate: AI -> education inequality 0.567; education inequality -> HCBED -0.006; indirect -0.003; direct 0.088; total 0.084
results.uncertainty: AI->edu inequality SE 0.3105 (p<0.1); -0.006 SE 0.0016 (p<0.01); indirect SE 0.002 (p<0.1)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16, Mechanism test (2): 'Sobel-goodman mediation tests ... -0.003*'

heterogeneity.finding: Positive significant effect in 'developed' subsample (0.058, N=358), no significant effect in 'developing' subsample (-0.031, N=1376). Authors attribute this to lower AI penetration per capita and infrastructure/education access limits. Subsample is not a formal interaction test and the classification criterion is not stated.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Models (2)-(3) and text p.8-9; Fig. 3 per-capita AI index

heterogeneity.finding: Time period: coefficient is +0.172 during COVID-19 (2020-21) and -0.024 in 2017-19; authors interpret as AI-enabled remote education and shift from substitution to assistance. Pandemic-period education quality measures may be affected by other contemporaneous shocks.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Models (4)-(5), p.8; text p.9

heterogeneity.finding: AI dimension: Education, Diversity, Policy & Governance and Economy pillars positively related to HCBED; R&D and Infrastructure pillars not significant.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4 Models (8)-(13), p.11; text p.11

income_group_results.high: Not reported by World Bank group; 'developed' subsample (N=358, about 6 countries by obs/60): AI coef 0.058 (SE 0.023)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately; pooled in 'developing' subsample: AI coef -0.031 (SE 0.034), not significant
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately; pooled in 'developing' subsample (e.g., India): not significant
income_group_results.low: not covered (authors state low-income countries lack data)

n_specifications_reported: about 35 (5 subsample models, 8 robustness models, 12 sub-indicator models, 3 IV models, 2 mediation sets)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('AI influences HCBED', 'solves the two-way causality issue'). The IV is industrial robot stock/installations, whose exclusion from education outcomes is argued only briefly and is doubtful (robots proxy for general economic/industrial development and can affect education demand through wages and automation exposure). Only about 1 year of within-country variation in a 5-year window; PSM is mentioned but no PSM results are reported. Controls include Legatum education-quality sub-indices that are components of the outcome.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5.4 p.13, Table 5 p.14: 'use of industrial robot prevalence as an instrumental variable (IV) is appropriate and justified'; Table 3 controls Pre_edu, Prim_edu etc.

exposure_measurement.why: AI Vibrancy score is a composite of R&D, investment, talent, policy and infrastructure indicators for the national ecosystem, not adoption or use in education. Authors concede possible 'generalization bias'. Index is dominated by country size (total, not per capita) and shows little within-country variation. Weighted pillars include internet speed and supercomputers.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 4.1 p.4; Limitations p.18: 'using the AI Vibrancy Index as a proxy for AI's influence on educational development may introduce a degree of generalization bias'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 29 countries chosen by availability of returns-to-education estimates and AI indicators, mostly OECD/BRICS; only five years (2017-2021); no low-income and few lower-middle-income countries; developed subsample covers only about 6 countries (358 obs / 60 months), developing about 23, which contradicts the stated mix and the selection criterion for 'developed' is not given.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 5.1 p.5; Table 3 observations 1376 vs 358; Limitations p.18

outcome_measurement.why: HCBED is the authors' own constructed index combining years of schooling, quality scores from Legatum, and country-specific returns to education from single-country literature estimates (which vary little over time). Annual data (index, AI score) are converted to monthly by quadratic interpolation, creating 1740 country-months from about 145 country-years, which artificially inflates N and deflates standard errors. Education quality drawn from a rankings index.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 5.1 p.6: 'transformed certain annual and quarterly variables into monthly frequency using quadratic interpolation'; Table 2 N=1740; Section 4.2 p.4-5

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Standard errors do not appear clustered by country; observations are interpolated monthly and 'Year FE' on monthly data is unclear; highly collinear controls (VIF 8.4 for lnGDP, about 6.8 for adult/primary/secondary education quality); many subsample and indicator regressions; sub-indicators estimated one by one in logs; Table 6 R2 around 0.99 vs 0.598 in Table 3 for the same specification, unexplained. Interpretation misstates units ('1% increase').
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 2 VIF column p.7; Table 3 p.8 'Standard errors in parentheses'; Table 6 p.16 R-squared 0.9916 vs Table 3 0.598

selective_reporting.why: Positive full-sample result is emphasised, but null developing result, negative pre-COVID result, and non-significant pillars/IV-related caveats are reported. PSM is announced but not reported; text reports the developed coefficient 0.058 as significant at 10% while the table marks 5%, and some tables show coefficients rounded to 0.000. Full country list and classification not tabulated.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 5.4 p.13 'implementing the propensity score matching strategy' with no PSM table; Table 3 vs text p.8

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Elsevier Technology in Society 2025. Outcome is education/human capital (family 5); inequality mediator (family 4) is a secondary result. Several internal inconsistencies for a human reviewer: 1740 vs 1734 observations; Table 2 N inflated by interpolation; text speaks of 'within the specified 20 months' and 'HCBED ... from over 0.6 to less than 0.8' while data span 60 months; text says 'a 1% increase' but variables are in levels on a 0-1 scale; developed coefficient significance mismatch (** in table, 10% in text); R2 0.9916 in Table 6 vs 0.598 in Table 3 for the same model; Hypothesis 1 states AI contributes to HCBED 'by aggravating income inequality' based on a Sobel test with Gini on unclear scale and no mediator-to-outcome identification. Coverage of income groups: no low-income and few lower-middle-income countries, so evidence on the 'payoff' for poorer countries is thin. No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

title: ICT and Productivity Growth in Transition Economies: Two-Phase Convergence and Structural Reforms
decision_rationale: Quantitative growth-accounting and shift-share study of ICT capital, ICT production and ICT use on labour productivity growth for about 23 economies (8 CEE/Russia, 14 EU-15, US), so it meets exposure, sample and outcome rules. It is purely descriptive and largely reuses estimates from Van Ark and Piatkowski (2004), so own estimation is limited.
technology: ICT in general (ICT capital, ICT-producing and ICT-using industries)
exposure_measure: Contribution of ICT capital deepening to labour productivity growth (percentage points, growth accounting); labour productivity contribution of ICT-producing and ICT-using industries (shift-share); ICT penetration (phones, mobiles, PCs per 1000) used only inside a reform indicator.

sample.n_economies: 23 in Table 1 (8 CEE/Russia, 14 EU-15 members, US); industry decomposition only for 4 CEE countries, Russia, EU-15 aggregate and US
sample.economies_or_groups: Bulgaria, Czech Rep., Hungary, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia; EU-15 (14 countries shown); United States
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (mix of transition and advanced economies; paper gives no income classification)

design.estimator: Growth accounting (Cobb-Douglas, share-weighted inputs) and shift-share industry decomposition; descriptive comparison of averages; one fitted log line (R2 = 0.05) in Figure 2
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: none; no regression controls. Reform indicators (composite z-score of 3 to 4 variables) are compared by rank only.

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT capital to annual labour productivity (GDP per person employed) growth, 1995-2001
results.estimate: CEE average 0.6 pp of 3.5% LP growth (17% share); EU average 0.4 pp of 1.1% (36%); US 0.7 pp of 2.2% (34%); Czech Rep. 0.8, Hungary 0.7, Romania 0.3, Russia 0.1 pp
results.uncertainty: not reported (accounting contributions, no standard errors)
results.evidence: Table 1, p.10-11: 'ICT capital intensity' column (3); CEE row 0.6, European Union row 0.4

results.indicator: Contribution of TFP growth to labour productivity growth
results.estimate: CEE average 2.0 pp vs EU 0.3 pp and US 1.1 pp (TFP, not ICT specifically, is the largest convergence source)
results.evidence: Table 1, column (4); text p.12: 'most important source of convergence ... has been the higher contributions of total factor productivity'

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT-producing industries to labour productivity growth
results.estimate: US 0.98 pp, EU-15 0.58, Czech Rep. 0.68, Hungary 0.68, Poland 0.21, Slovakia 0.15, Russia 0.08 pp
results.evidence: Table 2, p.15

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT-using manufacturing and ICT-using services to labour productivity growth
results.estimate: ICT-using manufacturing 0.46 to 0.98 pp in CEE vs about 0 in EU-15 and US; ICT-using services -0.58 to 0.92 pp in CEE vs 0.47 EU-15 and 1.29 US
results.evidence: Table 6, p.22: 'ICT Using Manufacturing' and 'ICT Using Services' rows

heterogeneity.finding: Structural reform composite indicators (A1 for phase 1, A2 for phase 2) are ranked alongside ICT contributions; countries with higher reform scores (Czech Rep., Hungary, Slovenia) show larger ICT contributions than Romania and Russia. No statistical test.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 6 p.26 and Tables 4, 7; 'insufficient observations to carry out a comprehensive statistical analysis'

heterogeneity.finding: Within CEE, countries with higher productivity levels show somewhat larger ICT capital contributions; fit is weak.
ICT contribution is concentrated in manufacturing (restructuring phase); ICT-using services in CEE and EU-15 lag the US.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 5, p.20-23

income_group_results.high: not reported (EU-15 and US, treated as advanced comparators, ICT capital 0.3 to 0.8 pp)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (income groups not assigned by the paper)

n_specifications_reported: not applicable (no regressions; about 8 tables of accounting results)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Descriptive accounting with causal narrative ('ICT led to a divergence rather than convergence', two-phase hypothesis); no strategy against reverse causation or omitted factors such as FDI, privatisation and labour shedding, which the authors themselves say drive TFP.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 6 p.26-27; footnote 4 p.4 on labour shedding

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital services via growth accounting is a recognised measure, but CEE ICT deflators are based on US deflators excluding computers and semiconductors, and Russia's data are 'not fully comparable'.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Footnote 15 p.13; note to Table 2 p.15

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 8 transition economies, selected by data availability; industry-level results for only 4 CEE countries plus Russia; short window 1995-2001 at the dot-com peak; the reform-linkage inference rests on 8 to 10 observations.

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity as GDP per person employed (real estate excluded) is standard, but Russian industry classification and sources differ and growth periods differ across countries (1993 vs 1995 start).
outcome_measurement.evidence: Note to Table 5 p.21; period headers of Tables 2 and 6

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Industry grouping into ICT-producing, ICT-using and other and the composite reform indices (equal-weight z-scores) involve analyst choices; no robustness checks reported.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 4 note p.18; Table 7 note p.24

selective_reporting.why: Results are descriptive and reported for all included countries, but most numbers are lifted from the authors' earlier work and the narrative stresses favourable cases (Czech Rep., Hungary).
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 3 p.10 'Piatkowski (2004) and Van Ark and Piatkowski (2004) provide growth accounting results'

venue_quality_concern: possible (TIGER working paper / MPRA deposit, not peer reviewed)
notes: Footnote 3 says the paper builds on Van Ark and Piatkowski (2004), GGDC Research Memorandum GD-69, and Tables 1 and 5 to 6 take their figures from that source and from Perminov and Egorova (2004) for Russia; check overlap with GD-69 if that paper is also in the corpus (possible DUP of numbers, not of the paper). Table 1 has 14 EU-15 rows (Luxembourg absent). A footnote refers to 'Table 4' but means Table 1. Authors state the reform hypothesis is not statistically tested. No instruction-like text found.

title: Does ICT Participate in Economic Convergence among Asian Countries: Evidence from Dynamic Panel Data Model
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel (system GMM) study of 24 Asian economies relating a composite ICT index (fixed and mobile telephony, broadband, internet) to income per capita and convergence; meets the 10-economy threshold for non-AI technology and the output outcome family.
technology: ICT in general (composite index of fixed telephone lines, mobile cellular subscriptions, fixed broadband, fixed internet subscribers, internet users)
exposure_measure: ICT Maturation Index (ICTMI) = fixed telephone lines per 100 + 0.2 x (mobile subscriptions per 100 + fixed broadband subscribers + fixed internet subscribers per 100 + internet users per 100), from ITU 2011 (Table 1, p.9). Also an interaction ICTSERT = ICTMI x tertiary enrolment.

sample.economies_or_groups: 24 Asian countries incl. Bangladesh, Brunei, China, Indonesia, India, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Cambodia, Korea, Kuwait, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Philippines, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Thailand, Tajikistan, Yemen (p.11)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (list spans high-income, middle-income and low-income Asian economies; paper gives no income classification)
sample.years: 2000-2010 per text (abstract says 2001-2010); estimation uses 216 observations

design.estimator: Two-step system GMM (xtabond2, small-sample correction) on a dynamic conditional-convergence model of log GDP per capita; Windmeijer-type robust errors implied
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged income, initial income YPC(0), tertiary enrolment interaction, population aged 15-64, urban population, trade openness, electricity consumption per capita, year dummies; country effects removed by GMM transformation. ICT goods imports (% of goods imports) used as an additional external instrument.

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita (PPP, constant 2005 intl $) on ICT Maturation Index
