results.estimate: 0.0119 (coefficient on ICTMI in system GMM; paper reads it as 0.119% income per 10% ICTMI, though the functional form of ICTMI, logged or in levels, is unclear)

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita on ICT x tertiary enrolment interaction (ICTSERT)
Conditional convergence: initial income coefficient YPC(0) in ICT-augmented model
results.estimate: -0.0584 (lagged income coefficient 0.9617, SE 0.0487)

heterogeneity.finding: Positive and significant ICT x tertiary-enrolment interaction: ICT is more productive where tertiary enrolment is higher. Not tested against secondary enrolment (ICTSERS dropped without estimation).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.13 'ICTSERT ... statistically significant and has positive influence on national income'

heterogeneity.finding: Electricity consumption (coefficient 1.2082, p<0.001) is described as complementary to ICT, but no ICT x electricity interaction is estimated.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 'electricity consumption has strong complementarily with ICT'

n_specifications_reported: 1 (a single system GMM table, Table 4); OLS/IV/Hausman diagnostics only as tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM is the only identification strategy. Instrument count (30) exceeds number of countries (24), contradicting the paper's own rule of thumb that instruments should not exceed groups; Hansen p=0.222 is therefore weak evidence. ICT goods imports as external instrument is not credibly excluded from income. The initial-condition regressor YPC(0) is time-invariant and would be absorbed by country effects in a standard setup. Causal wording ('ICT participates in convergence') with a lagged-income coefficient of 0.96.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.12 Table 4 'Instruments = 30 ... Countries = 24'; p.12-13 instrument discussion; p.12 'Number of instruments < number of observations' only

exposure_measurement.why: Composite index with ad hoc weights (1 for fixed lines, 0.2 for others) and overlapping components (fixed internet subscribers, broadband subscribers, internet users); Table 1 defines internet users using mobile broadband subscriptions (definitional error). Functional form (log or level) of ICTMI not stated though results are read as elasticities.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 24 Asian economies chosen by data availability; short panel (about 9 usable years, 216 observations); includes oil exporters and small economies. Text elsewhere says i=1..11 and 11 years, inconsistent with 24 countries.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.10 'dimensions of dataset are 24 countries ... 11 years ... mostly dictated by the availability of data'; p.10 'i = 1, ..., 11'

outcome_measurement.why: Log GDP per capita PPP from WDI, but the paper variously calls the dependent variable GNI, GDI and GDP; table header says 'Gross National Income'.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.9 Table 1 row 1; p.12 Table 4 header; p.10 'per capita gross domestic income (GDI)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Single specification reported, so little visible forking, but model choices (instrument set, which variables treated as endogenous, ICT weights, logs) are not documented and no sensitivity to instrument count or lag depth is shown. HDI is listed in abstract and Table 1 but absent from the estimated model.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.12 Table 4; abstract mentions human development

selective_reporting.why: Only the favourable model is shown; ICTSERS (secondary enrolment interaction) was 'not empirically tested'; no OLS/FE/difference-GMM comparisons reported. Interpretation misreads coefficients (constant -0.1483 described as the initial condition; trade coefficient is negative, but text calls trade 'positive contributor').
selective_reporting.evidence: p.13 'ICTSERS is not empirically tested'; p.13 'initial condition variable comes with a negative sign (-0.1483)'; p.14 'Trade openness ... positive contributor ... (-0.558%...)'

venue_quality_concern: possible (regional journal, Informatica Economica; numerous internal inconsistencies between text and tables, e.g., 11 vs 24 countries, 2000 vs 2001 start, dependent variable naming)
notes: Convergence interpretation is questionable: lagged income coefficient is 0.9617 (little adjustment) and the initial-condition regressor is collinear with fixed effects. Economic magnitude is small: coefficient 0.0119 on ICTMI with SE 0.0052. Income-group classification of the 24 countries is not given by the paper, so no income-group split is possible. No injected instructions found in the text.

title: Technological Learning, Policy Regimes and Growth in a `Globalized' Economy: General Patterns and the Latin American Experience
decision_rationale: Largely a conceptual and narrative essay with descriptive tables and correlations. The ICT section (Section 4) only reports diffusion statistics and runs no estimation of ICT effects on any outcome. The one calibrated model (trade/technology multiplier) concerns trade liberalisation and technology gaps in 7 Latin American countries, so the exposure is also outside the ICT scope (E2 would also apply).
exposure_measure: not applicable (ICT diffusion shown descriptively: Internet users, PCs, mobile subscribers, ICT investment shares; main empirical object is trade liberalisation and a productivity-gap multiplier)

sample.n_economies: not applicable
sample.economies_or_groups: OECD, NICs and Latin America in descriptive tables; 7 Latin American countries in the multiplier model
sample.income_groups_covered: not applicable

design.estimator: not applicable (descriptive statistics, pairwise correlations in Tables 4-5, period-average elasticities in Tables 16-20)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: not applicable

n_specifications_reported: not applicable

confounding_reverse_causation.why: excluded

exposure_measurement.why: excluded

selection_of_countries_years.why: excluded

outcome_measurement.why: excluded

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: excluded

selective_reporting.why: excluded

venue_quality_concern: possible (LEM working paper, Sant'Anna School; not a peer-reviewed journal version)
notes: Section 4 states 'the impact of the ICT revolution is still quite limited and asymmetric' but supports this only with descriptive tables (Tables 8-15, Figs 4-5). Section 5.2 and Appendix estimate trade/technology multipliers for Latin America. Text is a LEM working paper (2004/01). No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: The Effect of Technology Adoption on Financial Inclusion: A Cross-country Panel Analysis between China and Nigeria
decision_rationale: Panel of 20 countries (2005-2020) estimating the association of internet use and mobile cellular subscriptions (plus ATMs) with financial inclusion (family 5), with own estimation; meets the at-least-10-economies rule for non-AI technologies.
technology: ATMs (not a listed technology; covariate of interest)
exposure_measure: Individuals using the internet (% of population), mobile cellular subscriptions (per 100 people), ATMs (per 100,000 adults); World Bank data (pp.4-5).

sample.economies_or_groups: China, Nigeria plus 18 'randomly selected' countries (Poland, Botswana, Ecuador, Uganda, Burkina Faso, Zimbabwe, Tunisia, Singapore, Argentina, Seychelles, Uzbekistan, Haiti, Rwanda, Cote d'Ivoire, Zambia, Lesotho, Turkey, Georgia)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low); no income-group classification stated in paper

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, fixed effects, random effects and feasible GLS (FGLS, correcting heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation) for three separate models, each interacting one technology variable with China and Nigeria dummies
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: GDP growth, GDP per capita, unemployment rate, population; FGLS has no country effects; FE column has country effects; no year effects; variables in levels

results.indicator: Financial inclusion (commercial bank depositors per 1,000 adults) on internet users, baseline group (18 other countries), FGLS
results.estimate: 2.33 depositors per 1,000 adults per unit of internet users (levels; paper misstates as '2.33%')
results.evidence: Table III col (4), p.6: INTT 2.33(0.000)

results.indicator: Financial inclusion on mobile cellular subscriptions, baseline group, FGLS
results.estimate: 0.70 (levels; Table V gives 0.71)
results.evidence: Table III col (4), p.6; Table V col (4), p.8

results.indicator: Financial inclusion on ATMs (supplementary, not a listed exposure), baseline group, FGLS
results.evidence: Table III col (4), p.6

results.indicator: Internet x China and internet x Nigeria interaction (difference from baseline), FGLS
results.estimate: China 10.42, Nigeria 4.18 (differences relative to the other countries, not country-specific effects)
results.evidence: Table IV col (4), p.7

results.indicator: Mobile x China and mobile x Nigeria interaction, FGLS
results.estimate: China 4.38, Nigeria 2.63 (differences relative to baseline)
results.evidence: Table V col (4), p.8

results.indicator: Fixed-effects interactions (contradict FGLS)
results.estimate: ATM x China 10.78, mobile x China 21.26, internet x Nigeria 36.88
results.evidence: Table III col (2) p.6; Table IV col (2) p.7; Table V col (2) p.8

heterogeneity.finding: China (upper-middle) and Nigeria (lower-middle) are contrasted with the other 18 countries by dummy interactions; under FGLS the differences are statistically insignificant, while FE gives several significant differences. The authors interpret insignificant interactions as 'insignificant positive effects' in China and Nigeria, which is a misreading of interaction terms.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section D, p.8: 'the coefficient is insignificant, therefore there is no difference between China and Nigeria'

income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (China only, via interaction; insignificant under FGLS)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported (Nigeria only, via interaction; insignificant under FGLS)

n_specifications_reported: 12 regression columns (3 models x 4 estimators)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('effect', 'impact', 'engender') with levels regressions; headline FGLS has no country or year effects; reverse causation (banking development drives ATMs, internet and mobile use) not addressed; Hausman test favours FE but FGLS (pooled) is used for inference.

exposure_measurement.why: Internet users and mobile subscriptions are standard World Bank measures; mobile subscriptions are SIM counts (values up to 198 per 100), not users; ATMs used as a technology proxy though outside the listed exposures.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 20 countries, said to be chosen 'at random' but selected with China and Nigeria as focal cases, no sampling frame given; the 18 comparison countries are heterogeneous; period limited to 2005-2020 by ATM availability.

outcome_measurement.why: Single supply-side indicator: depositors with commercial banks per 1,000 adults; does not capture mobile-money or digital accounts; range 0.999 to 3000.9 in descriptives, with negative minimum for ATM (-3.1) implying data errors.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four estimators and three models; results diverge across estimators (FE vs FGLS) and the one favoured is not the one chosen by the diagnostic test; coefficients in levels but interpreted as percentages; inconsistent diagnostics (Wooldridge F(1,19) vs F(1,9); sign flip on POPL in Table V RE).

selective_reporting.why: Country-difference conclusions rest on FGLS only, while significant FE interactions are not discussed; conclusion that technology raises inclusion 'regardless of income level' is not tested.

venue_quality_concern: possible (European Journal of Business and Management Research; short article with interpretation errors and table inconsistencies; not clearly indexed in leading economics databases)
notes: Interaction terms are misread as country-specific effects, so the headline statement that technology has 'insignificant positive effects' in China and Nigeria is not supported by the design. Table I has garbled entries (POPL mean 9.4, min 82858, max 1.4; ATM min -3.1). Table III FE shows '1..54' typo. Abstract says GDP growth negative. Hausman and Breusch-Pagan results conflict (text says LM favours pooled OLS in one place and random effects in another). Financial inclusion is the only outcome (family 5); no income-group classification beyond the China/Nigeria dummies. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extractor.

title: Total Factor Productivity, Demographic Traits and ICT: Empirical Analysis for Asia
decision_rationale: System GMM panel of 24 Asian countries (2000-2010) with a composite ICT index as exposure and TFP as outcome. Meets ICT exposure, at least 10 economies and an output/productivity outcome; income groups are mixed within Asia.
technology: ICT in general (composite maturation index including fixed broadband, internet, fixed telephone, mobile)
exposure_measure: ICTMI = ICT Maturation Index, author-constructed composite inspired by the ITU ICT Development Index; the listed components are fixed broadband subscribers, fixed internet subscribers, internet users, fixed telephone lines and mobile subscriptions per 100. Construction method (weights, scaling) not reported. ICTSERT = ICT x tertiary enrolment interaction.

sample.economies_or_groups: Asian countries, 'few DCs and mostly UDCs'; country list not reported
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (not reported by group)

design.estimator: Two-step System GMM (xtabond2) with small-sample and robust options, lagged TFP as regressor
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged TFP, ICT x tertiary enrolment, population aged 15-64, urban population share, HDI, time dummies. ICT goods imports (% of goods imports, ICTM) named as external instrument. 29 instruments for 24 countries.

results.indicator: TFP on ICT Maturation Index (ICTMI)
results.estimate: 0.0156 (units and any log transformation not reported; TFP construction uses unreported factor share)
results.evidence: Table 5 (p.11) ICTMI 0.0156; coefficient on lagged TFP 0.9394

results.indicator: TFP on ICT x tertiary enrolment (ICTSERT)
results.evidence: Table 5 (p.11); text p.12 says significance 'only at 10%', which conflicts with the table

heterogeneity.finding: Positive ICT x tertiary enrolment interaction: ICT is more productive where tertiary enrolment is higher. Main effect of tertiary enrolment alone is not in the reported model.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5; p.12 'ICT has complementarity with tertiary level of education'

heterogeneity.finding: Urban population share positively related to TFP (0.0713, p=0.009); working-age share (0.0135, p=0.186) and HDI (0.0117, p=0.821) not significant. These are controls, not interactions with ICT.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 (p.11)

n_specifications_reported: 1 System GMM specification (IV tests shown in Tables 2-3 only for diagnostics)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with lagged TFP and an ICT-goods-import instrument addresses endogeneity in principle, but the instrument's validity is argued only through Hansen tests; 29 instruments versus 24 countries (instrument proliferation) and a Hansen p of 0.935 suggest weak diagnostics. AR(1) p=0.077 is not rejected at 5%.

exposure_measurement.why: Composite ICT index covers several ICT forms but its construction is not documented; the interaction term ICTSERT is included without the tertiary enrolment main effect.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.8-9 on ICTMI; Section 7 p.11 definition of ICTSERT

selection_of_countries_years.why: 24 Asian countries chosen 'depending on availability of data'; list not given; short 11-year window.

outcome_measurement.why: TFP is a residual 'YCD - alpha L - (1-alpha) K' with the factor share and the capital measure unreported, and units are not stated.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Only one final model is shown; no robustness checks, alternative lags or exclusion of the interaction. GMM tables (Table 4) and Table 1 are missing from the text and the table numbering jumps.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table numbering Tables 2, 3, 5 only; Table 5 p.11

selective_reporting.why: Text misstates results: says HDI is 'positive and statistically significant' while Table 5 gives p=0.821; says ICTSERT significant at 10% while table gives p=0.000; third C-test p given as 0.222 in text vs 0.822 in Table 5; text cites 240 observations while table shows 216.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Implied long-run effect of ICTMI from the dynamic coefficients would be about 0.0156 / (1 - 0.9394) = 0.26, but the paper does not report this; it is my arithmetic and not an extracted result. The paper cites Roodman (2009) as a source for the ICT-import instrument, which is a paper on too many instruments and does not appear to propose that instrument. Population aged 15-64 is described as 'youth' in the text. No embedded instructions to the reader were found in the text.

title: Digital Divide, Credit Financing and Financial Inclusion: Changing Patterns of Poverty, Employment and Income Inequalities
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel regressions on up to 148 countries with internet use, mobile payments and fintech credit as exposures and poverty, Gini, labour force participation, unemployment and growth as outcomes. Meets exposure, sample and outcome criteria.
technology: mobile telephony (mobile phone used to pay bills)
electronic payments / fintech and big-tech credit flows (context)
exposure_measure: INTRNT = individuals using the internet (% of population, WDI); MBLPMT = mobile phone used to pay bills (% age 15+, Global Findex); ELCPMT = electronic payments (% age 15+); FINTCBIG = credit flows by fintech and big tech companies (% of GDP); CRCRD = credit card users (% age 15+). Table 5.

sample.n_economies: 148 stated overall; regressions use 62 to 155 depending on table (70, 62, 64, 147, 148, 95, 155)
sample.economies_or_groups: Global unbalanced sample; countries not listed. Descriptive tables by World Bank region and by high/middle income.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (not reported by group in the regressions)
sample.years: 2008-2021 stated; individual tables use 2013-2019, 2008-2019, 2008-2020, or 2021 cross-section

design.estimator: Panel Least Squares (unbalanced) for Tables 7-12; OLS cross-section for Tables 13-14. Five alternative 'options' per equation, adding controls.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Controls vary by option: ease of doing business, domestic credit to private sector, GDP per capita or GDP growth, interest spread, NPL, new business density, corruption, tax rate. The estimating equation shows country and time effects, but tables do not report FE and the text says 'pooled data'; unclear whether FE were used.

results.indicator: Poverty headcount ratio at national lines (PVRTY) on internet users
results.estimate: -0.17 (option I) to -0.22 (options IV, V) percentage points of poverty per 1 pp internet users; -0.13 in option II
results.evidence: Table 7 (p.34), 70 countries, 235 obs, 2013-2019; text p.32 'significant and robust in all alternative options'

results.indicator: Poverty headcount ratio on fintech and big-tech credit flows (% GDP)
results.evidence: Table 7 (pp.33-34), FINTCBIG row

results.indicator: Gini index on internet users
results.estimate: -0.08 (I) to -0.13 (II, V) Gini points per 1 pp internet users
results.evidence: Table 8 (p.34), 62 countries, 336 obs, 2008-2019

results.indicator: Income share of lowest 20% on internet users and on mobile payments
results.estimate: INTRNT 0.01 (t=1.76 in I, 1.78 in III, insignificant in IV-V); MBLPMT 0.08 (II)
results.uncertainty: t = 1.76, 1.78, 1.29, 1.38 for INTRNT; t = 2.11 for MBLPMT
results.evidence: Table 9 (p.35), 64 countries, 361 obs; weak and not robust across options

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate on internet users and on mobile payments
results.estimate: INTRNT 0.08 (I), 0.06 (III), -0.03 (V, insignificant); MBLPMT 0.36 (IV), 0.25 (V) pp
results.uncertainty: t = 6.76, 2.96, -0.89 for INTRNT; t = 3.31, 2.47 for MBLPMT
results.evidence: Table 10 (pp.35-36), 147 countries, 1386 obs; INTRNT loses significance in option V

results.indicator: Unemployment rate on internet users
results.estimate: -0.03 (I), -0.01 (II), -0.01 (IV), -0.03 (V) pp per 1 pp internet users
results.evidence: Table 11 (p.36), 148 countries, 1529 obs, adjusted R2 0.05-0.09

results.indicator: Unemployment and labour force participation on fintech/big-tech credit flows
results.estimate: -0.32 on unemployment (one option); 1.08 and 1.65 on participation
results.evidence: Tables 10-11; text p.33 'flow of credit by fintech and big tech companies (FINTCBIG) are not significant'

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on fintech/big-tech credit flows
results.estimate: 0.86 to 1.15 pp growth per 1 pp of GDP in credit flows
results.evidence: Table 12 (p.37), 95 countries, 594 obs, 2013-2019

results.indicator: Perceived ability to arrange emergency funds in 30 days (30PSBL) on electronic payments and credit cards
results.uncertainty: t-statistics as given; p < 0.01 implied by three stars
results.evidence: Table 13 (p.37), OLS cross-section 2021, 155 countries; perception data

heterogeneity.finding: No interaction or subsample regression by income group. Only descriptive regional/income-group tables (Tables 1-4) are given, showing lower internet use and financial access in South Asia and lower-income groups.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 3-4 (pp.27-28), descriptive only

n_specifications_reported: approximately 40 columns (8 equations x up to 5 options)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Paper itself says the model has simultaneity (Figs 1-2) yet uses no instrument or timing strategy and gives causal language ('alleviate poverty'). Controls are ad hoc and change by option; FE use is unclear. Internet use and credit track national income.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4, p.30 'Simultaneity in the Model'; p.31 'Panel (unbalanced) Least Square (PLS)'

exposure_measurement.why: Internet users (% pop) is a standard measure; mobile payment and e-payment come from Findex survey waves (few years, merged with annual panel); fintech credit flows have narrow coverage and appear only for subsets of countries and years.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Unbalanced, availability-driven samples that differ strongly by table (62 to 155 countries); countries not listed. Cross-sections state 155 countries although paper says 148.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 4 p.31 'data of other countries could not be included'; Tables 7-14 headers

outcome_measurement.why: Poverty at national lines and Gini are sparse survey based and not comparable across countries; small within-country variation. Labour outcomes are WDI modelled series. Perception outcomes are survey based.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 5 definitions; Table 7 note 'national poverty lines'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Eight equations with different regressor sets, five options each, regressors dropped across options (internet and mobile payments never entered together), low adjusted R2 in several equations. 'Falsification tests' are only added controls.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 4 pp.30-31; p.32 'To conduct some falsification tests, some control variables have also been included'

selective_reporting.why: Conclusions say fintech credit creates employment and cut unemployment, while Tables 10-11 show FINTCBIG insignificant. Text says mobile payment lowers Gini but Table 8 reports no MBLPMT. Abstract says 'statistically significant and parameters are robust' although several coefficients lose significance across options.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; p.38 'effectiveness of the use of financial technology in poverty alleviation and creating employment'; Tables 8, 10, 11

venue_quality_concern: possible (article history shows received July 4, revised July 10, accepted July 13, 2023, a nine-day review cycle; single author affiliated with an employers' federation; many unrelated references)
notes: Internal inconsistencies: text says 8 equations in one place and '6 equations' in another; text says 'lowest 40 percent' for LWST20; equation numbers 8 and 9 cited for tables 8 and 9; abstract reports 148 countries while Tables 13-14 report 155. Table 7 column labels and several cells are misaligned in the converted text, so coefficient-to-option mapping for Tables 7, 11 and 12 is approximate. The data note states poverty and Gini results are 'robust'; this is the author's wording, not a tested result. Fintech credit is not one of the review's named exposures but internet and mobile payment are. No embedded instructions to the reader were found in the text.

title: TECHNOLOGICAL SOURCES OF ECONOMIC GROWTH IN EUROPE AND THE U.S.
decision_rationale: Own quantitative growth-accounting decomposition (statistical and model-based) of labour productivity and GDP growth in 10 OECD economies, separating ICT-specific technical change from non-ICT; meets the 10-economy minimum and family 1 (output and productivity). Borderline: decomposition and calibration, not regression estimation, and all economies are high income.
technology: ICT (investment-specific technical change in ICT capital: hardware, software, communication equipment)
exposure_measure: ICT investment-specific technical change, from quality-adjusted relative investment prices (EU KLEMS prices; non-ICT series built from Cummins-Violante US prices via Schreyer method); weighted by ICT capital or investment shares in growth accounting

sample.economies_or_groups: Austria, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, UK, US
sample.income_groups_covered: high only

design.estimator: Growth accounting (Solow, Jorgenson, Hulten) plus calibrated general-equilibrium balanced-growth decomposition; shares calibrated from cost shares, no regression
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Separate contributions of non-ICT capital, structures, labour hours and human capital (labour quality index); country-specific calibration of factor shares

results.indicator: ICT investment-specific technical change contribution to annual GDP growth, Jorgenson method (percentage points)
results.estimate: 0.22 to 0.39 pp per year across countries (Denmark 0.39, Sweden 0.33, US 0.31, Germany 0.22); 9.2% to 18.9% of GDP growth
results.evidence: Table 5, p. 1192, row 'ICT (a)'

results.indicator: ICT investment-specific technical change contribution to annual GDP growth, Hulten method (percentage points)
results.estimate: 0.39 to 0.63 pp per year (US 0.63, Denmark 0.63, Italy 0.39); 16.0% to 30.5% of GDP growth
results.evidence: Table 6, p. 1193, row 'ICT (a)'

results.indicator: ICT technical change contribution to labour productivity growth, equilibrium decomposition (percentage points)
results.estimate: 0.41 to 0.67 pp per year (US and Denmark 0.67, Italy 0.41); 15.8% to 49.5% of productivity growth (US 41.9%, Netherlands 49.5%, Austria 20.0%)
results.evidence: Table 7, p. 1194, rows 'ICT'

results.indicator: Relationship of TFP contribution to ICT intensity (cross-country and over time)
results.estimate: not reported (qualitative); strong negative correlation between ICT growth and TFP growth over time in high-ICT-growth countries
results.evidence: Section 3 Discussion, p. 1196: 'no evidence that the relative contribution of TFP depends on whether the country is an intensive user of ICT assets'

heterogeneity.finding: ICT contribution is similar in size to non-ICT contribution on average; largest ICT contributions in Denmark and the US, largest non-ICT in Germany. No income-group or institutional moderator tested (all high income).
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 2.4, p. 1194-1195: contributions of ICT and non-ICT technical change are 'of similar magnitude'

income_group_results.high: ICT technical change adds roughly 0.4 to 0.7 pp per year to labour productivity growth (equilibrium decomposition, Table 7)

n_specifications_reported: 3 statistical accounting methods plus 1 equilibrium decomposition (4 decompositions, by country)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Growth-accounting decomposition is an accounting identity with calibrated weights, interpreted as 'determinants' of growth; ICT contribution depends on the assumed weighting and does not address endogeneity of ICT investment.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3, p. 1195: ISTC contribution 'highly sensitive to the statistical method employed'

exposure_measurement.why: ICT technical change inferred from quality-adjusted investment price declines; non-ICT price series constructed by transferring US quality adjustment to Europe; ICT is one component, not adoption itself.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Ten high-income countries chosen by availability of EU KLEMS data; no developing economies; Spain's catch-up overlaps the sample.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p. 1180: 'only a subset of the countries reported in EU KLEMS has the variety of data required'

outcome_measurement.why: GDP and labour productivity from EU KLEMS national accounts.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Results vary by accounting method (Jorgenson ICT share 9-19% vs Hulten 16-31%); TFP turns negative in 7 of 10 countries under Hulten. Methods are all reported rather than one chosen.

selective_reporting.why: All three methods and the equilibrium decomposition are reported for all ten countries; no uncertainty measures provided.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Borderline for 'own estimation': descriptive decomposition and calibration, no standard errors or regressions. Included because it computes ICT-specific contributions to growth from data for 10 OECD economies. Abstract states ISTC explains over 50% of productivity growth on average; Table 7 shows 36% to 110% by country. Paper reports an ICT-TFP negative time correlation without a figure. Minor typographical inconsistency in Table 5 ('13..9'). No instruction-like text in the paper.

title: The Determinants of Total Factor Productivity in the EU: Insights from Sectoral Data and Common Dynamic Processes
decision_rationale: Own panel estimation (augmented mean group) of industry-level TFP on log ICT investment for 17 EU countries and 13 manufacturing sectors; meets the 10-economy threshold and the output/productivity outcome family.
exposure_measure: Log of ICT investment (labelled 'ICT' / 'ITC' in the text and tables) entered at industry-country-year level; the unit (e.g. share of GDP, per worker, euros), source and definition are not reported.

sample.economies_or_groups: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Netherlands, Sweden, UK, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Czech Republic, Estonia, Slovakia, Slovenia (text and figures also mention Hungary, which is not in the stated list of 17)
sample.income_groups_covered: mostly high; income-group classification not reported (EU members, core / South / East grouping noted but not used in results)

design.estimator: Two-step: (i) country-specific Cobb-Douglas value-added production functions estimated with the augmented mean group (AMG) estimator to obtain log TFP and a common dynamic process; (ii) log TFP regressed on determinants with Mean Group (MG), MG robust and AMG robust estimators; first-difference pooled AMG first step reported as a short-run check.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Log EU-25 exports to non-EU (openness), log FDI, log unit wages, human capital (secondary education as % of population), group-specific linear trends, common dynamic process (AMG). R&D and structural funds were dropped because not significant.

results.indicator: Log estimated industry TFP level on log ICT investment (AMG robust, preferred)
results.estimate: 0.00817 (elasticity; roughly +0.08% TFP per +10% ICT investment); text says the effect 'is small in economic terms'
results.evidence: Table 1, p.13, AMG Robust column, 'Ln ITC .00817** (.00414)'; text p.14: 'positively correlated to TFP, although the effect is small in economic terms'

results.indicator: Log estimated TFP on log ICT investment (MG, non-robust se)
results.uncertainty: se 0.00516, not significant at conventional levels
results.evidence: Table 1, p.13, MG column, 'Ln ITC .00707 (.00516)'

results.indicator: Log estimated TFP on log ICT investment (MG with robust se)
results.evidence: Table 1, p.13, MG Robust column, 'Ln ITC .00908*** (.00306)'

results.indicator: First difference of estimated TFP on first difference of log ICT investment (first-step pooled AMG)
results.estimate: 0.00386 (estimated TFP); 0.00194 for calculated (accounting) TFP
results.uncertainty: estimated TFP: se 0.00163, ** (p<0.05); calculated TFP: se 0.00129, not significant

heterogeneity.finding: The paper says it keeps three groups (core, South, East) for the empirical work, but no group-specific ICT estimates are reported in Section 4 or the tables.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 3, p.9: 'we keep the three distinct groups of EU members, core, South and East'; no corresponding table

income_group_results.high: Sample is EU members; pooled estimate only (see results); no split reported

n_specifications_reported: about 5 (three second-stage columns in Table 1, two first-difference columns in Table 2)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: AMG controls for common factors and cross-section dependence but ICT investment is not instrumented or lagged; high-TFP industries may invest more in ICT, and ICT capital is likely part of the capital input used to build TFP. Unit wages, also endogenous, are the largest regressor. Authors interpret coefficients as determinants and acknowledge correlation reading for wages.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4.2-4.3, pp.12-14; 'if we interpret this positive coefficient as correlation, it could be that industries with higher TFP pay higher salaries'

exposure_measurement.why: ICT investment is a reasonable capital-side exposure but its definition, unit, source and deflation are not described, and the variable is called 'ITC' in tables.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 4.2, p.12 (variable listed as 'log of ICT investment'); Table 1 label 'Ln ITC'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 17 countries chosen by data availability; period ends in 2007 so excludes the crisis; the country list is inconsistent with Hungary appearing in text and figures. Manufacturing only.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3, p.7; p.8-9 text mentions Hungary

outcome_measurement.why: TFP is a model-based residual from country-specific value-added production functions, including a common-factor term; results for calculated TFP are said to be similar but not shown. Estimation error in TFP is carried into the second stage without correction.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 2.2, pp.5-7; footnote 5, p.4: 'For brevity, we do not show the results here'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Variables (R&D, structural funds) were dropped because they were insignificant, and the openness proxy was chosen after testing; only a few specifications are shown, and the ICT result is similar across them.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 4.2, p.12: 'Since R&D has not statistically significant it has been excluded from the model'

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and conclusion state that human capital 'plays a role', but the human capital coefficient is insignificant in Table 1; dropped R&D and structural-fund results and the calculated-TFP robustness check are not shown.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p.1 vs Table 1, p.13, 'Human Capital .00354 (.00249)'

venue_quality_concern: possible (no journal or series named in the text; appears to be a working paper with typos, 'ITC' for ICT, and an unlisted country in the sample)
notes: The ICT elasticity is small (about 0.008). Table 1 lists N=1322 for MG and 1106 for AMG; the number of sectors times countries times years is not reconciled. Text says estimates are 'for the above mentioned 17 countries and their 13 sectors' but the first-step table has N=1158. The abstract says human capital plays a role though it is insignificant in the table. No instruction-like content found in the text.

title: The Role of ICT in the Productivity of Central and Eastern European Countries: Cross-country Comparison
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel estimation (LSDV fixed effects) of ICT spending and internet use on labour productivity for 21 EU countries, 1993-2011, with a CEE versus Western Europe comparison. Meets exposure (ICT in general), sample (21 economies, at least 10) and outcome (output/productivity) criteria.
exposure_measure: ICTS: total ICT spending (hardware, software and services, communications) as % of GDP, WITSA Digital Planet (editions 2002, 2006, 2010 listed in references), labelled 'ICT capital'; INTuse: internet users per 100 people (World Bank WDI). Both enter the regression as log(ICTS) and level INTuse.

sample.economies_or_groups: 7 CEE (BG, CZ, HU, PL, RO, SK, SI) and 14 Western/Southern/Northern EU members (3 Scandinavian, 2 Anglo-Saxon, 5 Continental, 4 Mediterranean); CY, EE, LV, LT, LU, MT excluded for lack of ICT capital data
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed within EU; predominantly high-income. Paper gives no World Bank income classification; CEE vs Western Europe is the only split

design.estimator: Fixed effects via least squares dummy variable (LSDV) regression, full sample plus sub-samples (7 CEE, 14 WE) and sub-periods (1993-1999, 2000-2007, 2008-2011)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country dummies (LSDV); controls log gross fixed capital formation % GDP, log public education spending per hour worked, log R&D % GDP, log trade openness, gross enrolment ratio, HRST % active population, log resident patents per million. Time effects not stated. Dependent variable is labour productivity per hour (appears to be in logs; equation 4 is garbled in the text).

results.indicator: Labour productivity per hour worked (log), elasticity w.r.t. log ICT spending % GDP, 21 countries, 1993-2011
results.estimate: 0.192 (log-log elasticity)
results.evidence: Table 4, p. 215, log(ICTS) 21 countries: '0.192***' (0.015)

results.indicator: Labour productivity per hour worked, elasticity w.r.t. log ICT spending, 7 CEE countries
Labour productivity per hour worked, elasticity w.r.t. log ICT spending, 14 Western European countries
Labour productivity per hour worked, coefficient on internet users per 100 people (level), 21 countries
results.estimate: 0.003 per additional internet user per 100 people (approx. 0.3% productivity per user-per-100, if dependent variable is log)

results.indicator: Labour productivity, log ICT spending, CEE sub-periods
results.evidence: Table 5, p. 217, CEE columns log(ICTS); Conclusion p. 218: 'ICT capital is only significant in CEE for 2000-2007'

results.indicator: Labour productivity, log ICT spending, Western Europe sub-periods
results.uncertainty: se 0.035; 0.019; 0.093. None significant at 5% as printed
results.evidence: Table 5, p. 217, WE columns log(ICTS)

heterogeneity.finding: ICT spending elasticity is larger in the 7 CEE (lower-productivity) economies (0.150) than in the 14 Western European economies (0.058). Region/development split, not an income-group classification.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4, p. 215: log(ICTS) CEE 0.150*** vs WE 0.058*

heterogeneity.finding: Public education spending per hour worked and HRST are positive and significant in the full sample and WE but not in CEE (EduS -0.016 ns; HRST 0.003 ns); gross enrolment significant in CEE (0.004**) and not in WE. Authors interpret as complementarities to ICT but do not test interactions.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4, p. 215-216; text p. 215: 'no identical tendency for CEE'

heterogeneity.finding: Time period: ICT, education, internet use and HRST become significant for CEE in 2000-2007, then lose significance in the 2008-2011 crisis period, when trade openness gains importance (0.123*). Sub-period samples are small (N=28 to 112).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5, p. 217; text p. 216: 'With the crisis, the sources of productivity have changed'

income_group_results.high: Not separated by income. Western EU (14 countries, mostly high-income): ICT spending elasticity 0.058* (se 0.026); internet users 0.002***
income_group_results.upper_middle: Not reported separately. Bulgaria and Romania (upper-middle in much of the period under World Bank classes, classification not given in paper) are pooled in the CEE sub-sample: ICT spending elasticity 0.150***

n_specifications_reported: 9 regressions (3 in Table 4, 6 in Table 5)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Static LSDV on log levels of 21 countries over 19 years with no instrument, lags, or unit-root/cointegration checks; ICT spending share is plausibly endogenous to productivity and income; common trends can drive spurious co-movement. Language is explanatory ('impact', 'role').
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4.3, p. 215: 'estimation of fixed effects models using least squares dummy variable (LSDV) regression'; no discussion of endogeneity

exposure_measurement.why: ICT expenditure as % of GDP (a flow, including services and telecom) is labelled 'ICT capital'; source reports (WITSA 2002, 2006, 2010 editions) suggest annual values may be interpolated, not stated. Internet users is a standard usage measure.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 3, p. 214: 'Total ICT spending ... as a percentage of GDP' / 'ICT capital'; references: WITSA Digital Planet 2002, 2006, 2010

selection_of_countries_years.why: 21 EU members only; six countries dropped for missing ICT data (all Baltics, CY, LU, MT); CEE sub-sample is 7 countries and sub-period CEE samples have 28-56 observations. Authors acknowledge small sample.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Table 2 note, p. 214; Conclusion p. 218: 'main limitation ... relatively small sample of countries'

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity per hour worked from the Conference Board Total Economy Database, PPP-converted; a standard outcome.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 3, p. 214: 'Labour productivity per hour worked in 2012 US'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Nine regressors in sub-period models with as few as 28 observations (adj R2 0.29); iid-type standard errors reported with no clustering or serial-correlation correction stated; no robustness section; variables enter in mixed logs and levels. Model equations are garbled in the text version.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 5, p. 217: CEE 2008-2011 Num. obs. 28, Adj. R2 0.291; no robustness discussion in Section 4.3

selective_reporting.why: All columns are shown, but the text and conclusion misdescribe some results: states R&D is 'positive and significant for CEE during 1990s and after the crisis' while Table 5 shows RDS CEE 0.046 and 0.029 without significance stars; says RDS significant 'only for the whole sample' while Table 4 shows it more strongly for WE (-0.064***); unexpected negative patent and R&D signs are noted but not examined.
selective_reporting.evidence: Conclusion p. 218 vs Table 5 p. 217 (CEE log(RDS) 0.046 / 0.043 / 0.029); text p. 215 on Table 4

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Revista de Economia Mundial 39 (2015), peer-reviewed; paper was presented at a conference first. The page header on p. 201 contains a stray template line from another article ('Migration Dynamics within the EU-15: Pull Factors and Choice of Destination'); ignore. Equations 1-4 are unreadable in the text conversion, so the exact functional form and whether the dependent variable is in logs is inferred (coefficients are labelled log(...) on the right-hand side; elasticity interpretation of log(ICTS) is the most likely reading but the dependent variable's transformation is not directly legible). Table 4 N: 399 = 21 x 19; 133 = 7 x 19; 266 = 14 x 19. Authors interpret the text as 'explanatory power dropped to 30%' referring to adjusted R2 of 0.291 in CEE 2008-2011. EU sample means this study adds little on the low and lower-middle income question; no AI exposure. No instructions directed at the reviewer were found.

title: Icts And Labour Productivity Nexus In Developing Countries: Evidence From Panel Estimation Approach
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 84 developing countries (upper-middle and lower-middle income) with own estimation of ICT effects on labour productivity (family 1); meets the 10-economy and outcome criteria.
technology: ICT in general (fixed telephone, mobile cellular and internet subscriptions)
exposure_measure: ICTs: fixed telephone, mobile cellular and internet subscriptions per 100 people (ITU database), entered as a single logged 'ICTs' variable; how the three series are combined is not stated.

sample.economies_or_groups: 84 developing countries: 46 upper-middle-income and 38 lower-middle-income (World Bank Atlas GNI per capita classification, 2016), chosen by GNI and data availability; country list not given in the text
sample.income_groups_covered: upper-middle, lower-middle (pooled; no low or high income)

design.estimator: Two-step System GMM (Blundell-Bond) with lagged dependent variable; dynamic panel quantile regression with non-additive fixed effects (Powell 2016) at 9 quantiles
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged log labour productivity, human capital index (PWT), domestic credit to private sector (% GDP), trade openness; country effects via GMM transformation; robustness adds population growth; interactions ICT x HC, FD, TO; instrument set and count not reported

results.indicator: Labour productivity (GDP per worker, log), ICT main effect, Model 1 two-step system GMM
results.estimate: 0.0144 (log-log; implied short-run elasticity of about 0.014; coefficient on lagged productivity 0.901, so implied long-run elasticity is about 0.15, calculated by the extractor and not reported by the authors)
results.evidence: Table 3, Model 1; text Section 4.1: 'a 1% increase in ICTs usage results in a 0.0144 increase in labour productivity'

results.indicator: Labour productivity, ICT x human capital interaction (Model 2)
results.estimate: 0.123 (ICT main effect 0.0175)
results.evidence: Table 3, Model 2

results.indicator: Labour productivity, ICT x financial development interaction (Model 3)
results.estimate: 0.0748 (ICT main effect 0.0175)
results.evidence: Table 3, Model 3

results.indicator: Labour productivity, ICT x trade openness interaction (Model 4)
results.estimate: 0.122 (ICT main effect 0.0172)
results.evidence: Table 3, Model 4

results.indicator: Labour productivity, ICT main effect with population growth added (robustness)
results.evidence: Table 5, Models 5-8

results.indicator: Labour productivity, ICT coefficient by conditional quantile (dynamic panel quantile regression)
results.evidence: Table 4; text Section 4.2: 'significant ... at all quantiles except for the 40th quantile'

heterogeneity.finding: Positive and significant ICT x human capital interaction in GMM (0.123); in quantile versions (Table 6) interaction is significant only at q10 (positive), q40 (negative, 10%), q70 (negative) and q90 (positive), so mixed.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Model 2; Table 6; Section 4.3.2

heterogeneity.finding: Financial development moderates the ICT effect positively in GMM (0.0748) although financial development alone has a negative coefficient (-0.107); in quantile versions the interaction is significant at most quantiles but negative at q60.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Model 3; Table 7

heterogeneity.finding: Trade openness moderates positively in GMM (0.122); in quantile versions interaction is significant only at q30, q60, q90 (positive) and negative at q80.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Model 4; Table 8

heterogeneity.finding: Productivity level: authors state ICT effect is larger in low and middle productivity countries than in the highest (q90 coefficient 0.00195 vs q10 0.00859), but q50 (0.00854) equals q10 and q40 is insignificant, so the pattern is not monotone.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4, Figure 1; Section 4.2

n_specifications_reported: about 44 columns: 8 GMM (Tables 3 and 5) plus 36 quantile equations (Tables 4, 6, 7, 8)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('impact', 'influence') with system GMM only; internal instruments, no external instrument or exogenous variation; instrument count and lag structure not reported (risk of proliferation with T=20, N=84); Sargan p-values of 0.11-0.17 are read as validity ('closer to 1'); the quantile estimator has no explicit treatment of ICT endogeneity.

exposure_measurement.why: Subscriptions per 100 people for three different technologies are combined into one logged 'ICTs' variable without stating the aggregation (sum, index or separate); subscriptions measure access rather than use or quality; fixed telephone is a declining technology.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1 and Eq. 5; Table 1 lists mobile, fixed telephone and internet separately

selection_of_countries_years.why: 84 countries selected by 2016 GNI classification and data availability; 1,219 observations from 84 x 20 = 1,680 possible, so the panel is unbalanced with unexplained gaps; country list not provided; only middle-income economies.

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity is GDP divided by total labour (source not named); Table 1 shows mean 1,185,371 and max 1.12e8, units not stated and implausible for a common-currency measure; human capital index described as 'years of schooling, weighted' with min 0.51; trade openness defined as imports plus exports over real GDP per capita (unusual).

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications (GMM, 4 interaction models, 4 quantile sets x 9 quantiles); interactions of logged variables not centred, so main effects are conditional on log of moderator equal to zero; control coefficients are unstable (human capital is +0.039 in Model 1, -0.067 in Model 2, -0.035 in Model 5); no estimates for sub-groups; claim that interaction coefficients 'have a greater influence than the impact of each variable individually' compares magnitudes of coefficients that are not comparable.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 3 and 5; Section 4.1 final paragraph; Eq. 6-9

selective_reporting.why: All quantiles and tables are shown, but the abstract and conclusion stress the GMM interaction results as uniformly positive while quantile interactions (Tables 6-8) are mixed; Figure 2 is missing (text in place of the figure reads 'The Powell command has no graph for quantile regression') although the text describes U-shaped and inverted patterns drawn from it.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; Section 4.3.2 and Figure 2 page 44; Conclusion

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Effect size is small (about 0.014-0.015 elasticity short-run). Reported units are log-log, but the text says 'a 1% increase in ICTs usage results in a 0.0144 increase in labour productivity' (loose wording). Text refers to 'Equation 4' for the quantile condition (should be Eq. 11) and 'Dua and Lang (2019)'/'Dua and Garg (2018/2019)' inconsistently. Table 1 reports 1,219 observations only in regression tables. Significance footnote shows '%%' typo. Abstract claims ICT significant at 'lower and intermediate' quantiles more than highest; Table 4 shows q50 about equal to q10. Authors recommend ICT adoption as policy for Industry 4.0, beyond what the design supports. No instruction-like text found.

title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness and Employment: A Global Panel Analysis
decision_rationale: Panel regressions on 78 countries (2019-2022) relating the Oxford Insights AI Readiness Index (an AI capability measure) to employment of highly educated workers. Meets AI exposure, at least 3 economies and a labour-market outcome.
exposure_measure: Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, composite of three pillars (Government, Technology Sector, Data and Infrastructure) with 9 indicators; also pillar and component scores. This measures readiness and capability, not actual AI use.

sample.economies_or_groups: Countries listed on p.64 (e.g. USA, Germany, Korea, Brazil, India, Egypt, South Africa, Rwanda, Zambia); China, UK and Japan excluded for missing data
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low are present in the list; no income-group breakdown reported)

design.estimator: Panel least squares with cross-section fixed effects (Hausman and redundant-FE tests said to favour FE); 15 models (3 outcomes x 5 regressor sets)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No control variables; only constant and country fixed effects (period effects mentioned as tested but not reported).

results.indicator: Employment rate of highly educated workers (total) on AI Readiness Index
results.estimate: 0.00034 (variables appear log-transformed per Table 1 magnitudes, but the text does not state transformation)
results.evidence: Table 2 (p.66), AI_READINESS 0.00034* Prob 0.000

results.indicator: Employment of highly educated workers (male) on AI Readiness Index
results.uncertainty: Prob. 0.141 (yet marked as 1% significant with an asterisk)
results.evidence: Table 2 (p.66); text p.66 says effect significant for all three categories

results.indicator: Employment of highly educated workers (female) on AI Readiness Index
results.evidence: Table 2 (p.66)

results.indicator: Total employment of highly educated on Pillar 1 Government
results.evidence: Table 3 (p.67)

results.indicator: Total employment of highly educated on Pillar 2 Technology Sector and Pillar 3 Data and Infrastructure
results.evidence: Table 3 (p.67); for male, Pillar 2 -0.00024 (p=0.013) and Pillar 3 -0.00036 (p=0.012)

results.indicator: Component-level effects (Pillar 1-3 components) on total, male, female employment
results.estimate: Coefficients of order 0.0001 to 0.0007 with signs varying by component and gender (e.g. AI human capital -0.00052 total, +0.0005 female)
results.evidence: Tables 4-6 (pp.67-69); text p.67 'inconsistencies in the impact of both components'

heterogeneity.finding: Gender split (male vs female highly educated employment) and pillar/component split. Authors state effects 'differ only slightly'; no formal test of difference. Opposite-signed component effects across genders.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4 p.70 'estimated impact on high-educated male and female employment differs only slightly'

n_specifications_reported: 15 models (one specification each); other FE/RE variants tested but not shown

confounding_reverse_causation.why: No control variables at all, no year effects reported, no strategy for reverse causation. The readiness index includes a human capital component, which overlaps mechanically with the education-based outcome. Only four years of within-country variation.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.1 eqs (1)-(15): 'a1 x AI Readiness Index + C + e'; Section 3.2 p.64-65

exposure_measurement.why: Government-readiness composite index (policy, data, infrastructure, human capital) is not AI adoption or use; the paper itself says use matters more than readiness. Index comparability across 2019-2022 editions is not discussed.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.61 pillars; Section 4 p.67 'practical use and its applications of AI are also important'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 78 countries retained only if complete data; China, UK and Japan dropped; 4 years only. Claim of 'representative' sample (60% of highly educated employment) is asserted without computation.

outcome_measurement.why: Outcome definition is unclear (stated as persons employed divided by total employed, i.e. a share of employment, called an employment rate); cited source URL points to a World Bank gender data indicator for female labour force share rather than ILO education-level employment. Table 1 variance is tiny (SD 0.004 on mean 1.18), consistent with log10 values, but transformation is not stated.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1 variable table p.62; Section 3.2 p.64 data source; Table 1 p.64

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: 15 models with strongly collinear sub-indices entered together; adjusted R2 about 0.999 because FE absorb nearly all variance; stationarity tests dismissed for short panel; Durbin-Watson used as 'robustness' evidence.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 2-6 (pp.66-69) Adj. R-squared 0.997-0.999; p.69 'The results are robust'

selective_reporting.why: Text and summary Table 7 contradict the regression tables: stars attached to insignificant coefficients (e.g. p=0.141, 0.642, 0.815); Table 7 says AI data representativeness significant for total employment although Table 6 gives p=0.815; Table 7 lists AI governance and ethics as positive and significant for male while Table 4 gives p=0.642; text says Pillar 3 significant for female but Table 3 gives p=0.437.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Abstract and conclusion claim AI literacy findings and that AI readiness has a positive effect on employment; AI literacy is never measured or tested, and pillar 2 and 3 effects are negative in several models, so the headline positive result rests on the composite index only. The coefficient size is very small (about 0.0003) and the unit/transformation is not stated; my inference that variables are log10-transformed comes from the Table 1 values (e.g. employment mean 1.18, AI readiness mean 1.84), not from the text. Many stars in Tables 2-6 are inconsistent with the reported p-values and are not a reliable guide. No embedded instructions to the reader were found in the text.

title: From Digital Divide to Employment Equity: How Digitalization Affects Women's Involvement in the Workforce in OECD Countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative country-panel study (22 economies, 2000-2021) of mobile cellular subscriptions and internet use against female labour force participation (family 3); meets the at least 10 economies rule. Reporting is thin: no estimated coefficients are presented.
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people (mb) and individuals using the internet as % of population (web), both World Bank.

sample.economies_or_groups: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Korea, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, Turkey, UK, US, Israel, Switzerland, Sweden, New Zealand, Finland, Denmark, Netherlands (described as 'OECD countries' though several are not OECD members)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle and lower-middle economies in the list; no income-group comparison)

exposure_measure: Robot volume as a share of the labour force (rvol_lf), from Statista and WDI. Table 2: 'Robot Volume as a share of labor force'.

sample.income_groups_covered: mixed, but dominated by high income; income groups are not reported by name

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, fixed effects, random effects, system GMM (Table 4); dynamic panel threshold regression of Seo and Shin (Table 5, Table 6)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged dependent variable; internet, resident patents per million, GDP per capita, advanced-education labour share (each in turn as threshold, the others as controls); time effects in the model equation

n_specifications_reported: not applicable

outcome_measurement.why: not applicable

notes: Borderline on E2: the title and framing link robots and AI, but the regressor is robot density (p. 906, Table 2) and the dependent variable is the LinkedIn-based relative AI hiring index (aihi). A reviewer may reconsider if robots are judged an AI-capability proxy; this is an exclusion on my reading of the stated criteria. For reference only, results (Table 4, p. 907): rvol_lf positive in linear models (pooled 48.347*, system-GMM 150.069***). Table 5 (p. 909): threshold coefficients change sign by regime, e.g. internet threshold 82.39 (lower -1779.863***, upper 2105.485***); GDP per capita threshold 47714.14 (lower 616.005***, upper -895.725***). Inconsistencies noticed: the abstract and text say 28 countries but Tables 5 and 6 report N=25; System-GMM uses 100 observations with only 6 years; the text interprets 2,105 as raising the AI hiring index 'by 2,105 times', which is a misreading of a coefficient on a share variable; Table 5 constant and some significance stars look inconsistent with standard errors (e.g. 2105.485 with SE 785.128 shown as ***, constant -7.314*** with SE 5.646); threshold CI for patents includes negative values [-329.231, 693.656]; no endogeneity instrument beyond GMM-style lags. No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

title: The Economic Value of Agentic AI: A Comparative Analysis of Its Impact on Growth and Business Productivity in Developed and Emerging Economies
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with own estimation of a composite AI adoption index (investment, adoption, patents) on firm productivity and GDP growth for 10 countries (above the 3-economy AI threshold), with an explicit developed vs emerging comparison. Meets all inclusion criteria, although data provenance and internal consistency are doubtful (see notes).
technology: artificial intelligence (composite AI adoption index; framed as 'agentic AI' but index is general AI)
exposure_measure: Country-year AI Adoption Index = equal-weighted mean of min-max normalised AI investment intensity, business adoption and AI-related patents (Section 3, p.32). Authors admit it 'does not isolate agentic systems' (p.28) and 'does not exclusively capture agentic systems' (p.40). Underlying series and exact sources for each component are not named beyond 'World Bank ... and OECD AI datasets'.

sample.economies_or_groups: Developed: United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, South Korea. Emerging: India, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (developed vs emerging dichotomy; no World Bank income-group split; includes high-income and middle-income economies plus Nigeria, lower-middle)
sample.unit: other (firm-level regressions for productivity, country-year for the mediation and growth models; number of firms and observations not reported)

design.estimator: Fixed-effects panel regression (firm FE for firm productivity; country FE for mediation, stage 1 and 2); interaction model AI x Developed dummy; quantile regression at tau 0.25, 0.50, 0.75; mediation by product of coefficients (no formal test).
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Firm models: firm size, capital intensity, firm FE. Macro models: capital formation, trade openness, inflation, country FE. Robust SEs. Time effects not mentioned. Table 7 interaction model: the Developed dummy main effect is not estimable with country FE and is not shown.

results.indicator: Firm-level productivity (revenue per employee), pooled
results.estimate: 0.18 (units of outcome and AI index scaling not stated; log specification not stated)
results.evidence: Table 3, p.35: 'AI Adoption 0.18 0.05 3.60 ***'

results.indicator: Firm-level productivity by group (developed vs emerging)
results.estimate: Developed 0.24; Emerging 0.11
results.uncertainty: Developed p < 0.01; Emerging p < 0.05; SEs not reported; no formal test of the difference reported
results.evidence: Table 4, p.35: 'Developed 0.24*** / Emerging 0.11**'

results.indicator: Firm financial performance (return on assets)
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: ROA is defined in Section 3 (p.32) and the abstract/objectives refer to financial performance, but no ROA results table appears in Section 4 (pp.33-39).

results.indicator: Macro productivity (GDP per person employed), mediation stage 1
results.estimate: 0.27 (units not stated)
results.evidence: Table 5, p.36: 'AI Adoption Index 0.27 0.06 4.50 ***'

results.indicator: GDP growth (annual %), effect of productivity (mediator), stage 2
results.estimate: Productivity 0.35
results.evidence: Table 6, p.37: 'Productivity 0.35 0.08 4.38 ***'

results.indicator: GDP growth (annual %), direct effect of AI index with productivity controlled
results.estimate: 0.09; implied indirect effect 0.27 x 0.35 = about 0.095 (computed by reviewer, not reported by authors)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.05, t = 1.80, p < 0.10; no test of the indirect effect
results.evidence: Table 6, p.37: 'AI Adoption Index 0.09 0.05 1.80 *'

results.indicator: GDP growth: AI index in emerging economies (baseline) and interaction with Developed dummy
results.estimate: AI index 0.15 (emerging); AI x Developed 0.18; total effect developed about 0.33 (0.15 + 0.18)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.05 and 0.06, both p < 0.01; SE of the sum not reported
results.evidence: Table 7, p.37: 'AI Adoption Index 0.15 0.05 3.00 ***; AI x Developed Dummy 0.18 0.06 3.00 ***'; abstract: 'approximately 0.33 ... (approximately 0.15)'

results.indicator: GDP growth, quantile regression effects of AI index
results.uncertainty: Stars only: developed ** / *** / ***; emerging none / ** / **; SEs not reported
results.evidence: Table 8, p.38

heterogeneity.finding: Developed economies show about twice the productivity effect (0.24 vs 0.11) and growth effect (about 0.33 vs 0.15) of AI than emerging economies; effects rise across growth quantiles, more steeply in developed economies. Interpretation as structural conditions (infrastructure, human capital, institutions) is asserted but none of these is tested as a moderator.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 4, 7, 8, pp.35-38; abstract: 'developed economies experiencing substantially stronger growth impacts (approximately 0.33) than emerging economies (approximately 0.15)'

income_group_results.high: Developed group (US, UK, Germany, Japan, South Korea): firm productivity effect 0.24***; growth effect about 0.33 (0.15 + 0.18 interaction); quantile growth effects 0.12**, 0.26***, 0.42***.
income_group_results.upper_middle: Not separated. Brazil, South Africa are in the pooled 'emerging' group: firm productivity 0.11**; growth 0.15***; quantile effects 0.04, 0.10**, 0.17**.
income_group_results.lower_middle: Not separated. India, Indonesia and Nigeria are in the pooled 'emerging' group (same estimates as above).
income_group_results.low: not reported (no low-income economy in the sample)

n_specifications_reported: about 8 (firm FE pooled, firm FE by group, mediation stage 1 and 2, interaction, 3 quantiles by 2 groups); ROA models mentioned but not reported

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('impact', 'effect', 'drives') with FE only; no instrument, lags or event timing. Authors concede reverse causality 'cannot be fully eliminated'. Country-level AI index regressed on firm outcomes and on growth; AI investment and patents plausibly respond to productivity and growth. Mediation via sequential regressions treats the mediator as exogenous. Time FE not mentioned, so common trends could drive results.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3, p.32 ('control variables help mitigate potential endogeneity'); Section 6, p.40 ('reverse causality ... cannot be fully eliminated')

exposure_measurement.why: Composite index not specific to agentic AI (authors admit this) yet the title, abstract and conclusions attribute effects to 'Agentic AI'. Components (investment, adoption, patents) have no named series, no units, and the 'business adoption' measure for Nigeria, Indonesia, South Africa etc. 2015-2024 is not documented. Min-max scaling applied within the sample would give a floor of 0 for the lowest country on each component, which is inconsistent with the reported index values (Nigeria 0.49 with the lowest value on all three components). Equal weighting is unvalidated.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3, pp.31-32; Table 1, p.33; Section 6, p.40 ('does not exclusively capture agentic systems')

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 10 hand-picked economies (5 developed, 5 emerging), chosen on 'data availability'; no low-income economy; very small cluster count for country FE and clustered or robust inference; group comparison rests on 5 vs 5 countries. Time coverage 2015-2024 claimed but AI adoption data of this kind are scarce for several of these countries and years.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3, p.31 ('Country selection is based on data availability')

outcome_measurement.why: Revenue per employee (firm) and GDP per person employed and annual GDP growth (macro) are standard outcomes, but the firm data source (World Bank Enterprise Surveys, which are mostly cross-sectional with irregular waves) is poorly matched to a firm-level FE panel; number of firms, waves and units (log or level) are not reported. Revenue per employee is nominal and not deflated, as far as stated. A country-level AI index is matched to firm outcomes without discussion of clustering.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: No observations or N, R-squared, clustering level, or time-effects reported; coefficient units unspecified; the Developed dummy is time-invariant and cannot enter a country-FE model, so the Table 7 specification is not as described; quantile regression with country FE not explained. Little robustness analysis despite the claim that 'additional model specifications confirm result stability' (none shown).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3, p.33 ('Additional model specifications confirm result stability'); Tables 3-8, pp.35-38

selective_reporting.why: ROA (financial performance) is announced as an outcome in the abstract, objectives and methods but no results are shown. Group comparison (Table 4) reports stars only with no SEs and no test of difference. Indirect effect is never calculated or tested. Abstract states firm-level beta 0.18 and 'productivity channel (beta = 0.35)' which mixes a regression coefficient of the mediator with the mediated effect. Every estimate is significant and in the hypothesised direction.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract, p.25; Section 3 p.32 (ROA defined); Section 4 pp.35-38

venue_quality_concern: possible (Asian Journal of Research in Computer Science, a computer science outlet publishing an economics paper; accepted about 9 weeks after receipt; five authors from different fields; heavy self-citation of the authors' own group, e.g. Ogunmolu, Olutimehin, Olaniyi, Ejoh, Henry 2026 papers)
notes: Decision rationale for risk rating: a 10-country sample with unreported N, no identification, an index that the authors say does not measure the stated exposure, and several internal inconsistencies make the conclusions untrustworthy. Internal inconsistencies noted: (1) Table 1 AI index values (e.g., Nigeria 0.49 with lowest raw values) are incompatible with min-max normalisation across the sample. (2) The country-level data are claimed to come from OECD AI and World Bank Enterprise Surveys for Nigeria, Indonesia, South Africa etc. for 2015-2024 with no data appendix; reported coefficients are round numbers, and t-statistics in every table equal coefficient/SE exactly (e.g., 0.18/0.05 = 3.60; 0.15/0.05 = 3.00), which is unusual for real estimates. (3) Firm-level pooled effect is 0.18 but the macro stage 1 effect is 0.27 on a different outcome with no reconciliation. (4) No figures for the number of firms, observations or years actually used. (5) Table 7 total developed effect 0.33 is computed by summation with no SE. Disclaimer states no generative AI was used in writing. No instruction-like text directed at the reader was found in the paper. Evidence quality for the review: use as low-weight evidence on the sign (positive) and on the developed vs emerging gap, but do not use the magnitudes.

title: Bridging the digital divide: the growth implications of e-commerce for small and developing states
decision_rationale: Contains its own cross-country estimation (SURE, 126 countries, year 2000) linking internet hosts to log real GDP, with a descriptive comparison across the four World Bank income groups. Weak design, but it meets the eligibility rules (internet exposure, more than 10 economies, output outcome).
technology: internet (hosts, used as proxy for e-commerce adoption)
exposure_measure: Log of internet hosts per 10,000 inhabitants in 2000 (ITU), called a biased measure of e-commerce diffusion by the authors. A composite investment measure (CMI) combines telephone lines, gross enrolment and fixed capital formation by factor analysis.

sample.n_economies: 205 descriptive; 126 in regressions (93 large, 33 small, small = under 3 million population)
sample.economies_or_groups: Global cross-section, with small-state versus large-state split and World Bank four income groups in box plots (Fig 3: 54 low, 44 lower-middle, 28 upper-middle, 35 high)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low)

design.estimator: Seemingly unrelated regression (SURE) on a two-equation system (LHosts and LGGDP) in LIMDEP 7.0; factor analysis for CMI; scatter plots and box plots
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: CMI, small-state dummy; no other controls, no fixed effects (single cross-section)

results.indicator: Log real GDP (constant 1995 US$, level) on log internet hosts per 10,000
results.estimate: 0.423 (specification 1, with CMI); 0.395 (specification with small-state dummy and CMI). Units are log-on-log, but see notes.
results.evidence: Table 3, second block of 'Model specification 1' (LHOSTS 0.423) and second block of 'Model specification 2' (LHOSTS 0.395); Section 3.3, Simulations 2 and 4

results.indicator: Log internet hosts on log real GDP (reverse direction, adoption equation)
results.estimate: 0.396 (SE 0.062) without dummy; 0.399 (SE 0.064) with dummy
results.evidence: Table 3, first blocks; Section 3.3 Simulation 1: 'GDP is found to be a positive and significant determinant of Internet hosts'

heterogeneity.finding: Descriptive only: internet hosts differ more between World Bank income groups than between small and large states; the income-adoption slope is steeper for large than for small states (Figs 3, 4a, 4b). No formal test.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 3.1 p.11: 'the extent of the digital divide is greater between income groups than it is between small and large states'

heterogeneity.finding: Small-state dummy (under 3 million): not significant in the hosts equation in specification 3 (6.814, SE 47.011) and weakly negative in specification 4 (-76.790, SE 49.069); strongly negative in the GDP equation (-209.499, SE 48.835; -179.145, SE 45.085).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (the text speaks of 'minimum thresholds' but none is estimated)
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3, Model specification 2; Section 3.3 Simulations 3 and 4

income_group_results.high: not reported (box plot of hosts only)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (box plot of hosts only)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported (box plot of hosts only)
income_group_results.low: not reported (box plot of hosts only)

n_specifications_reported: 4 system estimations (8 regressions), plus about 8 sets of scatter plots

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Single cross-section with GDP level and internet hosts jointly determined. SURE only exploits error correlation between equations and gives no exogenous variation; the paper itself says the two are endogenous and then reads coefficients as growth effects. CMI is built from the same variables that drive both sides. No controls for institutions, geography or population in the GDP equation.

exposure_measurement.why: Internet hosts per 10,000 are a poor measure of e-commerce or of use in a country (hosts are tied to domain registration, which the authors acknowledge is biased). E-commerce itself is never measured.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.9: 'a biased measurement of the state of e-commerce diffusion'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Regression sample falls from 205 to 126 states because of missing data; one year (2000) only; non-random loss, and small-state sample is 33.

outcome_measurement.why: Outcome is level of real GDP (constant 1995 US$), not growth, although the title and text refer to growth. Reported magnitudes look inconsistent with a log outcome (small-state dummy of -209 on LGGDP, constants of 23 to 82).
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 1 (LgGDP = log of real GDP); Table 3

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Unusual SURE set-up with the dependent variable of one equation as the regressor in the other; two versions with and without the dummy. The authors admit the size-dummy result 'may be affected by data specification and other statistical problems'. Table headings repeat ('Model specification 1' twice). Identical t-ratios (6.425, 6.196) appear in both equations, which suggests duplication or a mechanical artefact.

selective_reporting.why: All four simulations are shown, but no robustness checks, no diagnostics, and text describes Simulation 2 loosely (e.g. says 'regresses CMI on hosts'). Draft paper not peer reviewed.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 3.3, Simulation 2; cover note 'should not be cited or quoted'

venue_quality_concern: possible (unreviewed working paper prepared for a conference; author note says draft should not be cited)
notes: Abstract and introduction describe the paper as a synthesis plus research agenda; the empirical part is small and labelled 'initial'. Title speaks of growth but the model estimates GDP levels in a single year. Only the LHosts-to-LGGDP coefficient is treated as the payoff estimate; the CMI coefficient mixes telephone lines, schooling and capital formation and is not an ICT exposure estimate. Table 3 oddities: reported SMALL coefficients of -209.499 and -179.145 are implausible for a log outcome, and t-ratios are duplicated across the two equations. Possible duplicate or later version in a journal not checked. No instruction-like content found in the text.
