n_specifications_reported: about 36 (Table 2: 4; Table 3: 5; Table 4: 6; Table 5: 5; Table 6: 7; Table A3: 5; Table A4: 4)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('isolate the causal effect'), but the sole external instrument is the regional average of internet penetration, whose exclusion restriction is not defended (regional diffusion can be correlated with regional structural change and common shocks); the other instrument is lagged internet penetration. Footnote 3 argues reverse causality is absent for the manufacturing equation because the outcome is sectoral and the regressor national, which is not a valid argument. FE-IV estimates are larger than FE, unexplained. Table 6 Models 5-7 report no instrument tests.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2 p.318-319; Section 4.3 p.319-322; footnote 3 p.319; Table 4 notes; Table 6

exposure_measurement.why: Internet penetration is a single access proxy for 'digitalisation'; the authors acknowledge this. Data source is given inconsistently (ITU in text, WDI in Table A1). Internet penetration is 0 at the minimum and 1230 observations versus 1398 for other variables, so early years have many zeros/missing; log of zero values not discussed.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.2 p.318; Table A1; Table 1; conclusion p.325

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample is restricted to the ETD's 51 economies, mostly developing, with only 6 high-income; unbalanced panel with 36-49 countries depending on specification; the 1990-2018 window is set by data availability. Income groups are not separately estimated, only through an interaction. Sample size is inconsistent: 51 stated, Table A2 note adds to 50.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.318; Table A2 note; Tables 2-6 observation counts

outcome_measurement.why: Structural change is computed from the standard McMillan-Rodrik decomposition on ETD sectoral value added and employment, and manufacturing employment share is measured directly. The paper concedes manufacturing share is an imperfect industrialisation indicator.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications with varying control sets across models and estimators (about 36). Control sets differ between models (for example GCF is -0.019 insignificant in FE but -2.4 significant in FE-IV, with unexplained scale differences), the stated 'doubling' interpretation of a log coefficient is incorrect, and the preferred model is not declared. Significance of the headline FE effect is only 10% in Model 4. Some tables list no country FE row. Table 6 Model 5 omits year FE.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 2-6, A3-A4; p.319: 'A doubling of internet penetration is associated with a 0.14-unit increase'

selective_reporting.why: The abstract reports a 0.14 to 0.18 range drawn from FE models, omitting the larger FE-IV estimates (0.20-0.34), and states that the effects are stronger for low and lower-middle-income economies, although the main effect is insignificant in the income interaction. Manufacturing employment effect in SSA is insignificant, and appendix tables report only a few of the many specifications. Robustness text claims all results hold, but Table 3 Model 5 has insignificant forward linkage and backward linkage coefficients.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; Table 3 Model 5; Table 5 Model 1; Table A4 Model 4

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Journal of Digital Economy 5 (2026) 314-329, KeAi/Elsevier, peer reviewed, received 2 Sep 2025, accepted 22 Mar 2026. Funded by UNU-WIDER. Internal inconsistencies for the reviewer: (1) the abstract and p.319 say a 'doubling of internet penetration' raises SC by 0.14 units, but the regressor is a log, so the coefficient is a semi-elasticity (a doubling would imply about 0.095 on 0.137). (2) Text p.322 says KP p<0.05 'ensures' the model is not under-identified, and Table 4 shows p=0.00 and Hansen p>0.05, but instrument strength (Cragg-Donald F) is not reported. (3) Table 5 text numbering of Models 3-4 is loose (Model 4 uses lagged SC and the structural-development interaction). (4) Table 5 Model 1 reports a negative interaction on a binary dummy but the main effect is insignificant. (5) The structural change effect applies to the within-year percentage-point contribution to productivity growth; units of SC are percent. (6) The manufacturing employment results are interpreted as 'digital-led deindustrialisation' in developing countries, but the full sample includes six high-income economies and the SSA subsample shows no effect. Outcome families: both outcomes coded to family 2 (structural change); manufacturing employment share could also be read as family 3 (labour market). No instructions embedded in the text were found.

title: The Race between Technological Progress and Female Advancement: Changes in Gender and Skill Premia in OECD Countries
decision_rationale: Structural-econometric study with its own GMM/IV estimation of ICT-capital/labour substitution on cross-country cross-industry panel data from 11 OECD economies; exposure is ICT capital (ICCT) quantity and its falling relative price; outcomes are gender and skill wage gaps and labour shares (families 3 and 4). Sample of 11 meets the at least 10 economies rule for non-AI technology, but all are high income.
technology: ICT capital (computing equipment, communications equipment, software; called ICCT capital)
exposure_measure: Quantity of ICCT capital (k_i) and ICT investment-specific technological change, measured as the fall in the relative price of ICCT investment (q_i, ratio of ICCT investment price to output price); EU KLEMS capital services by asset type, rental prices computed from Jorgenson user-cost formula (internal or external rate of return).

sample.economies_or_groups: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States; four non-primary sectors (manufacturing, utilities, construction, services)
sample.income_groups_covered: high (all 11 are advanced OECD economies; no income-group comparison)

design.estimator: Multi-level nested CES sectoral production function; five first-difference (5-year differences) cost-minimisation equations estimated jointly by GMM with country-clustered SEs; sectoral parameters aggregated to aggregate Morishima elasticities of substitution (bootstrap SEs, 500 reps); effects of ICCT technological change are model-based counterfactuals (steady-state comparison) rather than reduced-form coefficients; preliminary OLS and first-difference IV regressions (eq. 23).
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: First-differencing removes country-specific fixed effects; instruments are lagged population size by demographic group and lagged ICCT investment price relative to consumption; robustness adds collective bargaining coverage, employment protection, minimum wages, external-rate-of-return rental prices (markups), country-specific trend polynomials. Wages adjusted for age and education composition.

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Uses IV (lagged group population, lagged ICCT investment price) and first differences, and shows robustness to institutions, markups and country trends, which is more than a standard panel. But the exclusion restriction for lagged ICCT price is not tested and the headline effects are counterfactuals derived from a maintained nested-CES structure (steady-state, competitive markets), not directly identified causal effects of ICT adoption on outcomes.

exposure_measurement.why: ICCT capital and its investment price come from EU KLEMS asset-level capital accounts, a direct measure of ICT capital stock and price decline. Rental prices are constructed and rely on assumptions (internal rate of return), partly checked with external rate of return.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 11 high-income countries with EU KLEMS 2008 coverage, 1980-2005, which stops before smartphones, broadband diffusion and AI; countries included when data available; no developing economies, so results do not speak to income-group differences.

outcome_measurement.why: Wages are labour compensation divided by hours, adjusted for age and education composition; education-based skill classification (college versus not) is coarse but standard. Labour shares built from the same accounts.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Results depend on the chosen four-level nesting order, the consumption elasticity set at 0.9 from Baqaee and Farhi, the choice of lagged population instrument (chosen because 'more precise'), and the labour-supply elasticity scenario; authors argue alternatives are rejected by tests (Table A1) and report robustness.

selective_reporting.why: Several instrument choices, robustness controls, labour-supply scenarios and country-level results are reported, including cases where effects are small or insignificant (non-ICCT capital, aggregate labour share). venue_quality_concern: possible (text is arXiv:2005.12600v9, October 2025, a preprint; no journal named in the text; acknowledges anonymous referees)

Effects are structural counterfactuals, not reduced-form estimates. Labels such as 'OECD countries' cover only 11 economies. Family coding: wage gaps coded as labour market (3), income shares as distribution (4). No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Trade Convergence and Deglobalisation: A Cross-country Analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (FE regressions, beta/sigma convergence, GE inequality) of a government AI readiness index on trade ratios for 28 economies (12 advanced, 16 EMDE), with an explicit AE vs EMDE comparison. Borderline on outcome family: the outcomes are Trade/GDP, merchandise trade/GDP and digital service trade/GDP, which are not a listed outcome as such; they are included only because the paper frames digital-service versus merchandise trade as a shift in trade structure (family 2). A reviewer may prefer E3.
exposure_measure: Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index (AIRI), total score from 3 pillars (Government, Technology, Data and Infrastructure), 10 dimensions, 39 indicators; entered in logs. It measures government readiness to deliver AI public services, not AI adoption or use by firms.

sample.economies_or_groups: 12 advanced economies (USA, Singapore, UK, France, Korea, Japan, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Austria, Israel, Czech Republic) and 16 EMDEs (China, Russia, India, Chile, Hungary, Turkiye, Colombia, Viet Nam, Ukraine, Mexico, Armenia, Sri Lanka, Georgia, Kenya, Lao PDR, Ghana)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (advanced vs emerging/developing; EMDEs span upper-middle and lower-middle income; no clearly low-income country); income groups are not formally classified in the paper
sample.years: 2020-2023 for regressions (112 obs); 2005-2023 for GE inequality measures (without AIRI)

design.estimator: Fixed-effects panel regression of ln(trade ratio) on ln(AIRI) interacted with AE/EMDE group dummies (Breusch-Pagan LM and Hausman tests used for choice); beta-convergence panel regressions (absolute and conditional on ln AIRI); sigma-convergence via standard deviation; Generalised Entropy measures (MLD, Theil, half CV) with within/between decomposition.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country fixed effects; controls ln REER, ln FDI, ln GDP per capita (some columns omit GDP or FDI/REER); time dummies mentioned for convergence equation only. Standard errors not stated to be clustered.

heterogeneity.finding: AIRI elasticity is larger for AEs than EMDEs for all three outcomes (0.916 vs 0.853; 0.445 vs 0.303; 0.558 vs 0.364). heterogeneity.finding: Authors argue EMDEs with weak AI readiness (Ghana, Kenya, Georgia) fall into a 'low level equilibrium trap' in digital services and rely on merchandise trade; EMDEs with improving AIRI (China, India) are expected to expand digital service trade. This is narrative interpretation; no estimate by AIRI level within EMDEs is reported.
heterogeneity.evidence: pp.13-14: 'low growth in AIRI spells low growth (or even negative) in trade flows among EMDEs'

income_group_results.high: Advanced economies (12; mostly high income): ln AIRI elasticity 0.9158 (Trade/GDP), 0.4451 (digital service trade/GDP), 0.5584 (merchandise trade/GDP), all significant at 1% (Table A2). Sigma and beta convergence found for all three ratios.
income_group_results.upper_middle: Not separated. Included in the EMDE group (e.g. China, Mexico, Turkiye, Colombia, Russia); EMDE elasticities 0.8534, 0.3032, 0.3644 (Table A2).
income_group_results.lower_middle: Not separated. Included in the EMDE group (e.g. India, Viet Nam, Kenya, Ghana, Lao PDR, Sri Lanka); pooled into the EMDE estimates.
income_group_results.low: not reported (no low-income country appears to be in the sample; classification not given)

n_specifications_reported: about 20 regression columns (3 FE columns in Table A2; 18 beta-convergence regressions in Table A3), plus descriptive sigma and GE tables; the paper also refers to a 'robustness check' control set that is not reported

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('AI can accelerate trade') drawn from FE regressions of trade ratios on a readiness index with no instrument or timing strategy. Reverse causation is plausible (trade-open, digitalised economies score higher on readiness), the sample is 4 years, and the AIRI has little within-country variation, so FE identification is thin. GE and sigma analyses attribute inequality patterns to AIRI without including it.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Conclusions p.16: 'AI can accelerate trade as the coefficient of AIRI is positive and highly statistically significant'; Eq. (1) p.9; Limitations p.16

exposure_measurement.why: AIRI measures government readiness to deliver AI public services, not AI adoption, investment or capability in the private sector or trade. Only 2023 scores and ranks are shown (Table 1), and the paper does not explain how the index varies over 2020-2023. Scores may be partly constructed from digital infrastructure and data indicators correlated with digital trade.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.5 'AIRI attempts to examine country-wise readiness of the government to deliver AI as public services'; Table 1 (2023 only)

selection_of_countries_years.why: 28 countries chosen as 'representative' with no stated rule; 12 AEs and 16 EMDEs. Only 4 years (2020-2023), all in the COVID shock and recovery. Trade/GDP values extrapolated for Japan, USA, Viet Nam (2023) and for Lao PDR for the whole period. No low-income countries.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.9 'year, 2020-2023'; Table 2 note on extrapolated values; p.16 limitation 'data on AIRI is only available from 2020 onwards'

outcome_measurement.why: Trade/GDP, merchandise trade/GDP (World Bank) and digital service trade/GDP (WTO) are standard measures, but none is a productivity or welfare outcome, and extrapolated values enter the data. Trade/GDP is mechanically affected by GDP, which is also a control and in the denominator.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Controls differ across columns in Table A2 (GDP absent in digital column; the 'controls included after the robustness check' row implies a search over controls), AIRI is interacted with group only, and no test of the AE-EMDE difference is given. Several coefficients carry significance stars that do not fit their reported SEs (ln REER -0.0832 with SE 0.0712 marked *; ln REER and ln FDI SEs inconsistent in scale). Conditional beta-convergence regressions have very small SEs (0.0043) and within R2 near 0.99 on 36-84 observations, which suggests specification problems (e.g. mechanical correlation of lagged level, AIRI and the constant).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table A2 rows LNREER, LNFDI and 'Controls included after the Robustness check'; Table A3 conditional columns

selective_reporting.why: Control-variable results are 'not discussed' beyond the table, robustness checks are mentioned but not shown, and the narrative stresses significant results. Non-significant EMDE digital-service convergence is reported. Between-group R2 values in Table A2 are near zero, which is not discussed. The correlation text and the Table A2 column order are inconsistent.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.11 'regression result of the control variables ... corroborates the theoretical literature, hence not discussed here'; Table A2 R2 rows

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Foreign Trade Review (Sage, Indian Institute of Foreign Trade), 2025. Table A2 column header order (Trade, Digital service, Merchandise) differs from the text order (Trade, Merchandise, Digital), so the assignment of coefficients to digital vs merchandise outcomes follows the table header and may be wrong. Table A2 shows within R2 of 0.8584 for Trade/GDP but 0.0561 and 0.1868 for the others, and between and overall R2 near zero. The abstract and text call the AE/EMDE split '28 nations in two sets' (12 + 16). Claims of 'deglobalisation' and 'polarisation' rest on descriptive GE time series (2005-2023) that do not include AIRI, and the link to AI is asserted, not tested; GE measures also rise sharply for 2020 (COVID). The text cites 'Baldwin et al., 2004' where the reference list has 2024. Outcome fit is borderline (trade ratios, not output, labour, poverty or welfare); family 2 was used for the digital-versus-merchandise composition framing. The 'pollution haven' and 'low level equilibrium trap' interpretations are speculative. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extraction.

title: AI capability and labor productivity in low- and middle-income countries: An absorptive capacity approach
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 63 low- and lower-middle-income economies (2005-2019) estimating the association of a PCA-based AI capability index (AI-related hardware imports plus digital/financial/electricity readiness) with labour productivity. Meets AI sample threshold (>=3 economies) and outcome family 1; the AI exposure is a loose proxy, which is handled in risk of bias rather than eligibility.
technology: artificial intelligence (AI-related hardware imports, capability index)
ICT in general (internet use, fixed broadband, mobile cellular subscriptions as index components)
exposure_measure: National 'AI Capability Index' = first principal component (PCA, standardised) of six variables: annual (flow) or 3-year cumulative (stock) per-capita AI-related hardware imports (23 HS 6-digit categories from CEPII BACI, selected using UNCTAD ICT goods list, expert judgement and ChatGPT), plus internet users (% pop), fixed broadband per 100, mobile cellular per 100, electricity access (%), and account ownership (%). Five of six components are general ICT/infrastructure/finance indicators. Alternative interaction specification uses log AI imports per capita x a PCA Domestic Readiness Index; a narrow index uses only GPU/TPU/FPGA/ASIC/memory HS codes.

sample.economies_or_groups: Low- and middle-income countries; initial panel of 80 LMICs, effective sample 63 with complete data; country list not given in the main text. Heterogeneity analysis only splits low-income vs lower-middle-income.
sample.income_groups_covered: low and lower-middle (the income dummy is LMI=1, low-income=0); upper-middle inclusion unclear

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, random effects, two-way fixed effects (preferred; country-clustered robust SEs); interaction FE models; two-step system GMM (xtabond2, Windmeijer-corrected, collapsed instruments, 30-35 instruments); FE with regressors lagged 1-6 years.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year FE; controls: gross fixed capital formation, human capital index, population growth, strength of legal rights index, R&D % GDP, FDI % GDP, trade % GDP. GMM treats lagged productivity and the AI index as endogenous using own lags. Authors explicitly say estimates are associations, not causal.

n_specifications_reported: approximately 80 regression columns (Tables 4-8, 10-13 and D.1-D.6, including pooled/RE/FE, GMM, lags, narrow indices)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Two-way FE plus controls, a system GMM with internal instruments, and 1-6 year lags are used, and the authors repeatedly disclaim causality. But the index is a generic digital/infrastructure development composite, so time-varying omitted factors (reforms, structural change, overall development) and reverse causation (richer countries import more hardware and have better connectivity) are not excluded; GMM instruments are internal lags only, and the AI index is a lagged regressor in GMM. No external instrument or event timing.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Sec. 5.6, p.14-15: 'does not fully address potential simultaneity'; Sec. 5.7, p.16-17: 'does not eliminate endogeneity arising from time-varying omitted factors'; Sec. 6.4: 'results remain associative'

exposure_measurement.why: Only 1 of 6 index components is AI-related (per-capita imports of 23 dual-use ICT hardware HS codes, partly selected with ChatGPT; includes laptops, phones, monitors, keyboards). The other five are general ICT, electricity and financial inclusion. PCA first component therefore mostly measures general digital/infrastructure development; the authors state it does not capture realised AI use. Narrow index (GPU/TPU/ASIC etc.) gives similar results but still reflects imports of chips that are largely general electronics and is also mixed into the index with the same readiness variables. Readiness variables come from an imputed dataset.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Sec. 4.1.1, p.7 and fn 2-4: 'many of these goods are not uniquely AI-specific'; Sec. 4.1, p.7: 'does not capture realized AI use or economic outcomes'; Table 1, p.6

selection_of_countries_years.why: 63 of an initial 80 LMICs retained based on data availability for all variables; effective N=871 of up to 945 country-years (unbalanced), yet descriptive statistics show 1200 obs for many variables, indicating the 80-country panel was completed by multiple imputation (MICE). Country list not shown in main text. No bias analysis of excluded countries; sample restricted to 2005-2019, pre-generative AI, so results describe general ICT/hardware accumulation.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sec. 4, p.6: 'effective sample ... comprises a robust panel of 63 LMICs'; Table 2, p.7 (obs 1200 vs 1093 for labour productivity)

outcome_measurement.why: Log real GDP per worker from WDI is a standard measure, but the paper defines it inconsistently (GDP / total labour force in Table 1; GDP per capita divided by total employment in Sec. 4.3; real GDP per worker in Sec. 5.1). Text states ICT 'significant' contribution can be identified in one place (p.12) but no ICT test is significant at conventional levels. No instruction-like text found.

title: The nonlinear link between AI and energy poverty: Empirical evidence from global data
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country panel (64 economies, 2000-2019, high/upper-middle/lower-middle income) estimating the association of an AI proxy with an energy poverty index (electricity access, clean cooking, per capita energy and electricity), which is a living-standards/resource outcome. Borderline on exposure: the AI measure is industrial robot stock, and the paper itself says results are evidence on industrial automation rather than AI broadly; kept because the paper frames and tests it as AI (with an AI-patent robustness check).
technology: artificial intelligence (proxied by industrial robot stock per million employees; AI patent stock in robustness)
exposure_measure: Natural log of IFR total industrial robot stock per million employees (lnRobot_Stock); robustness uses AI patent stock (WIPO/OECD). Authors state it captures embodied automation, not software AI.

sample.economies_or_groups: Balanced panel of 64 countries listed in Appendix A (28 high-income, 24 upper-middle, 12 lower-middle); selected by IFR and energy-poverty data availability; Sub-Saharan Africa underrepresented
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle (no low-income countries)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects with country-clustered SEs; system GMM (Blundell-Bond, collapsed instruments, lags t-2 to t-3); quadratic specification with Lind-Mehlum U test; interaction models; stepwise mediation with bootstrap; 2SLS and Bartik shift-share IV and spatial lag as robustness
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: ln GDP per capita, urbanization, industry share, trade openness, FDI; country and year fixed effects; lagged dependent variable in GMM

results.indicator: Composite energy poverty index (0-1; geometric mean of electricity access, clean cooking access, per capita electricity use, per capita energy supply; higher = more poverty), quadratic in lnRobot_Stock, preferred system GMM with controls
results.estimate: Inverted U. lnRobot_Stock 0.0517, lnRobot_Stock^2 -0.0044; turning point lnRobot_Stock 5.88 (about 358 robots per million employees). Two-way FE with controls: 0.0370 and -0.0030, turning point 6.17.
results.uncertainty: GMM p=0.017 and p=0.016 (** level); Lind-Mehlum p=0.039; AR(2) p=0.198; Hansen p=0.387. FE with controls p=0.051 and 0.057; Lind-Mehlum p=0.047.
results.evidence: p.13 Table 6 col 4: "lnRobot_Stock 0.0517** (0.017) ... lnRobot_Stock2 -0.0044** (0.016)"; Turning point 5.88

results.indicator: Marginal effect of lnRobot_Stock on EP_Index at lnRobot_Stock=7.0 (about 1,100 robots per million employees), GMM col 4
results.estimate: About -0.010 per unit of lnRobot_Stock; a further 1 SD (1.89) rise implies about -0.019 EP_Index units (about 10% of EP SD 0.19). At the sample mean (5.21, on the rising arm) the marginal effect is small and positive.
results.uncertainty: not reported (no SE or CI given for the marginal effect in text; Fig. 7 shows 95% CI)
results.evidence: p.12 Section 4.2: "At lnRobot_Stock = 7.0 ... marginal effect on EP_Index is approximately -0.010"

results.indicator: Alternative specifications of the inverted-U (robustness): AI patent stock, electricity access rate as DV, excluding oil exporters, excluding 2008-10, 2SLS, Bartik IV, spatial lag
results.estimate: Inverted U retained in all eight reported checks; linear coefficient 0.0420 to 0.0552, quadratic -0.0034 to -0.0048, turning points 5.75 to 6.18 (2SLS 0.0535/-0.0045, TP 5.94; Bartik 0.0494/-0.0042, TP 5.88)
results.uncertainty: Significance stars only: * to *** (10% to 1%); no SEs shown in text; full tables said to be in an Online Appendix
results.evidence: p.17 Table 10: "Inverted U Confirmed? Yes" for all rows; "full coefficient tables are available in the Online Appendix" (p.16)

results.indicator: Energy intensity (MJ per $ PPP GDP) as mediator: Step 1 AI to energy intensity, quadratic
results.estimate: Linear -0.152 (FE), -0.168 (GMM); quadratic +0.013 (FE), +0.014 (GMM); bootstrap indirect effect -0.004 (FE), -0.005 (GMM)
results.uncertainty: *** on linear terms, ** on quadratic; bootstrap 95% CI [-0.008,-0.001] (FE) and [-0.009,-0.001] (GMM)
results.evidence: p.15 Table 8 Panel A and Table 9: "Energy Efficiency FE -0.004 [-0.008, -0.001]"

results.indicator: Renewable energy share of final consumption as mediator: Step 1 AI to renewable share, quadratic
results.estimate: Linear +0.118 (FE), +0.130 (GMM); quadratic -0.008 (FE), -0.009 (GMM); bootstrap indirect effect -0.002 (FE), -0.003 (GMM) on EP_Index
results.uncertainty: *** on linear, * on quadratic; bootstrap 95% CI [-0.005,-0.001] (FE), [-0.006,-0.001] (GMM)
results.evidence: p.15 Table 8 Panel B and Table 9: "Renewable Energy Sys-GMM -0.003 [-0.006, -0.001]"

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of lnRobot_Stock^2 with human capital is positive (0.002, p about 0.065-0.078), read by the author as higher human capital flattening the curve and lowering the EP level (main effect of HC -0.120 to -0.135***). Median-split grouped regressions: low-HC group has larger coefficients (GMM 0.0890/-0.0090***, TP 4.94) while high-HC group is insignificant (GMM 0.0310/-0.0020, TP 7.75). Text turning points by HC: about 5.0 (low) and 5.83 (high).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (turning points 4.94-5.17 low HC; 7.75-9.00 high HC in grouped regressions)
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 Table 7 cols 1-2: "lnRobot_Stock2 x Z 0.002* (0.078) / 0.002* (0.065)"; p.20 Table B1

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of lnRobot_Stock^2 with institutional quality (rule of law, government effectiveness) positive (0.001, p about 0.082-0.091); main effect of Z -0.095 to -0.110***. Grouped: low-institution group significant (GMM 0.0950/-0.0100***, TP 4.75), high-institution group insignificant (0.0280/-0.0020, TP 7.00).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (turning points 4.75-5.07 low institutions; 7.00-11.00 high institutions)
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 Table 7 cols 3-4; p.21 Table B2

heterogeneity.finding: No formal income-group split in the regressions; income groups appear only descriptively in Fig. 4(b). Authors state results mainly characterise middle- and high-income economies and have limited applicability to Sub-Saharan Africa. No low-income country is in the sample.
heterogeneity.evidence: Abstract and p.19 Section 5.4; Appendix A note: "high-income (n = 28), upper-middle-income (n = 24), and lower-middle-income (n = 12)"

income_group_results.high: not reported separately (sample includes 28 high-income countries; only pooled results)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (24 countries in pooled sample)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (12 countries in pooled sample)
income_group_results.low: not applicable: no low-income countries in the sample

n_specifications_reported: about 35 (Table 6: 4; Table 7: 4; Tables B1-B2: 10; Table 8: 8 plus Table 9: 4; Table 10: 8 rows)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors explicitly frame results as conditional associations, not causal. Sys-GMM, a 2SLS with frontier-country patent stocks and a Bartik shift-share instrument are offered, but exclusion restrictions are argued only verbally, no first-stage statistics or overidentification results are reported in the text, and it is unclear how the quadratic term is instrumented. Robot adoption is strongly tied to income and industrialisation (r=0.71 with GDP per capita).
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.10 Section 3.3.3 ("robust conditional associations rather than identified causal parameters"); p.16-17 Section 4.5 IV description; p.17 Table 10

exposure_measurement.why: Industrial robot stock per million employees is a measure of manufacturing automation, not AI in the sense of machine learning or generative AI; the author concedes it does not capture software AI. Patent stock is the only alternative and is also imperfect. Robot stock is near zero in many low-income economies.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.9 Section 3.1: "central findings should be read as evidence on industrial automation rather than AI broadly construed"; p.19 Section 5.4

selection_of_countries_years.why: Balanced panel of 64 countries chosen by data availability and IFR coverage; no low-income countries and almost no Sub-Saharan Africa (only South Africa appears in the list despite the note saying 'fewer than 10'). Turning point is derived mainly from industrialised economies. 20-year window.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.9 Section 3.1; p.20 Appendix A country list and note; p.19 Section 5.4

outcome_measurement.why: Composite index of four standardised sub-indicators combined by geometric mean; two components (per capita electricity use and energy supply) measure consumption levels that rise with income and industrialisation, so the index partly reflects development. Direction coding of these components within a poverty index is not explained. Electricity-access-only robustness is provided.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.10 Table 4: "geometric mean of four standardised sub-indicators"; p.17 Table 10 Alt. DV: Electricity access

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Quadratic functional form chosen a priori but the U-shape is tested only within one parametric form; many specifications (FE and GMM, with and without controls, interactions, groups, robustness). GMM instrument count not reported. The Table 7 interaction coefficients differ greatly in magnitude from baseline (linear 0.12 vs 0.05), and the 'three-way interaction' label actually refers to two-way interactions of AI and AI^2 with a moderator.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.10 Eq. 1-3; p.14 Table 7 (linear 0.095-0.121, quadratic -0.006 to -0.011); p.13 Table 6

selective_reporting.why: All eight robustness checks and both mechanism channels confirm the hypotheses; the full robustness tables are not in the paper (Online Appendix). Heterogeneity interaction terms are significant only at the 10% level yet read as support. Marginal effects quoted in text for human capital levels do not reproduce from Table 7 (see notes). Table notes contain leftover revision language.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.16 Section 4.5 ("full coefficient tables are available in the Online Appendix"); p.14 Table 7 and Section 4.3 text

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Exposure is industrial robots labelled as AI: borderline for the AI exposure criterion; included because the paper tests AI patents as well and frames the study as AI, but a human reviewer may prefer to reclassify as automation. Internal inconsistencies found: (1) Table 7 text gives marginal effects at the sample mean of lnRobot_Stock of about -0.010 (mean HC), +0.008 (HC -1 SD) and -0.028 (HC +1 SD); recomputing from Table 7 col 2 (0.121, -0.011, interactions -0.018 and 0.002, SD of HC 0.58) gives roughly +0.006 at mean HC, +0.005 at -1 SD and +0.008 at +1 SD, so the stated values and their ordering do not reproduce (my own calculation, check). (2) Descriptive ranges differ between text and Table 5 (text: human capital 1.6-4.4, institutions -1.8 to 1.9; Table 5: 1.81-4.39 and -1.43 to 2.11). (3) Appendix A note says fewer than 10 Sub-Saharan African countries but only South Africa is a Sub-Saharan country in the list (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia are North African). (4) Table notes (Tables 5, 6, 10) and text refer to earlier versions ('previously 5.21', 'formerly Table 3', 'Coefficients are now reported to four decimal places so the implied turning point is internally consistent') indicating post-hoc rounding to match the headline turning point; two-decimal coefficients would not give 5.88. (5) Reference list problems: Dong et al. (2021) is cited as digital finance IV study but listed as a low-carbon energy transition causality paper; Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson 'colonial origins' given as 2007 vol 91(5). (6) Policy section says the high-capacity marginal effect is about three times larger than for low-capacity countries, while Section 4.3 shows the low-capacity effect positive. Result contrasts with Zhu et al. (2025) cited in the paper (AI effect stronger in low-income countries). Data available only on request. No prompt-injection or directive text found in the paper.

title: Exploring the Moderating impact of ICT Infrastructure on Trade Openness-Sectoral Growth Nexus in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA)
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (PMG/ARDL) of 26 SSA economies with ICT infrastructure (internet, mobile, fixed-line, composite index) as exposure and sectoral value added (output / structural change) as outcome; meets the 10-economy threshold.
exposure_measure: Individual internet users (% pop), mobile cellular subscriptions per 100, fixed telephone subscriptions per 100, and a PCA-based ICT infrastructure index (ICTINF); each interacted with trade openness (trade/GDP).

sample.economies_or_groups: 26 Sub-Saharan African countries (names not listed in the text read)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported

design.estimator: Pooled Mean Group ARDL (PMG/ARDL), long-run and short-run; Pesaran CD, CIPS/CADF unit root, Pedroni and Kao cointegration tests
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Gross fixed capital formation/GDP (labelled human capital investment), labour participation, FDI/GDP, GDP per capita (log); country-specific short-run heterogeneity; no instrument.

results.indicator: Agriculture value added: long-run trade openness (ln TO) in models with ICT interactions
results.estimate: -0.0921 to -0.1807 (log-level coefficients, columns 1-4)
results.evidence: Table 9, Long Run LNTO; text p.113: 'a 1% increase in LNTO associated with a 0.13-0.18% decline in agricultural sector growth'

results.evidence: Table 9, column 4, ICT_INF

results.evidence: Table 9, column 3, FTS

results.evidence: Table 9, column 3, TO_FTS; interactions with IUI, MCS, ICTINF not significant

results.evidence: Table 10, Long Run, columns 1, 2, 4; text p.115: 'ICT_INF emerges as a positive and significant driver in model 4'

results.estimate: TO_ICTINF -0.0648; TO_IUI -0.0154; TO_MCS -0.0013

results.indicator: Industry value added: trade openness (ln TO)
results.evidence: Table 10, Long Run LNTO

results.indicator: Services value added: ICT infrastructure index (ICT_INF) and internet use (IUI)
results.evidence: Table 11, Long Run, columns 1 and 4 (ICT_INF figures identical to Table 10)

results.indicator: Services value added: trade openness x ICT interactions
results.estimate: TO_IUI -0.0328; TO_MCS -0.0013; TO_ICTINF -0.0648
results.evidence: Table 11, Long Run interaction rows

results.indicator: Sector value added: short-run effects of trade openness, ICT and interactions (all three sectors)
results.estimate: mostly insignificant; e.g. agriculture short-run LNTO 0.0940 to 0.1232
results.evidence: Tables 9-11 Short Run; text p.114: 'trade openness, ICT variables, and their interactions are largely insignificant'

heterogeneity.finding: ICT effect positive and significant for industry and services in the long run, but not for agriculture, where only fixed-line (negative alone, positive when interacted with trade) is significant.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 9-11; Conclusion p.118: 'ICT infrastructure generally supports industrial and service sector growth in the long run'

heterogeneity.finding: Trade openness moderates ICT: interaction terms are negative in industry and services, so the ICT coefficient falls as openness rises (authors interpret ICT and openness as substitutes). Sign of net effect depends on the level of ICT.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 3.2 eq. 7 and Tables 10-11; text p.117: 'each 1% increase in openness lowers ICT's contribution to service growth by 0.03%-0.06%'

n_specifications_reported: 12 main long-run/short-run model columns (4 ICT measures x 3 sectors)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: PMG/ARDL with contemporaneous ICT and trade; no instrument or event timing. The text claims the model accounts for endogeneity, but the Conclusion concedes results are correlational. Interaction terms are not separately identified.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4.3 p.113; Conclusion p.118: 'results remain correlational and cannot establish definitive causality'

exposure_measurement.why: The PCA ICT index is internally inconsistent: Table 3 shows ICTINF with skewness and kurtosis identical to MCS and a correlation of 1.000 with MCS, and Tables 6-7 show ICTINF test statistics identical to IUI. It is unclear what the index captures. Fixed-line telephony is included, which the authors admit may overstate relevance.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 2, Table 3, Table 4 (ICTINF row), Table 6, Table 7; Limitations p.118

selection_of_countries_years.why: 26 SSA countries chosen by data availability; balanced panel 1992-2023 (26 x 32 = 832 observations). Methods text gives two different periods (1992-2023 and 1991-2022). Country list not shown in the text read.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.107 'Data availability dictated the choice of economies and periods'; Section 3.3 p.109; Table 9 N=832

outcome_measurement.why: The dependent variables labelled 'sectoral growth' are sector value added as a share of GDP (mean 21.3, 26.1, 45.9), not growth rates; interpretation as growth effects is inconsistent. Shares are legitimate structural-change measures but the paper does not treat them as such.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 3 (Agric. sector value added mean 21.3032; Serv. 45.8963); text p.110: 'Agriculture growth (AGRV) shows a mean of 21.3%'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four alternative ICT measures each entered one at a time with interactions in three sectors; variables of mixed order I(0)/I(1) fed to PMG; ICT/trade enter partly in logs and partly in levels; control sets and column contents differ; table numbering in text (4.10, 4.12, 4.13) does not match the tables. Uncorrected multiple testing.

selective_reporting.why: Table 10 (industry) and Table 11 (services) report identical coefficients and standard errors in columns 2-4 for long-run and short-run rows (e.g. LNTO -0.0396, -0.1151, -0.0978; ICTINF 0.2594), which is implausible for different dependent variables and suggests a copy-paste error. Text then reports the same 0.26 ICT effect for both sectors. Unclear whether reported results are the actual estimates.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 10 columns 2-4 versus Table 11 columns 2-4; p.116 and p.117 text on ICT_INF 0.2594

venue_quality_concern: possible (NIU Journal of Humanities, a humanities-titled journal with an economics paper; apparent duplicated result tables; at least one irrelevant citation)
notes: Outcome is sector value-added share, so results are about structural composition as much as output. Duplicated columns across Tables 10 and 11 and the ICT index inconsistency should be checked by a human; effect estimates for industry and services cannot be told apart in 9 of 12 columns. Reference list contains a mismatched citation: Varriale et al. (2024) is 'Coal and Mines in the Era of Fascist Ventennio in Italy' but is cited in the text as a study of renewable energy and growth in the E-7. Several citations (e.g. Swammy and Dharni, 2020) look unrelated to the claims. Text claims on ICT index percent effects treat a standardised PCA index as a log. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

title: The Digital Maturity Paradox: The Divergent Impact of Network Readiness and FDI Across Development Tiers
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country OLS on 121 economies with an explicit developing vs developed comparison; exposure is the Network Readiness Index (ICT capability) and the outcome is GDP per capita growth (family 1).
technology: ICT in general (composite Network Readiness Index)
exposure_measure: Network Readiness Index 2023 (Portulans Institute), 0-100 composite of ICT capability, min-max rescaled to [0,1] (NRIT). Composite index, not a direct adoption or investment measure.

sample.economies_or_groups: 76 developing and 45 developed economies (2023 World Bank classification); Malta and Singapore flagged as outlier hubs and dropped in a robustness run (N=43)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (binary split developing vs developed; sub-groups of low, lower-middle, upper-middle not separated)

design.estimator: Cross-sectional OLS with HC1 (White) robust standard errors, estimated separately for developing and developed cohorts; Chow breakpoint test for the split; VIF, RESET, BPG, Cook's D, DFBETAS diagnostics
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Only FDI inflows (% GDP, IHS-transformed) and trade openness (% GDP, IHS-transformed); no income level, human capital, institutions, investment or population controls; no fixed effects; no lags.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth (2023, IHS-transformed) on Network Readiness Index (NRIT), developing economies N=76
results.estimate: 1.106 (coefficient on min-max NRI in IHS(growth) units; roughly a full-range move of NRI across the sample)
results.evidence: Table 4, p.10: 'Normalized Network Readiness (NRIT) 1.106 *** (0.0027)'

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on NRIT, developed economies N=45
results.uncertainty: p = 0.0895 (10% level only); adj R2 = 0.0161; overall F p = 0.3072

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on NRIT, developed economies excluding Malta and Singapore N=43
results.evidence: Table 6, p.13: 'Normalized Network Readiness (NRIT) -0.734 * (0.0895) | -0.693 (0.1166)'

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on FDI inflows (control, not the exposure of interest), developing / developed
results.estimate: developing 0.246; developed 0.036 (N=43: -0.050)
results.uncertainty: developing p = 0.0116; developed p = 0.6724; N=43 p = 0.5433
results.evidence: Table 4, p.10 and Table 6, p.13

heterogeneity.finding: NRI coefficient is large and positive in developing economies and negative and weak (10% level) in developed economies; the sign reversal is read by the authors as saturation of digital returns. Chow test rejects equal coefficients across the split.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (exogenous split at the World Bank high-income boundary, observation 77; no endogenous threshold estimated)
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.3.4, p.13: 'Chow Breakpoint Test (CBPT) at the high-income transition boundary (Observation 77) ... F = 11.91, p < 0.01'

income_group_results.high: Developed cohort (N=45): NRIT -0.734 (p=0.0895), not robust once Malta and Singapore are dropped (-0.693, p=0.1166); model jointly insignificant (F p=0.3072)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort, NRIT +1.106, p=0.0027)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort)

n_specifications_reported: about 3 (developing, developed, developed excluding two outliers), plus diagnostics

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Single-year cross-section of growth on a contemporaneous composite readiness index with only FDI and trade as controls; no income level, human capital, institutions or investment controls; no instrument or timing. NRI is strongly correlated with income and development, so it proxies for general development. Authors use causal language ('growth multiplier', 'catalysts', policy prescriptions).
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.5 Eq. (3), p.7; Section 5.2, p.15 policy prescriptions based on 'growth elasticity of network readiness (beta = 1.106)'

exposure_measurement.why: NRI is a composite that includes technology, people, governance and impact pillars; it is not a measure of ICT adoption or investment and may mix in outcomes. Min-max rescaling makes the coefficient hard to interpret.

selection_of_countries_years.why: One year (2023), 121 economies chosen by NRI availability; 2023 growth is a noisy single-year observation that includes post-pandemic rebound and shocks. Developed group includes small hubs (Malta, Singapore); developed mean growth of -0.37% in 2023 looks unusual and is not discussed. Sample splitting at the group boundary is then 'validated' by a Chow test at that same boundary.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.2, p.6; Table 3, p.8; Section 4.3.4, p.13

outcome_measurement.why: WDI real GDP per capita growth is standard, but it is a one-year rate and is passed through an inverse hyperbolic sine transform, which is unusual for a growth rate near zero (approx. identity for small values) and complicates the reading of 'elasticity'.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Missing trade values imputed with group medians (landlocked/coastal); split by development tier chosen by the authors; outlier exclusion after looking at diagnostics; very low explanatory power (adj R2 0.016 in developed cohort). Developed-cohort NRI result significant only at 10%. No test of the NRI coefficient difference with an interaction term beyond the Chow test.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.4, p.7; Section 4.4, p.13; Table 4, p.10

selective_reporting.why: Few specifications and results are reported in full, including null ones, but the interpretation overstates weak evidence ('conclusive empirical weight', 'mathematically proves', 'fully supported') and the abstract headlines the 10%-level negative coefficient.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract and Section 4.4, p.14: 'The Fitness Gap mathematically proves that advanced economies have entirely outgrown infrastructure-led development'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Treat as descriptive cross-sectional association, not causal. title: The relationship between inequality and poverty in developing countries: mitigating role of virtual social network and internet access in schools
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country Tobit study of 57 developing economies in which the use of virtual social networks and internet access in schools (internet use, survey-based) moderate the effect of inequality on the poverty headcount (family 4). Meets the at least 10 economies rule.
technology: internet (use of virtual social networks; internet use in schools)
exposure_measure: Two Global Information Technology Report executive-survey indices, each scored 1-7: extent to which virtual social networks (Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn) are used in the country, and extent to which the internet is used in schools for learning; not a measure of subscriptions or users. Appendix notes that zero is assigned when there is no official data.

sample.n_economies: 57 (stated); regression uses 43 observations
sample.economies_or_groups: 57 non-OECD developing countries with available data (footnote 1 list, e.g. Bangladesh, Benin, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, Philippines, Ukraine, Vietnam, Yemen, Zimbabwe)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (non-OECD developing economies, predominantly low and lower-middle income; no income-group split)

design.estimator: Double-censored Tobit regression (censoring at 0 and 100 percent) of poverty headcount on Gini, technology indicator, Gini x technology interaction and controls; marginal effects (dy/dx) also reported; thresholds computed as ratio of Gini coefficient to interaction coefficient.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Remittances (% GDP), log population, gender parity in school enrolment, adult literacy; no country or time fixed effects; no instruments. Authors state that cross-sectional dependence, reverse causality and unobserved country and time heterogeneity are 'shortcomings in the present study'.

results.indicator: Interaction of virtual social network use with Gini on poverty headcount (% of population, national poverty lines)
results.estimate: -33.506 (Tobit coefficient), -32.607 (dy/dx); unconditional Gini effect +118.022 / +114.855; implied technology threshold 3.5224 (on a 1-7 scale, sample mean 4.83)
results.uncertainty: p-values: 0.004 (coefficient), 0.002 (dy/dx); Gini main effect p=0.024 / 0.016; no confidence interval for the threshold; Fisher test 3.87***
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12, Models 1-2, row '[Social Network] x Gini'

results.indicator: Interaction of internet use in schools with Gini on poverty headcount
results.estimate: -54.278 (coefficient), -52.841 (dy/dx); Gini main effect +132.410 / +128.906; implied threshold 2.4394 (sample mean 3.24)
results.uncertainty: p-values: 0.027 (coefficient), 0.018 (dy/dx); Gini main effect p=0.080 / 0.067; Fisher test 3.11**
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12, Models 3-4, row '[Internet in Schools] x Gini'

results.indicator: Unconditional (own) effect of technology indicators on poverty headcount, at Gini = 0
results.estimate: Social network +18.257 (dy/dx +17.767); internet in schools +28.820 (dy/dx +28.058). Reviewer calculation from the table: at the sample mean Gini of 0.501 the implied marginal effect of the technology measure is still positive (about +1.5 for social network, +1.6 for internet in schools)
results.uncertainty: p=0.006 and 0.003 (social network); p=0.022 and 0.014 (internet in schools)
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12; text p.11: 'the unconditional effects of the moderators ... are not relevant for the outcome of the study'

heterogeneity.finding: The effect of inequality on poverty is modelled as conditional on the technology level: positive below a threshold and negative above it. Thresholds 3.52 (virtual social networks, range 2.571-6.234) and 2.44 (internet in schools, range 1.339-5.050) are said to be below the sample means. No heterogeneity by income group, region or institutions is examined.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 3.5224 (virtual social network index); 2.4394 (internet in schools index)
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4, p.10-11; Table 1 p.12

n_specifications_reported: 2 regression specifications (one per technology indicator), each shown as coefficient and marginal effect, so 4 columns

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Pooled Tobit with four controls, no country or time effects, no instruments; poverty, inequality and technology use are jointly determined with income, yet the abstract uses causal language (technology 'mitigates' the effect of inequality). Authors concede reverse causality and cross-sectional dependence are unaddressed.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Conclusion p.14: 'adopt the relevant estimation techniques that take into account apparent concerns of cross-sectional dependence and reverse causality'; Section 3.2 p.9

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is a perception-based executive survey score of how widely social networks are used and how far the internet is used in schools; it does not measure adoption, users or access. Appendix says zero is assigned when official data is missing, which, if present in the regression sample, would be a gross measurement error (reported minimum is 2.571, so unclear). Correlation between the two indices is 0.84.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Appendix 1 notes p.15; Appendix 2 p.15; Appendix 3 p.15

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample determined by availability of GTIR data and by non-OECD status; 57 countries named but only 43 observations in regressions (poverty has 84 observations over five years), so the estimation sample is small and countries entering it are not identified.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.7 and footnote 1; Appendix 2 p.15 (Poverty 84 obs); Table 1 p.12 (Observations 43)

outcome_measurement.why: Poverty headcount at national poverty lines (WDI) is not comparable across countries and years and is available for few observations. Gini from GCIP is described as measuring 'distribution of wealth' although it is an income measure.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Tobit with limits 0 and 100 although observed poverty ranges only 0.4-66.5, so no censoring occurs and the choice is not warranted by the data; about 43 observations for 7 regressors and an interaction; thresholds are point estimates from ratios with no confidence interval; interaction result relies on Gini scaled 0-1.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.2 p.9; Appendix 2 p.15 (poverty min 0.400, max 66.500); Table 1 p.12

selective_reporting.why: Only two models are shown, no robustness checks or alternative estimators. The positive unconditional effects of the technology variables on poverty are reported but set aside as 'not relevant', while the abstract emphasises the mitigating role.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 4, p.11 (paragraph on unconditional effects); Table 1 p.12

venue_quality_concern: possible (working paper of the first author's own research centre, EXCAS WP/24/011, stated as forthcoming in International Journal of Social Economics; heavy self-citation)
notes: Parentheses in Table 1 are p-values, not standard errors (inferred from layout, e.g. constant -40.802 (0.339); not stated explicitly in the table note). The 57-country list and 43 regression observations are not reconciled. Net-effect arithmetic in the text (threshold 3.5224) checks out against the coefficients. Not a payoff-for-technology study in the usual sense: technology enters as a moderator of the inequality-poverty link. No instruction-like text found.

title: IMPACT OF MOBILE PHONES AND INTERNET USE ON FINANCIAL INCLUSION: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE FROM THE EU POST-COMMUNIST COUNTRIES
decision_rationale: Own panel cointegration and causality estimation of mobile subscriptions and Internet use on financial inclusion indices for 11 economies (meets the 10-economy threshold for non-AI technology). Outcome is financial inclusion (family 5).
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people and individuals using the Internet (% of population), World Bank (Table 1)

sample.economies_or_groups: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Czech Republic, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia (EU post-communist)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (single regional group, EU post-communist members)

design.estimator: Westerlund-Edgerton (2008) panel cointegration test with structural breaks; AMG (Augmented Mean Group) long-run coefficients; Dumitrescu-Hurlin (2012) panel Granger causality; CIPS unit root, CD and slope-homogeneity pretests
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No control variables; two bivariate-style models (FIA or FMA on MOBILE and INTERNET); country-specific coefficients and break dates; AMG common dynamic process handles cross-section dependence

results.indicator: Financial institutions access index (FIA: bank branches and ATMs per 100,000 adults), effect of mobile subscriptions, panel AMG
results.estimate: 0.0015297 index units per 1 additional subscription per 100 people (authors call it 'very low')
results.uncertainty: significant at 5% (** in Table 7a); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7a, Panel row; text p.733: '1 unit change in mobile cellular subscriptions led a 0.0015297 increase'

results.indicator: FIA, effect of Internet users (% pop), panel AMG
results.uncertainty: no significance stars (not significant); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7a, Panel row, INTERNET column

results.indicator: Financial markets access index (FMA: market cap outside top 10 firms, number of debt issuers), effect of mobile subscriptions, panel AMG
results.uncertainty: no significance stars; se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7b, Panel row, MOBILE column

results.indicator: FMA, effect of Internet users (% pop), panel AMG
results.estimate: 0.0025709 index units per 1 percentage point of Internet users
results.uncertainty: significant at 10% (* in Table 7b); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7b, Panel row, INTERNET column; text p.733: 'Internet usage positively influenced financial markets access'

results.indicator: Country-level long-run effects (11 countries x 2 outcomes x 2 exposures)
results.estimate: Mobile to FIA significantly positive in Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovenia (largest Latvia 0.0070) and negative in Czech Republic (-0.0014). Internet to FIA positive in Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Rep., Hungary, Poland; negative in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovenia (e.g. Latvia -0.0157)
results.evidence: Table 7a and 7b; text p.734: 'The effect of Internet usage rate on financial institutions' access is negative in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Slovenia'

results.indicator: Short-run Granger causality (first differences)
results.estimate: DMOBILE to DFIA: W=4.77, Zbar=2.93; DINTERNET to DFIA: Zbar=2.07; reverse DFIA to DINTERNET: Zbar=1.97; no significant causality involving FMA, no reverse causality from FIA to mobile
results.uncertainty: p=0.0034 (mobile to FIA); p=0.0381 (Internet to FIA); p=0.0485 (FIA to Internet); FMA links p=0.26 to 0.94
results.evidence: Table 8, p.734

heterogeneity.finding: Effects differ in sign and significance across countries (e.g. mobile to FIA positive in 5 countries, negative in Czech Republic; Internet to FIA negative in 4 countries). Authors note a Central Europe vs South-East Europe/Baltic grouping by financial development but do not test it.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 7a-7b; Introduction p.724-725; Section 3 p.734

n_specifications_reported: about 4 main long-run models (2 outcomes, each with panel + 11 country estimates), plus 8 causality tests and 3 versions of cointegration test (no break, level break, regime shift)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: No control variables (income, banking regulation, financial development) and causal 'impact' wording; the causality test itself shows feedback from financial institutions access to Internet use, and no instrument or timing design.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 2.2; Table 8 (DFIA does not Granger-cause DINTERNET rejected at p=0.0485)

exposure_measurement.why: Standard World Bank indicators (subscriptions per 100 people; % Internet users), but subscriptions count SIMs, not users, and the two exposures are entered jointly without interaction.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 11 post-communist EU members chosen by transition history; N=11 and T=22 limit the power of the panel tests; authors acknowledge the small sample as the main limitation.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 2.1 p.728; Conclusions p.735: 'main limitation of our research is the sample size'

outcome_measurement.why: FIA is branches and ATMs per 100,000 adults (supply of outlets) and FMA is market capitalisation outside the top 10 firms plus number of debt issuers (market depth). Neither measures household account ownership or use; authors admit no single indicator captures inclusion.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 2.1 p.727-728: 'not a single indicator that can capture accurately the multidimensional concept of financial inclusion'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Several test variants and break structures; cointegration is rejected for 'no break' only weakly in Model 1 (Zf p=0.091) and not rejected for level-break; Model 2 shows no cross-section dependence yet the same dependence-robust AMG estimator is applied. Short T relative to the number of break parameters.

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and conclusions foreground significant country results; conclusions claim 'significant positive influence' on both indices 'in both the short and long run' although panel Internet to FIA is negative and insignificant, panel mobile to FMA is insignificant, and no short-run causality involves FMA.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Internal inconsistencies for the reviewer: (1) text p.732 says no-cointegration is rejected 'for both models for no break and regime shift', but Table 6a Model 1 Zf(N) no-break p=0.091 and the level-break tests are not significant; (2) Conclusions say Internet positively affects FIA in several countries 'but weak in the panel' while Table 7a panel coefficient is negative (-0.0012) and insignificant; (3) Table 5 first-difference CIPS statistics for D(FIA) and D(INTERNET) with trend (0.079, 0.094) are positive and flagged significant, which looks like a reporting error. Standard errors are not given for coefficients. No instruction-like text found.

title: Impact of Economic Integration and Information and Communication Technology on Economic Growth for European Union: Dynamic Panel GMM Approach
decision_rationale: Dynamic panel GMM on 27 EU countries (at least 10 economies) with internet users and mobile subscriptions as ICT exposure and GDP per capita as outcome (family 1).
technology: internet use (users per hundred, labelled ICT usage)
exposure_measure: Natural log of internet users per hundred population (IU) and log of mobile phone subscriptions (MS), from World Bank/ITU; interacted with log trade/GDP (economic integration).

sample.economies_or_groups: EU member states (Figure 1 lists the United Kingdom as well; text says 27 EU countries)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (EU countries only; no income classification given)

design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged log GDP per capita, log trade/GDP, log human capital (PWT), log employment (persons engaged), log inflation; time effects not mentioned; 18-21 instruments

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita (labelled economic growth) vs log internet users (Model 1)
results.estimate: 0.16262 (log-log coefficient)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (1), p.10; 'impact of ICT on economic growth positive and significant' p.11

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita vs log mobile phone subscriptions (Model 3)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (3), p.10

results.estimate: IU -4.14710; lnEI x lnIU +2.15698; lnEI 3.82505 (conditional effect depends on trade level; marginal effect at mean not reported)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (2), p.10

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita vs log mobile subscriptions, with interaction with economic integration (Model 4)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (4), p.10

heterogeneity.evidence: Conclusion p.12: 'has not discussed any level or precise thresholds for ICT'

income_group_results.high: not reported (EU-27 sample pooled; no income split)
income_group_results.low: not applicable (no such economies in sample)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Difference GMM with internal lags addresses simultaneity in principle, but instruments are not specified (text says 'lagged dependent variable is used as an instrumental variable'), the series are highly persistent, and Hansen p = 0.097 and 0.110 are borderline in Models 1 and 4. AR(1) not rejected at 5% in Models 1 and 4 (p = 0.056, 0.146). Causal 'impact' language used.

selection_of_countries_years.why: EU-27 only (homogeneous, high/upper-middle income); 3-year averages leave 6 periods and 162 obs, but only 138 enter the regressions without explanation; Figure 1 includes the UK while text says 27 EU countries.

outcome_measurement.why: Dependent variable is log GDP per capita (a level) described as 'economic growth'; price basis (constant or current) not stated.

selective_reporting.why: All four models are shown, but conclusions emphasise a positive ICT effect while ICT coefficients are negative in Models 2 and 4; no robustness section.

venue_quality_concern: possible (Business and Economic Research, Macrothink open-access journal; received 29 July 2021, accepted 24 September 2021, published 5 October 2021; peer-review rigour cannot be judged from the text)

Table 4 header reads 'Two-Step Difference GMM'. Regression N is 138 versus 162 in the descriptive table. Marginal ICT effect at mean trade level in the interaction models is not reported. confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Equation 2, p.627; Table 6, p.628; Abstract p.621

exposure_measurement.why: Standard ITU subscription and user counts, but they are saturated in rich countries and measure access rather than use or intensity; units are only given as '%'.

notes: Internal inconsistencies: Table 6 labels the constant (8.421) as 'Economic growth (EG)'; text quotes a fixed-telephone coefficient of -0.8696 while the table and Equation 3 give -0.028; the broadband discussion says a negative effect while the coefficient is positive and says growth will increase 'by -0.023510'; the discussion states 'negative effect' yet concludes 'no significant effect'. title: Reducing Gender Inequality in Education in Developing Countries: Do Information and Communication Technologies Matter?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (Driscoll-Kraay, quantile, system GMM) of mobile phone and internet diffusion on male-to-female primary and secondary gross enrolment ratios in 64 low and lower-middle income economies; meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies) and outcome (family 5, schooling) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (fixed broadband and ICT service exports as alternative measures)
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people; share of individuals using the Internet (WDI). Robustness: fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people and ICT service exports as % of service exports.

sample.economies_or_groups: 64 developing countries described as low-income and lower-middle income (list in Appendix A, e.g. Angola, Bangladesh, India, Egypt, Tunisia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam)
sample.income_groups_covered: low and lower-middle (as stated by authors); group membership not reported per country, and some listed countries (e.g. Tunisia, Jordan, Sri Lanka) may be upper-middle in parts of the period

design.estimator: Country fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors (baseline); OLS (Appendix B); trimming outliers; quantile regression (Q10-Q90); two-step system GMM with lagged dependent variable; quadratic ICT term; ICT x GDP growth interaction
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE; controls GDP growth, government education spending (% GDP), population growth, trade openness; no year fixed effects reported. GMM uses internal lagged instruments only.

results.indicator: Gender inequality in primary education (male/female primary gross enrolment ratio; higher = more inequality to the detriment of women) on mobile subscriptions per 100
results.estimate: -0.001 per additional subscription per 100 people (rounded; baseline FE, Driscoll-Kraay); mean of outcome 1.072 (SD 0.128)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.000 (reported to 3 decimals), p<0.01, N=845, 64 countries, within R2 0.355
results.evidence: Table 3 col 1, p.6: 'Mobile phone -0.001*** (0.000)'

results.indicator: Gender inequality in primary education on internet users (% population)
results.estimate: -0.001 per percentage point of internet users (rounded)
results.evidence: Table 3 col 2, p.6: 'Internet -0.001*** (0.000)'

results.indicator: Gender inequality in secondary education (male/female secondary GER) on mobile subscriptions per 100
results.estimate: -0.003 per subscription per 100 people; outcome mean 1.170 (SD 0.363)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.000, p<0.01, N=638, 61 countries, within R2 0.412
results.evidence: Table 3 col 3, p.6: 'Mobile phone -0.003***'

results.indicator: Gender inequality in secondary education on internet users (% population)
results.estimate: -0.004 per percentage point
results.evidence: Table 3 col 4, p.6: 'Internet -0.004*** (0.001)'

results.indicator: System GMM (dynamic) effect of mobile/internet on primary and secondary gender inequality
results.estimate: Mobile: -0.0001 (primary), -0.001 (secondary); Internet: -0.0004 (primary), -0.001 (secondary); lagged dependent var 0.59-0.88
results.uncertainty: Primary mobile p<0.01; other three p<0.05; Hansen p 0.41-0.69; AR(2) p 0.12-0.33; instruments 26-56 vs 59-62 groups
results.evidence: Table 7, p.9: 'Mobile phone -0.0001*** ... Hansenp 0.685'; text: 'smaller marginal effects in absolute value'

results.estimate: Fixed broadband -0.002 (primary), -0.004 (secondary); ICT exports -0.002 (primary), -0.004 (secondary)

results.estimate: Linear term negative, squared term positive: mobile -0.002 / +0.00001 (primary), -0.006 / +0.00003 (secondary); internet -0.004 / +0.00004 (primary), -0.013 / +0.0001 (secondary). Implied turning points: 100 mobile subs per 100; internet 50% (primary) and 65% (secondary)
results.uncertainty: All reported p<0.01; turning points computed from rounded coefficients, no CI for the threshold
results.evidence: Table 8, p.9 and text p.10: 'threshold of 100 subscriptions per 100 people for mobile phones'

results.indicator: ICT x GDP growth interaction on gender inequality
results.estimate: Mobile x GDP growth -0.00002 (primary), -0.0001 (secondary); Internet x GDP growth -0.00003 (primary, n.s.), -0.0002 (secondary)
results.uncertainty: Mobile primary p<0.1; mobile secondary p<0.01; internet primary not significant; internet secondary p<0.05
results.evidence: Table 9, p.10: 'Mobile phone x GDP -0.00002* ... Internet x GDP -0.00003'

heterogeneity.finding: Effects stronger in secondary than primary education (about -0.003/-0.004 vs -0.001). Text says opposite ('stronger effects ... on primary education') in conclusion and policy section, contradicting Table 3 in absolute coefficient terms (outcome scales differ).
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 5.2 p.7: 'ICTs have stronger effects ... on primary education than on secondary' vs Table 3 coefficients

heterogeneity.evidence: Section 5.4.1, p.10: 'beyond the threshold of 100 mobile phone subscriptions per 100 people, the diffusion of mobile phone exacerbates gender inequality'

heterogeneity.evidence: Table 6, p.8 and Section 5.3.3

heterogeneity.evidence: Table 9, p.10

income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (sample described as low and lower-middle; no group split)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately; pooled estimates only
income_group_results.low: not reported separately; pooled estimates only

n_specifications_reported: about 50 (Table 3: 4; Table 4: 8; Table 5: 4; Table 6: 20 quantile coefficients; Table 7: 4; Table 8: 4; Table 9: 4; Table B1: 4)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors use causal language ('direct causal effect') but the baseline is a country-FE panel with four controls and no year effects, so common trends (ICT diffusion and enrolment parity both rising 2001-2022) and omitted variables (income level, urbanisation, schooling policy) can drive the result. Authors acknowledge reverse causality (skills bias). System GMM uses internal instruments only, with up to 56 instruments for 62 groups in one model, and gives smaller coefficients.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4 p.5: '𝛼 is used to capture the direct causal effect'; Section 5.3.4 p.8; Table 7 p.9

exposure_measurement.why: Mobile subscriptions per 100 (counts SIMs, exceeds 100 in sample, max 174) and share of internet users are standard but are not gender-specific and do not capture access by girls or school-age children; the mechanism concerns gendered access. Internet user data have many missing years.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3 p.4; Table 1 p.5: Mobile phone max 174, Internet obs 1671

selection_of_countries_years.why: 64 low and lower-middle economies, 2001-2022, but unbalanced: 638-862 obs used in main models vs roughly 1,400 possible country-years; missingness not discussed. Outlier-trimming robustness cuts the top and bottom 5% of the outcome distribution (selects on the dependent variable). Income classification is not applied per country; some listed countries are upper-middle income.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3 p.4; Table 3 obs rows p.6; Section 5.3.1 p.7

outcome_measurement.why: Male/female gross enrolment ratio (not net enrolment, completion or learning). Ratio below 1 (min 0.72-0.84) means girls ahead, so a lower ratio is not always 'less inequality'; interpretation of negative coefficients as reduced inequality is not qualified. GER can exceed 100% because of repeaters and over-age pupils.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3 p.4: 'ratio of male to female primary school gross enrollment'; Table 1 p.5 (min 0.842 and 0.723)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many estimators and variants (DK, OLS, trimming, quantile, GMM, quadratic, interaction) but headline spec is the pre-stated baseline. Four controls, no time effects, no lags in baseline. Threshold from quadratic form is computed from rounded coefficients without a test of the turning point or CI. Descriptive text in Section 3 contains units inconsistencies (GDP min stated -0.46% vs -46.082 in Table 1).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 4 p.5; Section 5.4.1 p.9-10; Section 3 p.5 vs Table 1

selective_reporting.why: Nearly every specification supports the main finding, with all primary coefficients rounded to -0.001 and SE 0.000, limiting inspection of precision. Table 6 shows Q10 mobile-primary at -0.001 with SE 0.0001 and no star, which looks inconsistent. Text on relative effect size (primary stronger) contradicts the tables. No pre-registration or placebo checks.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 6 panel A p.8; Section 5.2 p.7 and Section 6 p.10

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Included under family 5 (schooling / gender gap in enrolment), technology stream H (mobile and internet). No text attempting to direct the extractor was found. Reported inconsistencies: (1) conclusion says ICT effects are stronger on primary than secondary education, but coefficients in Table 3 are larger for secondary (-0.003/-0.004 vs -0.001) though the secondary outcome has a larger SD; (2) text states GDP growth min -0.46% and max 34% while Table 1 gives -46.082 and 33.629; (3) Table 2 footnote reads '***p < 0.0'; (4) Table 4 note shows only *** though 8 columns; (5) Table 7 first column has 56 instruments for 62 groups. Authors claim to be first to study ICT and gender gap in education. Sample is low and lower-middle only so no high-income comparison and no estimated income-group heterogeneity; the U-shape turning point for mobile (100 per 100) lies within the sample range (mean 50, max 174). Appendix B OLS results reported (coefficients similar). Wiley journal Sustainable Development, 2026.
