title: Digital transformation and income disparities: A threshold analysis in developing countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (dynamic panel threshold, System GMM) of a composite ICT/digital index (internet, mobile, digital payments etc.) on Gini and Theil inequality across 45 economies, so it meets the exposure, sample (>=10 economies) and outcome (family 4) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (composite digital economy index: internet use, mobile subscriptions, digital payments, secure servers, tertiary enrolment, years of schooling)
exposure_measure: Digital Economy Index (DIG), 0-1 scale, built with Entropy Weight-TOPSIS from six indicators: internet users %, mobile subscriptions per 100, tertiary enrolment, mean years of schooling, digital payments % adults, secure servers per million (Appendix B, A.2). Also used as the threshold variable.

sample.economies_or_groups: 45 'developing' economies per World Bank classification (Appendix A): 12 Africa and Middle East, 7 East Asia and Pacific, 14 Europe and Central Asia, 12 Latin America and Caribbean (e.g. China, India absent; includes Chile, Uruguay, Romania, Bulgaria, Malaysia, Russia, Brazil, Nigeria, Kenya)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (described only as 'developing'; income-group breakdown not reported; sample appears to span lower-middle to upper-middle and some economies now classed high-income; no obvious low-income economies)

design.estimator: Dynamic panel threshold model (Hansen 1999 / Seo-Shin 2016 / Kremer et al. 2013 framing), threshold found by SSR grid search with 300-replication bootstrap; coefficients estimated by two-step System GMM (Blundell-Bond) with collapsed, limited instruments; lagged dependent variable included.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country effects (mu_i), lagged Gini/Theil, relative development (normalised GDP per capita), average years of schooling, trade openness, government expenditure % GDP, R&D % GDP, informal employment share. No time effects mentioned. Instruments are internal lags only.

results.indicator: Gini coefficient, regime 1 (DIG below 0.48), dynamic threshold System GMM
results.estimate: beta1 = 0.125 (Gini on 0-1 scale per unit of DIG index, 0-1 scale); sign inferred from text 'positive and significant' because the minus/plus signs are lost in the converted table
results.evidence: p.60 Table 6 and Sec. 4.3.1: 'In Regime 1 (DIG < 0.48), the coefficient for digitalization is positive and significant (β1 = 0.125, p < 0.05)'

results.indicator: Gini coefficient, regime 2 (DIG above 0.48), dynamic threshold System GMM
results.estimate: beta2 = -0.087 (magnitude 0.087 in Table 6; negative sign stated in text, lost in table conversion)
results.evidence: p.59 Sec. 4.3.1: 'The coefficient becomes negative and significant (β2 = 0.087, p < 0.10)'; p.60 Table 6

results.indicator: Gini coefficient, linear (no threshold) System GMM full sample
results.estimate: 0.015 (sign not recoverable from converted table)
results.evidence: p.59 Sec. 4.3: 'coefficient for digitalization is statistically insignificant (0.015)'; p.60 Table 6 column 3

results.indicator: Theil index, two regimes (threshold near DIG = 0.50), robustness
results.estimate: regime 1: 0.095 (inequality-increasing); regime 2: 0.071 (inequality-reducing, sign from text); controls not shown
results.uncertainty: stars only: regime 1 p < 0.05, regime 2 p < 0.10; SEs not reported
results.evidence: p.61 Sec. 4.3.3 and Table 7: 'inequality-increasing effect below the threshold (β1 = 0.095) and an inequality-reducing effect above it (β2 = 0.071)'

results.indicator: Threshold existence test (Gini): single vs linear
results.estimate: single threshold gamma = 0.48, 95% CI [0.45, 0.51]; F = 42.15. Double threshold F = 18.72, gamma = 0.65 [0.62, 0.68], not significant
results.evidence: p.59 Table 5 and Sec. 4.2: 'F-statistic of 42.15 with a p-value of 0.008'

heterogeneity.finding: Effect of digitalization on Gini depends on the level of digital maturity: inequality-increasing below DIG = 0.48, inequality-reducing above (inverted-U 'Digital Kuznets Curve'). Mean DIG is 0.458, so roughly half the sample-years are in each regime (regime counts not reported).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.59 Table 5; abstract: 'at low-to-moderate levels of digitalization (index <= 0.48), technological advancement exacerbates income disparity'

heterogeneity.finding: R&D expenditure reduces inequality only in the high-digitalization regime (significant in regime 2, not regime 1); other controls have similar signs in both regimes (human capital and relative development inequality-reducing per text; informal employment inequality-increasing).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.60-61 Sec. 4.3.2: 'research and development expenditure only exhibits a significant negative effect on inequality in the higher digitalization regime'

income_group_results.high: not reported (not separated; sample labelled developing)

n_specifications_reported: about 4 (Gini linear and 2-regime threshold in Table 6, Theil 2-regime in Table 7; double-threshold test in Table 5)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with internal instruments, AR(2) and Hansen tests are reported, but no information on instrument count or lag depth, no external instrument, and the threshold variable (DIG) is itself endogenous. How Hansen threshold search and System GMM are combined is not explained. Causal language ('exacerbates', 'mitigates') is used.

exposure_measurement.why: DIG mixes ICT access/use with human capital (tertiary enrolment, mean years of schooling), which overlaps with the schooling control (CAP) and independently drives inequality. Definitions are inconsistent: Table 1 lists internet, mobile, digital payments and e-commerce readiness (sources ITU, Findex, WIPO), whereas Appendix B lists six different indicators (incl. schooling, secure servers) with no WIPO. Mean years of schooling is 15+ in Table 1 and 25+ in Appendix B. The threshold at 0.48 is an index-specific value with weights not reported.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.55 Table 1 and Sec. 3.2.2; p.67 Appendix B, A.2 table

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 'developing' economies are selected by the authors' own criterion, which includes economies such as Chile, Uruguay, Romania, Bulgaria and Malaysia. The panel is perfectly balanced over 2000-2023 for 45 countries, which is hard to reconcile with the sparse availability of survey-based Gini and Theil data. Country selection by 'data availability' is stated but not documented. Observation count of 1,035 equals 45 x 23, not 45 x 24, and is unexplained.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.54 Sec. 3.1; p.58 Table 4 (Obs 1,035); p.66 Appendix A

outcome_measurement.why: Gini taken from the World Bank PIP and Theil from 'ILO Labour Statistics; National Surveys' with a full annual balanced panel and no description of interpolation, harmonisation, or income vs consumption basis. Gini and Theil are described as 'sensitive to middle/tails' with a citation (Schutz 1951) that does not support this. Descriptive statistics are unusually round (min/max of SUP 10.0/45.0, INF 30.0/80.0, DIG 0.12/0.78).
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.55 Table 1 and Sec. 3.2.1; p.58 Table 4

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: A single main threshold specification with fixed set of six controls and no time effects; linear comparison is shown. Threshold regime coefficients on lagged dependent variable also vary by regime. Threshold search on the same variable used for causal claims and a bootstrap test designed for static panels (Hansen 1999) applied to a dynamic panel. No sensitivity to alternative index weights, sample or lag structure.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.56 Sec. 3.3 equations; p.57 Sec. 3.3.1; p.59 Sec. 4.2

selective_reporting.why: Gini results are reported in full (Table 6), but the Theil robustness table (Table 7) omits control coefficients, standard errors and the sign column, and only states diagnostics. Double-threshold estimate (0.65) is shown but dismissed. No alternative samples or exposure definitions reported, so absence of unfavourable results cannot be checked.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.61 Table 7 ('Controls included: Yes'); p.59 Table 5

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Text conversion dropped minus signs and replaced '=' with '5' (e.g. 'β2 5 0.087'); the signs of beta2 and of controls are taken from the verbal text (negative for regime 2, REL and CAP negative, INF positive), not from the tables, so check against the PDF. Abstract says DIG <= 0.48; Sec. 4.2 says DIG < 0.48. Table 5 reports a double-threshold value of 0.65 even though it is not significant. Regime-specific lagged dependent variable (0.854 vs 0.792) means the regimes are estimated as separate equations, which is not discussed. Number of observations per regime, instrument counts and bootstrap details are not reported. The paper states a 'quasi-experimental setting' but offers no quasi-experimental design. Reported data features (balanced annual Gini/Theil panel, round descriptive min/max, 1,035 obs for a 24-year window, mismatch between index definition in Table 1 and Appendix B) raise concerns about data provenance; a human should look at these before the headline threshold is used. Funding statement refers to an unrelated project on global public opinion in the AIGC era; first author affiliation is a vocational education company. No instructions embedded in the text were found. Journal is Acta Oeconomica (Akademiai Kiado), a recognised outlet, so no venue concern is recorded.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Employment: New Cross-Country Evidence
decision_rationale: Quantitative empirical study with own estimation (occupation-by-country regressions) of AI exposure (capability-based) on employment and hours in 23 OECD countries, which meets the 3-economy threshold for AI; outcomes are labour-market (family 3).
technology: artificial intelligence (occupational AI exposure, task/ability-based; Felten-Raj-Seamans measure extended with PIAAC)
exposure_measure: Occupation-by-country index of exposure to AI (0-1, min-max scaled), linking progress in nine AI applications (EFF, 2010-2015) to 52 O*NET abilities and then to 33 PIAAC tasks, measured at 2-digit ISCO-08 in 2012. It is a measure of potential automatability, not actual AI adoption (authors state this explicitly). Alternative indicators (Webb 2020, Tolan et al. 2021, job-posting share of AI skills) used for robustness.

sample.economies_or_groups: OECD countries: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Lithuania, Mexico, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Slovenia, Slovak Republic, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States (p.8 footnote 23)
sample.income_groups_covered: mostly high; Mexico is the only clearly non-high-income economy (income classification not reported in the paper)
sample.years: 2012-2019 (changes); exposure fixed at 2012 task content, AI progress 2010-2015
sample.unit: industry-country (country x 2-digit ISCO-08 occupation cells; 36 occupations, 822 cells in the all-occupation sample)

design.estimator: Cross-sectional OLS of 2012-2019 percentage change in occupation employment (and hours, part-time share) on AI exposure, robust SEs, unweighted; sample split into terciles of computer use
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country fixed effects in all models; in extended models share of employment in tradable sectors, offshorability, exposure to software and to industrial robots (Webb), 1-digit occupation dummies. Main Table 2 has no controls beyond country FEs.

heterogeneity.evidence: p.21-23 Tables 2-4: 'positive and statistically significant only for the subsample where computer use is high'

heterogeneity.evidence: p.11 'average score of AI exposure ... ranges from 0.52 (Lithuania) to 0.72 (Finland)'

income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (Mexico only, pooled in sample)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Exposure is fixed in 2012 from AI progress 2010-2015 and outcomes are subsequent changes, which limits simultaneity, and country FEs are used. But there is no instrument or quasi-experiment, occupation-level confounders remain (headline all-occupation result vanishes with controls), and the authors say causal nature needs further research and use associational language.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.21 'further research is needed to test the causal nature'; p.21 Table 2/3 controls

exposure_measurement.why: Capability-based potential exposure, not actual AI use or investment; it is built from US O*NET abilities and an MTurk correlation matrix, mapped to PIAAC tasks by authors' own binary judgement; 17 physical/sensory abilities are lost; other-technology controls (software, robots, offshorability) are US-based and imposed on all countries. Authors acknowledge these limits and show robustness to alternative indicators, with mixed results (Tolan indicator not significant).
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.6 'measure potential exposure and not actual AI adoption'; p.10 'indicator loses 17 abilities'; p.22 Table A.3 discussion

selection_of_countries_years.why: 23 OECD countries with PIAAC and LFS data, almost all high income; 36 occupations; IT professionals and technicians excluded by the authors; a few cells missing; 2012-2019 is a recovery period. Limits generalisation to developing economies.

outcome_measurement.why: Official labour force surveys (EU-LFS, US CPS, Mexican ENOE) with occupations harmonised to ISCO-08; some mapping from SOC and SINCO codes. Employment counts are not adjusted for sampling error in small cells.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Key positive result arises in a subsample (high computer-use tercile) defined by authors' split; other splits (wage, creative, social tasks, Goos classification) and alternative indicators were explored. Terciles are post-hoc stratifications, but split choice is motivated by theory and several are reported. Unweighted regressions, small clusters, SEs not clustered by country or occupation.

selective_reporting.why: Several results are described as 'not displayed' or 'available on request' (e.g., full-sample results with controls, weighted regressions). Authors do report non-robust findings (hours result lost with occupation FEs; Tolan indicator insignificant) and phrase conclusions cautiously.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.21 footnotes 56-57 'not displayed but available on request'; p.25 'not robust to the inclusion of the full set of controls'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: OECD-authored paper in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. The all-occupation employment coefficient (13.3**) is uncontrolled; with controls it is insignificant, so the abstract's 'no clear relationship' is the preferred summary. Exposure is a potential-automatability measure rather than adoption. Table 4 has 781 observations (22 countries) against 822 for employment. Job-posting outcome (demand for AI skills, UK and US only) is reported in Figure 15 and footnote 70 but is not an eligible payoff outcome and is not extracted. No injected instructions found in the text.

title: Cryptocurrency Adoption Patterns and Financial Inclusion Outcomes in Emerging Market Economies

exposure_measure: Cryptocurrency adoption rate, described as the percentage of people using cryptocurrency; data sources named as World Bank, IMF and CoinGecko; exact variable and construction not defined. results.estimate: not reported (no coefficient; only SEM R2 = 0.88, regression R2 = 0.85)
results.uncertainty: not reported (no se, ci or p-value; MSE 0.020 SEM, 0.025 regression; AIC 121.65 vs 125.23)

R2 of 0.88 is attributed to adoption 'and other related factors', so it is not an effect size for crypto.

exposure_measurement.evidence: Data Collection p. 54, Key Variables p. 55, Results p. 56: 'obtained from the World Bank, IMF, and CoinGecko'

selection_of_countries_years.why: The 15 countries are never named; selection is described in the future tense as 'stratified random sampling' based on adoption level, development and infrastructure, so the sample may be selected on the exposure.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sampling Strategy, p. 55: 'selected by using a stratified random sampling method'

outcome_measurement.why: Financial inclusion index is not specified (components listed loosely: digital financial services, bank accounts, mobile money); SEM latent variables with four observed variables, indicators not named.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Key Variables p. 55; Results p. 56: 'four observed variables were measured'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: No coefficients, standard errors or sample size for the models; fit metrics appear in-sample and Eq. 1 explains adoption, while Table 1 and Fig. 2 compare models for the financial inclusion index. The methods section reads as a proposal ('will be used').
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1, p. 57; Methodology pp. 53-56 in future tense

selective_reporting.why: Only goodness-of-fit numbers are reported; no effect sizes, uncertainty, robustness or cross-validation results despite being promised; results cannot be checked.
selective_reporting.evidence: Validation and Robustness Checks, p. 55 (promised); Results pp. 56-58 (not shown)

venue_quality_concern: possible (journal header says Vol. 12, No. 4, 2023 but the paper lists received 25 Sept 2025, accepted Nov 2025, published 30 Dec 2025 and cites 2025 references; several cited venues are low-profile outlets; internally inconsistent description of the study)
notes: The Methodology section is written as a plan (e.g., 'The countries will be selected', 'interviews will be carried out') while the Results section then reports completed analysis of 15 countries and 30 interviews; the two are not reconciled. Data window described as '5 years (2018-2023)' (that is 6). If 15 countries x 5-6 years were used, N is about 75-90, never stated. The 'regression model' in Eq. 1 predicts crypto adoption, yet the R2 of 0.85 is described in the abstract as variance in adoption explained by economic and technological factors, while Table 1 treats both models as explaining financial inclusion; this is contradictory. Reported R2 values are the only quantitative results; the abstract and conclusion read R2 = 0.88 as '88% of variance in financial inclusion attributed to crypto adoption', an overstatement. Adoption-determinant results (Eq. 1) are context only and have no coefficients. No text in the paper attempted to direct the reviewer.

title: FinTech Leapfrogging: A Comparative Analysis of Digital Payments and Cryptocurrency Adoption in Emerging and Developed Economies
decision_rationale: The paper states it uses Comparative Trend Analysis 'rather than using econometric regression' on ten purposively selected economies, reporting descriptive CAGRs, group averages and rankings. There is no estimation of an exposure-outcome relationship, and the content is about adoption patterns, not payoffs.
exposure_measure: not applicable

sample.economies_or_groups: India, Vietnam, Nigeria, Brazil, Philippines (emerging); US, UK, Germany, Sweden, Japan (developed)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (emerging vs developed, purposive)

design.estimator: not applicable (descriptive comparative trend analysis; CAGR, group means, scatter plot of Chainalysis rank vs unbanked share)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: not applicable

n_specifications_reported: 0 (no regressions)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: excluded

exposure_measurement.why: excluded

selection_of_countries_years.why: excluded

outcome_measurement.why: excluded

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: excluded

selective_reporting.why: excluded

venue_quality_concern: possible (single-author descriptive study built on Statista market projections; Globalization and Business journal; reliance on commercial projected values)
notes: Section 3.4: 'comparative trend analysis (CTA) approach ... rather than using econometric regression'. Statista figures include projections (data limitations, Section 3.5). Table 4 and the scatter plot are cross-sectional rank comparisons of 10 countries with no statistical test. Could serve as context only for the adoption question (digital payments and crypto), but has no estimation, so excluded under E4. No embedded instructions seen in the text (I read pages up to Table 4/Figure 7 in full and skimmed the remainder by keyword search).

title: Crypto-driven growth: A comparative study of Bitcoin and Ethereum on economic growth for multi-country analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of Bitcoin and Ethereum returns and trading volume on real GDP growth in 14 countries (more than 10), with own estimation (GM-FMOLS, Pedroni cointegration, Granger tests). Included under crypto-assets and output family, although the exposure is global market returns and volume rather than country-level adoption (flagged in risk of bias).
exposure_measure: Quarterly rate of return (BTCR, ETHR) and quarterly percent change in trading volume (BTCV, ETHV) of Bitcoin and Ethereum from CoinMarketCap. These are global market series, not country-level holdings, adoption or usage.

sample.economies_or_groups: 14 countries; the text names only Australia, Canada, China, Colombia, Indonesia, South Africa, United States, Saudi Arabia in the data description; full list not stated in the main text
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle at least; not reported by authors)

design.estimator: Panel group-mean FMOLS (six model variants), second-generation CIPS unit-root test, Pedroni cointegration, Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger causality
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: CPI quarterly growth, VIX percent change, WTI oil price change, gold price change; country-specific intercepts (FMOLS); no country-varying crypto exposure.

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Bitcoin rate of return (Model 1, GM-FMOLS)
results.estimate: 0.0252 (GDP growth per unit change in BTCR, both in decimal/percent change units as constructed)

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Ethereum rate of return (Model 3)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7 Model (3)

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Bitcoin trading volume change (Model 2 and Model 6)
results.estimate: Model 2: -0.0005 (p=0.3221, insignificant); Model 6: -0.0027 (p<0.01)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7; text p.415 'In Models 2 and 6, BTCV negatively and significantly affects growth'. Note Model 2 is insignificant, contradicting that sentence.

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Ethereum trading volume change (Models 4 and 6)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7

results.indicator: Panel Granger causality between crypto variables and GDP growth (short run)
results.estimate: Bidirectional causality BTCV and GDP; unidirectional from GDP to ETHR and ETHV; no statistics in main text (Appendix A)
results.evidence: p.418 section 4.2; p.421 Conclusion

n_specifications_reported: 6 FMOLS models (different combinations of crypto indicators), plus cointegration and causality tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Contemporaneous association between global crypto price and volume series and country GDP growth. The paper itself finds causality running from GDP to ETH returns and bidirectional with BTC volume. Same crypto series is applied to every country, so the variation is purely time-series and common across countries; it cannot be separated from the common global financial cycle (VIX, oil, gold are only partly controlled). Policy and growth-effect wording ('crypto-driven growth', 'effect') is not supported by the design.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.418 section 4.2 Granger results; Table 1 variable definitions; abstract 'significantly positive impact'

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is global Bitcoin/Ethereum price returns and percent change in global trading volume, identical across the 14 countries, not national adoption, holdings or usage. It does not capture crypto adoption in a given country (for example the China ban is ignored).
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.410 Table 1; p.409 'their trading volumes and rates of return are used as the main cryptocurrency indicators'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 14 countries chosen 'informed by prior studies'; list is not given in the main text. Window 2015Q3-2023Q3 includes COVID-19 GDP swings (GDP growth min -0.2255, max 0.2256), which may dominate the common time variation.

outcome_measurement.why: Seasonally adjusted quarterly real GDP growth from OECD, a standard measure, but quarterly, volatile and mixing units (decimal vs percent); descriptive statistics show kurtosis of 21.9 and the text claims data are normal for all variables except gold although Jarque-Bera is significant for GDP.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.410 Table 1; p.411 Table 2 'Jarque-Bera ... 6893.137*' vs text 'data for all variables are normally distributed'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Regressing a growth rate (near stationary) on percentage changes with FMOLS, which assumes I(1) variables; the unit-root section concludes variables are I(0) or borderline, so FMOLS cointegration logic is questionable. Cointegration among differenced/rate variables is conceptually odd. Several outcomes of Pedroni tests are mixed (panel v-statistic p=1.0). Choice of six models with different crypto proxies; no coefficient SEs.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.413 section 3.3 'data are either I(0) or borderline I(1)'; p.418 Table 8

selective_reporting.why: All six models reported, including the insignificant BTCV result in Model 2. But the narrative contradicts the table in places (BTCV described as negative and significant in Models 2 and 6; discussion says ETHV 'associated with higher volatility and potential downside risk' although Table 7 shows a positive significant coefficient), and abstract says positive impact 'except for Bitcoin's trading volume'. No SEs or country-level FMOLS estimates shown.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.415-416 text vs Table 7; p.419 Discussion 'ETHV is associated with higher volatility and potential downside risk'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Russian Journal of Economics, a regular journal; no concern flagged. Reported coefficients are tiny and units of the variables are inconsistent (Table 2 shows growth in decimals). Text states 14 countries but never lists them in the main text; Appendix A holds causality tables only. Internal inconsistencies: Jarque-Bera statement; BTCV Model 2 insignificant but described as significantly negative; Discussion reverses the sign interpretation of ETHV. Abstract says 'panel fully modified ordinary least squares'; methods use group-mean FMOLS. Eligibility judgment: included under crypto-assets exposure, but exposure is market-price based, so a human may prefer to reclassify as context or exclude (E2). No instructions embedded in the paper text.

title: FINANCIAL INCLUSION, MOBILE PHONE DIFFUSION, AND ECONOMIC GROWTH; EVIDENCE FROM AFRICA
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel of 32 African countries (2004-2016) estimating a structural equation model in which mobile phone penetration is a mediator between financial inclusion and GDP per capita growth; mobile telephony exposure, at least 10 economies, and an output outcome are all met.
exposure_measure: Mobile phone subscriptions per 100 adults (MOBILE), sourced from the ITU (Section 3.1). In the model mobile penetration is a mediator, and financial inclusion (PCA index FII) is the main exposure.

sample.economies_or_groups: 32 African countries; country list not given in the text; selection by data availability
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (African countries; mixed presumably, not stated)

design.estimator: Structural equation model (path analysis, maximum likelihood) with one financial inclusion index, one mobile penetration variable, two bank mediators (Boone, Z-score) and GDP per capita growth
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No controls and no country or year fixed effects reported; five observed variables only

results.indicator: Path MOBILE -> GDP per capita growth (GDPPCGR)
results.estimate: not reported (path coefficients are only in Figure 2, which is not in the text; sign is not stated in the text)
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'mobile diffusion influences economic growth given that the path MOBILE -> GDPPCGR is significant'. Table 2 simple correlation of MOBILE with GDPPCGR is -0.2198.

results.indicator: Direct path financial inclusion (FII) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported; described as insignificant and negative
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'The insignificant negative impact of financial inclusion on economic growth'

results.indicator: Indirect path FII -> MOBILE -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'indirect relationship from financial inclusion through mobile diffusion to economic growth with the significant path'. Sign of the product is not stated; 'positive' is inferred from the authors' reading that mobile mediates a growth-enhancing effect, so treat as unclear.

results.indicator: Path Boone indicator (bank competition) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'only the path running from Boone -> GDPPCGR is significant indicating an inverse relationship'

results.indicator: Path Z-score (bank stability) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'ZSCORE -> GDPPCGR path is insignificant'

n_specifications_reported: 1 (one SEM)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal mediation language (mobile mediates financial inclusion to growth) from a cross-country panel with no instrument and no controls. The authors' own text says the direction may run from financial inclusion to mobile phones, and the model imposes FII -> MOBILE while the cited literature reports MOBILE -> FII.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 2.4: 'possibility of a reverse causality from financial inclusion to mobile phone diffusion'; Figure 1; Section 4.2.1

exposure_measurement.why: Mobile subscriptions per 100 adults is a standard diffusion measure. Subscriptions can exceed 100 (maximum 176.7 in Table 1) and are not users. Financial inclusion is a PCA index that includes outstanding loans to GDP, which is partly a financial depth measure.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 32 countries chosen by data availability, country list not given, 394 observations versus 416 for a balanced panel (unbalanced). Short window 2004-2016.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1: 'data availability largely determines the selection of countries'; Table 1 Observations 394

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita growth from WDI is a standard output measure.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Single SEM with no controls, no fixed effects, no stationarity or panel dependence handling; Jarque-Bera p-values of 0.000 are read as confirming normality although they reject it; fit indices reported are internally odd (TLI 0.990 above CFI 0.955, SRMR 0.005). Simple correlation of mobile with growth is negative (-0.22) yet the paper reports a positive mediation story.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1 Jarque-Bera; Section 4.2.1 'Global model fitness indices: CMIN/DF 2.598, SRMR 0.005, TLI 0.990, CFI 0.955'; Table 2

selective_reporting.why: Coefficients, standard errors and the sign of the mobile -> growth path are not reported in the text (only in Figure 2, an image), so the headline cannot be checked. Only significant/insignificant is described.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 4.2: 'Figure 2 below presents the result'; no coefficient table in text

venue_quality_concern: possible (the introduction promises analysis of bank competition and stability but the abstract and title do not; the paper claims it is the first SEM study of this question; short 7-page paper; International Journal of Economics and Financial Issues)
notes: Path coefficients are only in Figure 2 and were not available in the text conversion; a human should check the figure for signs and magnitudes before using the MOBILE -> GDPPCGR result in quantitative synthesis. The FII -> MOBILE path is the main reported significant link. The paper treats insignificant FII -> growth as 'negative impact' of low financial inclusion, which is over-interpretation of a null. Table 1 shows all Jarque-Bera p-values as 0.000000 yet text says 'data are normally distributed'. The text also lists 'financial inclusion -> bank competition -> growth' hypotheses H1 to H5 but only partial results are described. No instruction-like text directed at a reader or reviewer was found.

title: The Employment Effects of Mobile Internet in Developing Countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative IV panel study of 3G mobile internet coverage (mobile data) in 14 developing countries (low, lower-middle and upper-middle income) with labour-market and sectoral-structure outcomes. Meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies, explicit spread of income levels) and outcome criteria.
exposure_measure: Population-weighted share of a sub-national region covered by 3G signal, from Collins Bartholomew Mobile Coverage Explorer 1x1 km binary grid maps (operator submissions via GSMA); set to 0 before 2006 or before the year the country adopted 3G (ITU).

sample.economies_or_groups: Armenia, Bolivia, Botswana, Brazil, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Indonesia, Iran, Mexico, Philippines, South Africa, Uganda, Zambia (Table C3)
sample.income_groups_covered: low, lower-middle, upper-middle (text p.7 says 'full spectrum' from low to upper-middle; no high-income country listed; Table C3 gives only 2015 GDP per capita, no income-group labels)
sample.years: 2000-2015 survey/census rounds (33 country-years in Table C3; 2 rounds in most countries); 3G data 2006-2017
sample.unit: other (sub-national region-year; 6,802 regions, 16,069 region-years in preferred sample)

design.estimator: Region and year fixed-effects panel regression, OLS and 2SLS IV; robustness with ANCOVA (state FE, baseline outcome and covariates), aggregated adjacent regions, placebo with future 3G coverage, full-sample.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Region FE, year FE, 2G coverage, rainfall, elevation. Instrument is above-median lightning strike frequency interacted with a time trend (first-stage coefficient -0.011, Table A1). Robust SEs; q-values for multiple testing.

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate, whole sample (fraction of 18-65 pop.)
results.estimate: IV 0.284 (10 pp more 3G coverage -> 2.8 pp higher LFP); OLS 0.066
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel A col 2 (p.23); text p.11: 'areas with 10 pp higher 3G coverage have 2.8 pp higher labor force participation'

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate, women
results.uncertainty: SE 0.218, p=0.024, q=0.017; first-stage KP F = 5.98 for the LFP columns
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel C col 2 (p.23); abstract: 3G 'significantly increases the labor force participation rate of women'

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate, men
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel B col 2 (p.23); text p.12: 'negative (-1.7 pp) but statistically insignificant'

results.indicator: Employment rate, whole sample
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel A col 4 (p.23)

results.indicator: Employment rate, men / women
results.estimate: IV men 0.310; women 0.132
results.evidence: Table 2 Panels B and C col 4 (p.23)

results.indicator: Own-account enterprise (OAE) share, whole sample
results.evidence: Table 2 col 8 (p.23); text p.13

results.indicator: Employer (hires workers) share, whole sample
results.estimate: IV -0.021; OLS -0.001 (ANCOVA robustness gives slightly positive 0.013)
results.evidence: Table 2 col 6 (p.23); Table B1 col 6 (p.32); text p.31 notes the sign differs

results.indicator: Wage-employed share, whole sample
results.uncertainty: SE 0.014, p<0.001 (whole); not significant in ANCOVA (Table B1 col 10: -0.025, SE 0.029)
results.evidence: Table 2 col 10 (p.23); text p.31: 'evidence on transition to wage employment is not as robust'

results.indicator: Unpaid work share, whole sample / men / women
results.estimate: IV whole -0.086; men -0.238; women +0.060
results.evidence: Table 2 col 12 (p.23); text p.14

results.indicator: Employment share in agriculture, whole sample
results.estimate: IV 0.088 (OLS 0.023); ANCOVA IV 0.035 (n.s.)
results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 2 (p.24); Table B2 col 2 (p.33)

results.indicator: Employment share in manufacturing, whole sample
results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 4 (p.24); Table B2 col 4 (p.33)

results.indicator: Employment share in services, whole sample
results.estimate: IV 0.060 (OLS 0.031); ANCOVA IV 0.052
results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 6 (p.24); text p.15: 'no strong evidence of major sectoral reallocation'

heterogeneity.finding: Gender: LFP effect is entirely among women (IV 0.492 vs men -0.168 n.s.); men shift from unpaid agricultural work to OAEs and service wage jobs, women into unpaid jobs, OAEs and service wage jobs.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 2 Panels B and C (p.23); text p.11-14

heterogeneity.finding: Effects concentrated in agriculture (male OAEs, unpaid work) and services (wage jobs); manufacturing effect small/insignificant; authors find no sectoral reallocation away from agriculture.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables A2-A4 (pp.27-29), Table 3 (p.24)

income_group_results.high: not applicable (no high-income country in sample)

n_specifications_reported: approximately 400 coefficients across Tables 2, 3, A2-A4, B1-B5 (about 12 outcomes x 3 gender panels x OLS/IV in main table, repeated across sector and robustness tables)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Region and year FE plus 2G control and a lightning-strike IV address reverse causality, but the exclusion restriction is not fully established (lightning correlates with rainfall, elevation, 2G rollout, and possibly agricultural conditions). IV estimates are several times larger than OLS. First stage is strong for most columns (KP F about 142) but weak for LFP (F = 5.98 for men and women). Placebo test with future 3G shows significant coefficients for wage employment (whole, women) and male unpaid work.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3 (pp.9-10); Table A1 (p.26); Table 2 F-stat row (p.23); Table B4 (p.37)

exposure_measurement.why: Coverage (network signal) is used, not actual use or adoption. Operator-submitted maps; 3G coverage set to zero before 2006 or before the national adoption year regardless of maps. Population weights fixed at 2001 distribution.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 14 countries with IPUMS data and 3G maps; mostly two or three survey rounds per country; some country-years drop out for missing data (Mexico 2005, South Africa 2011 and 2016); no high-income countries. Lightning data limited to +/-38 degrees latitude.

outcome_measurement.why: Harmonised IPUMS census/labour-force survey data, so comparable and large samples, but survey instruments change across rounds, LFP measured in a smaller subsample, and no wages, hours or income observed so welfare cannot be assessed.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 2.1 (pp.5-6); text p.5: 'we do not observe wages or hours worked'; Table 1 note on LFP sample (p.11 fn 11)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Single main specification with FE, reported alongside OLS; multiple robustness checks (ANCOVA, aggregation, placebo, full sample). Some results are not robust to ANCOVA (wage employment, employer sign). Many outcomes tested, but q-values are reported.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 4.7 (p.17); Appendix B.1 (pp.30-31); Table 2 q-value rows (p.23)

selective_reporting.why: Full tables reported for all outcomes, by gender and by sector, both OLS and IV; non-robust findings are acknowledged in text; placebo exceptions disclosed.
selective_reporting.evidence: Tables 2, 3, A2-A4, B1-B5; text p.31 and p.36

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: NBER working paper (No. 30741, Dec 2022), not peer reviewed at time of issue; may have been published later, not checked. Internal inconsistencies noted: text p.7 lists Rwanda as a low-income country in the sample but Rwanda is not in Table C3; Section 2.1 says ages 18-65 but Appendix C.1 says 18-24; 3G maps said to cover 2006-2015 (p.3) and 2006-2017 (p.6); lightning data said to end 2014 (p.7) and 2013 (p.47); Table 2 footnote says 'Keibergen-Paap' (sic). Table 3 and Table 2 IV first-stage F for LFP (5.98) is below conventional thresholds. Estimates are in fraction units; a 10 pp coverage change is a 20-25 percent increase on the 46 percent mean coverage. No instructions embedded in the text.

title: ICT capital and labour productivity growth: A non-parametric analysis of 14 OECD countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative DEA/Malmquist-type decomposition with bootstrap and distribution tests on 14 OECD economies; exposure is ICT capital and outcome is labour productivity growth, meeting the 10-economy rule for non-AI technology.
exposure_measure: ICT gross capital stock (K_ICT) from EU KLEMS, separated from non-ICT capital as a second DEA input (model m2) versus aggregate capital (model m1); ICT deflated with hedonic/harmonised indices.

sample.economies_or_groups: OECD members named in text: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Korea, Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, UK, USA (no full list given in a single place)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (all OECD members; mostly high-income)

design.estimator: Data envelopment analysis; Kumar-Russell decomposition of labour productivity change into efficiency, technology and capital accumulation; Simar-Wilson bootstrap bias correction; Maasoumi-Racine entropy test of equality of counterfactual densities (500 bootstraps)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: None; ICT effect inferred by comparing decomposition with ICT capital split out (m2) versus aggregate capital (m1); inputs are hours and capital stocks

results.indicator: Capital accumulation (KACC) component of labour productivity growth when ICT capital is separated (m2 vs m1)
results.estimate: not reported numerically in text (shown in Fig. 3); KACC distribution moves upward in m2 and ICT capital 'on average, exerts a higher growth rate than non-ICT capital'
results.uncertainty: Maasoumi-Racine test of m1 vs m2 counterfactual (y1995*KACC): p<2.22e-16 (Table 3)
results.evidence: Section 4.1 p.13 and Table 3 p.26

results.indicator: Technological change (TECH) component, m2 vs m1
results.estimate: not reported numerically; TECH values negative on average in m2 (Fig. 3); authors read this as lower capacity utilisation and implosion of the frontier rather than regress
results.uncertainty: Distribution difference y1995*TECH p=0.024; y1995*EFF*TECH p=0.012 (Table 3)
results.evidence: pp.13-14 and Table 3: 'the separation of ICT capital stock ... caused an implosion of the productive frontier'

results.indicator: TFP change when ICT capital is separated
results.estimate: not reported numerically; negative on average in m2 (Fig. 3)
results.evidence: p.13: 'The negative values for TFP growth obtained in model m2'

results.indicator: Efficiency change (EFF) distribution, m2 vs m1
results.estimate: not applicable (no difference estimated in levels)
results.evidence: Table 3, p.26; p.17: 'does not produce a significant difference in the EFF component'

results.indicator: Cross-country dispersion / convergence clubs in labour productivity
results.estimate: not reported numerically; ICT capital 'may be one of the factors' creating convergence clubs; mean labour productivity growth 1995-2005 across the sample about +21% (Korea +44%, Italy +2%)
results.uncertainty: Qualitative from density shapes; no separate test of clubs
results.evidence: Section 4.2 pp.15-16; p.11

heterogeneity.finding: Country-specific: Finland has the largest TFP gain (+20%); Korea and Japan have strong ICT-producing sectors but weaker ICT-usage effects; USA is only marginally hit by negative TECH while most European countries are hit more. These are descriptive remarks, not tests.

n_specifications_reported: 2 DEA models x 4 components; 4 counterfactual distribution tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Purely descriptive decomposition with no causal strategy; DEA components are not estimates of ICT effects, and the paper concedes non-parametric methods 'cannot quantify the contribution of ICT capital to TFP shifts'. Frontier positions are driven by all inputs and unobservables.

exposure_measurement.why: EU KLEMS ICT capital stocks use harmonised deflators for some countries, which the paper itself flags as imperfect (citing Timmer and van Ark).

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample reduced to 14 countries by ICT-data availability; only two end-years (1995, 2005) so results hinge on end points; a dot-com-era window.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3, p.10: 'The introduction of ICT capital restricted the sample to 14 countries'

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity as value added per hour from EU KLEMS with PPP conversion; fine for the purpose but DEA outputs are sensitive to input dimensionality.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3 p.10 and Section 4.1 p.11 (Nunamaker point)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: The ICT result comes from adding a second capital input, which mechanically changes DEA scores (more inputs raise efficiency), and the interpretation of falling TECH as capacity under-utilisation is speculative. Bootstrap bias-correction, bandwidth and component ordering are further choices. The robustness check (Spearman rank correlations) is weak.

selective_reporting.why: Numerical component values are shown only in figures; only distribution-equality p-values are tabulated; bias-correction rule is stated but not reported per country.

venue_quality_concern: possible (MPRA preprint dated 2012; the text contains unfinished draft notes; no peer-review evidence in the text)
notes: Draft note left in the body (p.4, after Eq. 1): an Italian-language author reminder about correcting formulas ('FINO ALLA FORMULA 16 VANNO CORRETTI'). It is not an instruction to the reviewer and was ignored. Inconsistency: the text says Spearman rank correlations 'are above 0.53' but Table 2 reports 0.49, 0.43, 0.47, 0.47. The text also claims the rank-correlation evidence shows the ICT contribution 'is effective', which does not follow. Abstract says 'positive' contribution to convergence clubs, while results show ICT capital raises KACC but lowers TECH and TFP in this DEA set-up. No numeric estimate of the ICT contribution is given in text or tables; only Table 1 summary statistics (mean K_ICT/K_GFCF 0.027 in 1995, 0.079 in 2005) and Table 3.

title: ICT capital–skill complementarity and wage inequality: Evidence from OECD countries
decision_rationale: Own GMM/IV estimation of a sector-level production function on 14 OECD economies (>=10 economies, non-AI); exposure is ICT equipment capital and outcome is the skill premium (distribution/labour market).
exposure_measure: Quantity of ICT equipment capital (k_i) and its rental price (r_i) from EU KLEMS, by country-sector-year; ICT equipment share rose from 0.2-2.4% in the 1970s to 5-21% in the 2000s.

sample.economies_or_groups: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Sweden, UK, US
sample.income_groups_covered: high only (advanced OECD economies; paper does not report income classification)
sample.unit: industry-country (country-sector-year, goods and service sectors; 682 observations)

design.estimator: Joint GMM on first-differenced (five-year) first-order conditions of a four-factor nested CES production function (ICT capital, non-ICT capital, skilled labour, unskilled labour); Shapley decomposition of the skill premium
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country-sector-specific polynomial trends in share parameters (orders chosen to fit each country-sector); differencing removes time-invariant country-sector wedges; robustness with collective bargaining coverage; shift-share IV built from the other sector's industries in other countries.

results.indicator: Elasticity-of-substitution parameters: sigma (ICT-skilled composite vs unskilled) and rho (ICT vs skilled); capital-skill complementarity requires sigma>rho
results.estimate: sigma=0.888, rho=-0.162 (difference about 1.05) under factor-biased technological change; sigma=0.642, rho=-0.053 under factor-neutral change
results.uncertainty: SE clustered at country-sector: sigma 0.029, rho 0.051 (Newey-West SE 0.026 and 0.057); factor-neutral sigma SE 0.248
results.evidence: p.15 Table 1; 'ICT equipment is much more complementary to skilled labor than unskilled labor even in the presence of factor-biased technological change'

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT capital-skill complementarity effect to change in the skill premium (w_h/w_u), decomposed with relative labour quantity and unobserved factor-augmenting technology effects
results.estimate: Not reported as a single coefficient; shown graphically (log changes, Figs 8-9). Complementarity effect widens the premium in all countries; the relative labour quantity effect narrows it; the rise in the US premium from the 1980s to 2000s is attributed mostly to the complementarity effect.
results.uncertainty: not reported (no confidence intervals for decomposition)
results.evidence: p.21 Sec 6.2.2: 'capital–skill complementarity effect associated with a rise in ICT equipment is large enough to account for a rise in the skill premium in almost all countries'

results.indicator: Observed factors (complementarity + quantity effects) track actual skill premium trend
results.estimate: Observed factors line up with actual trends in the goods sector of 8 of 14 countries and the service sector of 9 of 14; they do not line up in the goods sector of 6 countries and the service sector of 2 (Finland, Italy)
results.evidence: p.26 Sec 6.2.2: 'Unobserved factors cannot be disregarded as determinants of changes in the skill premium in these countries.'

results.indicator: Cross-country differences in change in the skill premium relative to the US explained by ICT equipment and labour quantities
results.estimate: Table 4 decomposition, e.g. goods sector log-point gaps vs US: data 0.225 vs model 0.182 for Australia; ICT component ranges from -0.501 (Austria) to 0.624 (Japan)
results.evidence: p.27 Table 4; 'differences ... attributable at least in part to ICT equipment in almost all countries'

results.indicator: Relative demand for skilled labour (ln(l_h/l_u)) and the contribution of the falling ICT rental price
results.estimate: e.g. US goods sector: change in ln(l_h/l_u) data 1.066, model 1.207; part due to r_i 2.538 (offset by w_h -4.600, w_u +2.795, technology terms 8.371 and -7.897)
results.evidence: p.29 Table 5; 'a fall in the rental price of ICT capital is large enough to account for a rise in relative labor quantity'

results.indicator: Effect of higher education expansion on the skill premium with versus without capital-skill complementarity
results.estimate: Impact of rising skilled labour on the log skill premium is 1.78x (goods) and 1.58x (service) larger on average when complementarity is accounted for; e.g. US goods -0.274 total (-0.154 complementarity, -0.121 quantity)
results.evidence: p.30-31 Table 6 and text

heterogeneity.finding: Complementarity effect is larger in the goods than the service sector in most countries; sigma and rho estimates are similar across sectors (goods sigma 0.847, rho -0.114; service sigma 0.889, rho -0.123).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.16 Table 2; p.26 'capital–skill complementarity effect was greater for the goods sector than the service sector in the majority of countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Country heterogeneity: the complementarity effect is particularly large in Denmark, Finland and the US; the quantity effect is particularly large in the UK; Finland's gap to the US is mostly unobserved technology.
Adding collective bargaining coverage to the wedge leaves sigma and rho almost unchanged (0.873, -0.119) and the coefficient is insignificant.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.15-16 Table 2 last row

income_group_results.high: All 14 economies are advanced OECD members; complementarity effect widens skill premium in all, sigma>rho pooled (Table 1)

n_specifications_reported: about 6 (baseline factor-biased, factor-neutral, goods only, service only, collective bargaining control; plus Czech/Slovenia exclusion mentioned in a footnote without table)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Shift-share IV uses other-sector, other-country industry growth to instrument factor quantities, which addresses simultaneity in principle, but validity (exogenous shares or shocks, no common global shocks) is asserted not tested; no first-stage strength or overidentification statistics reported in the main text; unobserved technology is a residual absorbed by flexible trends.

exposure_measurement.why: ICT equipment capital and user cost from EU KLEMS national-accounts data capture ICT investment directly; user cost computed without a competitive-market assumption.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 14 advanced OECD economies, data ending 2005, unbalanced panel ('as many countries and years as possible'); results do not speak to middle- or low-income economies or the post-2005 period.

outcome_measurement.why: Skill premium is high-skilled (college) versus all other workers, from labour compensation divided by hours including part-time, self-employed and family workers, with composition adjustment; not a standard wage-survey measure, and the paper notes it differs from other studies.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Polynomial order of the time-varying share parameters is chosen separately for each country-sector to fit the relative factor prices, so the model fit (Figs 4-7) is largely by construction and the split between observed-factor and unobserved-technology effects depends on this choice; decomposition depends on parametric nested-CES form and Shapley ordering.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.12 Sec 5.1.1 'We choose the orders of polynomials ... to fit the trends'; p.21 fn 9

selective_reporting.why: Few robustness specifications shown; no sensitivity of decompositions to alternative trend orders or instruments; footnote claims Czech/Slovenia exclusion leaves results unchanged without a table. Mixed fit across countries is reported honestly (Sec 6.2.2).

venue_quality_concern: possible (arXiv preprint v5 as supplied; peer-review status of this version cannot be confirmed from the text, although the acknowledgements thank anonymous referees)
notes: Structural estimation, so the headline is the pair of substitution parameters and a decomposition, not a reduced-form effect of ICT on wages. Outcome is relative wages (skill premium), so the sign 'positive' means ICT raises inequality. Sample is exclusively high income. No instruction-like text found in the paper. Possible duplicate/published version elsewhere; check against other records.

title: Does ICT Investment Matter for Growth and Labor Productivity in Transition Economies?
decision_rationale: Growth-accounting study of ICT capital contribution to output and labour productivity (own estimation, family 1 outcome) but covers only eight post-socialist economies, below the 10-economy minimum for non-AI technology, and does not compare income groups.

exposure_measure: ICT investment built from WITSA/IDC spending data, adjusted by assumed investment shares, deflated with harmonised US hedonic price ratios, converted to capital stock by perpetual inventory (geometric depreciation 0.295 hardware, 0.115 telecom, 0.315 software).

sample.economies_or_groups: Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia (transition economies)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (no income-group comparison; only a correlation of ICT contribution with GDP per capita PPP across the 8 countries)

design.estimator: Extended growth accounting (not regression)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: not applicable

n_specifications_reported: not applicable

exposure_measurement.why: excluded

selection_of_countries_years.why: excluded

outcome_measurement.why: excluded

title: The role of governance in the effect of the internet on financial inclusion in sub-Saharan Africa
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (system GMM) of internet use and a financial inclusion index in 42 sub-Saharan African economies, so it meets the 10-economy rule for non-AI technology. Outcome falls in family 5 (financial inclusion).
exposure_measure: Individuals using the internet (% of population), World Development Indicators.

sample.economies_or_groups: 42 sub-Saharan African countries (list not given in the text)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (SSA only; no income-group split)
sample.years: 2004-2019 in Section 3.3; abstract and conclusion say 2004-2020

design.estimator: System GMM (Blundell-Bond) dynamic panel with lagged dependent variable and internet x governance interactions; one-step or two-step not stated
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged financial inclusion index, log GDP per capita, education index, trade openness, gross capital formation, governance indicator; no explicit country/time fixed effects reported; internal (lagged) instruments, 19-20 instruments, 42 groups

results.indicator: Direct (unconditional) effect of internet users (% pop) on supply-side financial inclusion index (IFI: bank branches and ATMs per km2 and per 100,000 adults)
results.estimate: -0.0003 to -0.0005 per percentage point of internet users in Table 1 (five of six columns; RQ column 4.17e-06, not significant); -0.001 in Table 2 for economic, institutional and general governance columns
results.uncertainty: p<0.01 for -0.0003 (political stability, voice) and -0.0005 (corruption control); p=0.021 (govt effectiveness); p=0.007 (rule of law); p=0.979 (regulatory quality); p=0.860 (political governance composite)
results.evidence: Table 1 'Internet (INTERNET)' row; Table 2 same row; Section 4.1: 'the internet negatively and significantly affect on financial inclusion at the 1% level'

results.indicator: Interaction of internet with governance on financial inclusion index (conditional effect)
results.estimate: Table 1: INTERNET x VA 0.001, x RQ 0.001, x GE 0.001, x RL 0.0008 (significant); x PS -0.0001 and x CC -0.0004 (not significant). Table 2: x EG 0.0004, x IG 0.001, x GG 0.001 (significant); x PG -0.0001 (not significant)
results.evidence: Table 1 and Table 2 interaction rows

results.indicator: Net effect of internet on financial inclusion at mean governance
results.estimate: -0.0009 (voice and accountability), -0.001 (government effectiveness), -0.0008 (rule of law); composite indicators reported only as 'nsa'
results.uncertainty: not reported (computed from point estimates, no standard error)
results.evidence: Table 1 'Internet net effects' row; Section 4.1: '–0.0009 ([-0.0003]+ [0.001× –0.648])'

heterogeneity.finding: Internet effect on the supply-side financial inclusion index rises with governance quality: the internet x governance interaction is positive and significant for voice and accountability, regulatory quality, government effectiveness, rule of law, and for economic, institutional and general governance, but not for political stability, corruption control or the political governance composite.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 0.300 (voice and accountability), 0.300 (government effectiveness), 0.250 (rule of law); 2.500 (economic governance), 1.000 (institutional governance), 1.000 (general governance)
heterogeneity.evidence: Abstract and Table 1/Table 2 'Gov. thresholds' rows; Eq. (6) threshold = |alpha2/alpha4|

income_group_results.high: not applicable (sample is sub-Saharan Africa only)

n_specifications_reported: 10 (six governance indicators in Table 1, four composites in Table 2)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('the internet can be effectively complemented...') rests only on system GMM with internal lagged instruments; no external instrument and the paper does not say which regressors are treated as endogenous. The lagged dependent variable coefficient is 0.93-0.997, close to a unit root, which weakens lagged-level instruments. Sargan p-values of 0.96-1.000 are a sign of an overfitted instrument set. Governance and internet use are both likely to respond to financial development.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2; Table 1 'Financial inclusion (IFI) (-1)' row and Sargan/Hansen rows

exposure_measurement.why: Share of individuals using the internet is a standard WDI measure, but the argument is about internet quality and cost, which it does not capture. Mobile internet and fixed broadband are not separated.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.3: 'individual using the internet (% of population)'; Introduction on cost and quality

selection_of_countries_years.why: 42 SSA countries, 2004-2019, unbalanced (426-435 observations against about 672 possible). Country list is not given, and the text states both 2004-2019 and 2004-2020. No income-group breakdown.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.3; Table 1 'Observations' row; Abstract vs Section 3.3

outcome_measurement.why: The index uses only four supply-side access indicators (branches and ATMs per km2 and per 100,000 adults), min-max normalised within the sample. It omits account ownership, digital payments and mobile money, which are the channels through which the internet would act. A negative internet coefficient may reflect substitution away from branches and ATMs. The text also refers to 'eight dimensions' but lists four.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1, Eqs. (1)-(3); text 'we measure financial inclusion using eight dimensions such as: (i)...(iv)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Six governance indicators and four composites are interacted separately, with thresholds computed from ratios of rounded coefficients (0.0003/0.001). A threshold of 2.5 sits at the edge of the WGI range. No sensitivity checks beyond the composite re-grouping.

selective_reporting.why: The abstract reports thresholds only for the significant interactions and states the internet 'can be effectively complemented'. It does not say that the direct internet effect is negative in nearly every column and that net effects at mean governance are negative (-0.0008 to -0.001). Thresholds above the sample mean governance (-0.65 to -0.75) imply most observations are below them.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; Table 1 'Internet net effects' and 'Gov. thresholds' rows; Table 1 note on means

venue_quality_concern: possible (AGDI working paper WP/23/004, not peer reviewed in this form; assignment lists year 2022 while the working paper is dated January 2023)
notes: Several internal inconsistencies: years 2004-2019 vs 2004-2020; 'eight dimensions' vs four; the narrative says 'an increase in internet users by one person decreases financial inclusion' while the variable is % of population; the second-step or one-step choice, collapse of instruments and the instrument list are not stated; the text states Fisher statistics but no country list. Table 1 'Internet net effects' and thresholds are shown only for voice and accountability, government effectiveness and rule of law. No instruction-like text found.
